An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, when combining this result with that of a different decay channel, $B^0_s\rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$, at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV, resulting in a 7 TeV and 8 TeV combined lifetime of 1.408 ± 0.035 picoseconds, a significant improvement was achieved compared to the 2012 prediction of 1.437 ± 0.069 picoseconds. Additionally, when considering all available data at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies and accounting for variations in production rates, the measured lifetime was found to be 1.437 ± 0.025 picoseconds. This outcome leads to a 0.3 sigma deviation from the Standard Model prediction made by various numerical packages such as HMFX, YENI, and others that utilize next-to-leading order quantum chromodynamics calculations to estimate the influence of possible $B^0_s$ decay system anomalies on this measure. It is also reported that none of the constraints provided by this result significantly impede the operating parameter space of several theories beyond the Standard Model, specifically those involving $c$ charmed quark scenarios, such as $T$ and $V_c$ scenarios, as determined by various numerical packages such as HMFX, YENI, and others that utilize next-to-leading order quantum chromodynamics calculations to estimate the influence of possible $B^0_s$ decay system anomalies on this measure. It is also noted that this outcome results in a modified $B^0_s$ decay rate to a photon pair to be less than 7.2 × 10^{-4} at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies. Moreover, an upper limit has been set on the branching ratio of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay into double pions at a 90% confidence

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. The paper's initial section reviews the stochastic control problem and discusses its numerical representation, including the application of the finite element method for spatial discretization and a different approach using rough path theory. The paper then explores (1) the convergence properties of the numerical solution with respect to time and rough path parameters, (2) an alternative solution using the Monte-Carlo method and dynamic mesh technique, and (3) presents results for two real-world applications. The numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods. The paper's conclusions highlight the value of the rough path theory in modeling stochastic control problems and suggests future directions for related research. The implemented methods are made publicly available as part of a numerical tool developed in the FEniCS project. The tool addresses optimal control problems involving stochastic partial differential equations and can be used with multiple spatial and temporal integration libraries. The source code is shared under the MIT license and is easily accessible via the Larch solver manager for the FEniCS Suite. The paper's results and the accompanying code serve as a starting point for further exploration and enhancement of numerical methods related to stochastic control problems. The research paper's findings are further discussed in the author's Ph.D. thesis written in German. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we narrowed our data set to extremely energetic observations above 8 EeV and discovered that this anisotropy signal becomes even more pronounced, exhibiting an 8.1 sigma significance level. Moreover, we identified quadrupolar and higher-order anisotropy patterns in our data, characterized by an octupolar component with a 3.2 sigma significance level and showing alignment with the Galactic plane, as well as a periodic variation linked to the Earth's movement around the Galactic center, exhibiting a 2.8 sigma significance level and affecting quadrupolar and higher-order anisotropy patterns. To minimize potential biases, we employed an independent approach using only newly detected cosmic rays from 2010 to 2015, and our findings remained consistent. Our study suggests that extremely energetic cosmic rays exhibit complex anisotropy patterns influenced by the Earth's location within the Galactic plane and near the Galactic center. Consequently, we propose that particle accelerators positioned at the Earth's location, such as active galactic nuclei, can modulate cosmic ray anisotropy through their massive particle streams. Moreover, our findings indicate that the birthplace of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays is likely linked to the Galactic center, possibly associated with the presence of dark matter. Finally, our study reveals that the arrival directions of cosmic rays with energies above 16 EeV exhibit a significant pattern of quadrupolar anisotropy, characterized by a 4.0 sigma significance level and showing alignment with the Galactic plane. This finding is consistent with, yet independent of, a recent analysis of such cosmic rays and may have important implications for our understanding of these cosmic events. Our study paves the way for enhanced anisotropy investigations at the most energetic levels and highlights the importance of maintaining data accessibility for final results of such research. Moreover, to verify our findings, we suggest adopting an open-access approach for publishing research based on new cosmic ray detection data sets. This approach will enable the scientific community to conduct independent analyses and verify research results. In addition, we plan to make available detailed descriptions of our analysis methods, encompassing data selection, anisotropy pattern estimation, and significance level computation, along with the primary data used for our study

Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. Additionally, our study has yielded new nonstandard metric formulas for all the spheres $S^n$, projective spaces $RP^n$, and $U(2)$. These metric formulas relate the motion on these manifolds to their isometries. Furthermore, our results indicate that both the Dirac and Harper models can be viewed as motion on flat manifolds with torsion. Lastly, our research shows that the Hall effect corresponds to motion on a flat line with zero torsion. Consequently, our approach offers a novel geometric way to examine quantum mechanics on noncommutative spaces by transforming the issue into an ordinary quantum problem via a change of variables. This allows us to visualize the difficulties as obstacles in momentum space. The accuracy of our general formula for the deformed Hamiltonian is verified by applying it to well-known models such as the Harper model, Harper-Dirac model, Beyer model, Atland-Dotain model, Harper-Dotain model, Harper-Dirac-Dotain model, Atland-Dotain-Dirac model, and Harper-Dotain-Dirac model. The resulting Hamiltonians contain all known limiting cases. The ultimate goal is to use this approach to examine more complex systems such as lattice models in which the interaction between different sites is not negligible. The new metric formulas introduced here may also impact our comprehension of metric properties associated with geometric singularities. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. To further explore the benefits of federated learning, we conducted additional experiments under more realistic data scenarios and observed comparable performance. A particularly notable outcome involved a scenario where a single dataset contained significant anomalies, such as cells with incorrect labels or image corruption, which can represent a common challenge in real-world image classification scenarios. In this scenario, we discovered that federated learning not only prevented the model from learning from the anomalies but also enabled the production of accurate models at a faster rate. This achievement was attributed to the incorporation of a technique that limits the model's training on unreliable data. Overall, our study demonstrates the potential of federated learning to facilitate rapid development of high-performance image analysis models in histopathology. Additionally, we have made the code and datasets used in this study publicly available for further research purposes.

In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. Experimental evidence confirming the efficacy of this approach was obtained through a 14.9km terrestrial cable test, demonstrating a maximum 2.9dB NLBER performance improvement when using WDFE-MLSE over conventional DFE. To further highlight the benefits of this method, simulations were conducted in a 50km underwater cable scenario, featuring a dual-mode transmission system using WDFE-MLSE for the higher data rate signal, thereby enabling successful reception of both signals in a 36GHz bandwidth even in the presence of burst errors. This groundbreaking research paves the way for the efficient transmission of high-speed data signals in underwater cables through optimal use of WDFE-MLSE. To facilitate practical implementation, computer-generated algorithms for optimizing WDFE parameters in various underwater cable scenarios are also provided, along with suggestions for further research strategies. Ultimately, this study offers an innovative solution to the long-standing challenge of chromatic dispersion in submarine cables and presents potentially applicable technologies to mitigate the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in other fiber-optic communications systems. To facilitate future research, the measured data from this experiment has been made available online. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our results show that TCNs can reach state-of-the-art performance on time-series classification tasks, outperforming recurrent networks and other competing methods. Moreover, our method enables the creation of smaller models that excel in data-limited settings. Furthermore, our technique can be integrated into a resource-aware training framework, allowing for the simultaneous optimization of model size and performance. Our method is versatile and applicable to various TCN architectures, prompting us to release an open-source framework called Time2Net that offers customizable TCN models and related training frameworks. This framework is now publicly accessible on GitHub. Our technique has far-reaching implications as it could serve as a cornerstone for developing other efficient deep learning models using pruning-based dilation optimization. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. Additionally, our analysis provides a method to transition from Zinbiel algebras to their associated Malcev algebras, allowing us to leverage this information to achieve greater understanding of the properties of Zinbiel algebras. Specifically, our research demonstrates that the dimension of a finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra is at most 2^n, where n represents the dimension of its associated Malcev algebra. Consequently, no new finite-dimensional solvable Zinbiel algebras can exist over fields like Q, R, or C, as their dimension would need to be less than two degrees lower than that of their Malcev algebras, a condition that cannot be met. Furthermore, our research enables the classification of infinite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras based on their characteristics. Alongside, we outline the grounds for believing that certain of these infinite-dimensional algebras are nilpotent. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and their associated logics. These tools, particularly tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse application of ALBA's rules is then demonstrated to be computationally equivalent to running the actual algebraic model finding algorithm for the logic in question, leading to a fundamental insight where the computational cost of determining whether a given structure is an model of a given logic is equivalent to the cost of determining whether a given first-order sentence is equivalent to a given formula of the logic. This fundamental insight is further distilled into a theorem known as the 'equivariance' theorem, providing a theoretical framework that equates the computational cost of determining first-order validity within a given model to determining the validity within the same model of a given formula's equivalence to its corresponding first-order sentence. This framework further enables the development of new algorithms tailored to determine first-order validity within a given model by leveraging existing algorithms for determining equivalence within the same model for a given formula and its corresponding first-order sentence, itself determined by ALBA for inductive formulas and amenable to extension across multiple semantic frameworks. As such, these newly developed algorithms rely entirely on existing tools from the correspondence theory. As a concrete illustration, we present a new algorithm for determining first-order validity within models of the logic of provability, itself derived by reverse application of ALBA to its existing model finding algorithm. This novel algorithm for determining first-order validity within the logic of provability leverages ALBA's rules and algebraic language to offer a fundamentally more transparent and maintainable alternative to the current state-of-the-art, itself based on the algorithm set out in the book 'Modal Logic for Computer Scientists' by the same authors. Additionally, we propose a new methodology for a sub-system of the logic of provability, itself amenable to extension across multiple semantic frameworks, based on the unified correspondence theory and set out a new theorem known as the 'equivariance' theorem for a sub-system of the logic of provability, providing a computational framework that equates the computational cost of determining first-order validity within a given model

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, unknown, or contradictory. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for calculating data quality, (c) techniques for handling data integration in presence of inconsistencies, (d) approaches for evaluating our framework through benchmark tests, and (e) proposing an effective plan for addressing the central problem of this research. Moreover, we outline potential extensions of this research, along with an effective strategy for handling certain forms of dependencies. Lastly, we provide an open-source implementation of our data management approach, along with the testbed and example use cases, all available at https://github.com/jayantpoddar/inconsistencies- handling for further collaboration and feedback. This research is an initial step towards creating data management solutions that can effectively handle inconsistencies in data tables and, hence, is highly relevant for various pressing problems concerning data quality, query validation, data merging, as well as data quality assessment. category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas. Specifically, the review will cover progress on silicon microstrip sensor development, where the goal is to achieve below 100 e- reverse bias current for power consumption reduction, and participation in global efforts to standardize calorimeter readout objectives and develop joint R&D projects. Additionally, the review will explore potential collaborations with global research initiatives and outline strategies for securing necessary funding from various sources. Lastly, the review will outline a proposed plan for the R&D schedule, participation strategy, and funding allocation to ensure optimal utilization of available resources and effective integration with global efforts. This review is intended to serve as a starting point for ongoing discussion and development within the SiD collaboration on detector research and development. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. Building on this insight, I plan to investigate the co-authorship network within the archive's community, as well as develop methods for visualizing the dependency graph and assessing the centrality of content within the archive. Ultimately, my research aims to provide actionable recommendations for improving the archive's organization and structure. To achieve this, I will apply my analysis results to a set of carefully selected case studies, drawn from various areas within the archive, and identify potential solutions to enhance content accessibility and understanding. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code and models are available online at https://github.com/zyang0126/Refine-RPN.

Researchers utilized acoustic lenses composed of PMMA to increase the detection area of sensitive devices and improve resolution but discovered these lenses introduced image distortion. This problem was investigated and a new lens material called Stycast 1090SI was proposed as an alternative. The acoustic properties of this novel material were examined alongside PMMA to determine its feasibility. Computational simulations and practical tests using two different materials, PMMA and Stycast 1090SI, showed both materials significantly enhance the detection capabilities of sensitive devices. Notably, the Stycast lens exhibited lower levels of distortion compared to the PMMA lens, which could have implications for photoacoustic tomography technology. Further analysis indicated that both materials have comparable acoustic properties, yet the structure and anisotropic properties of PMMA may contribute to the observed distortion. In contrast, the uniform composition of the Stycast lens may reduce stress on sensitive devices and minimize the impact of anomalies, resulting in clearer images. Ultimately, the success of these lenses highlights the potential for innovative materials to enhance the performance of photoacoustic tomography systems. This could enable the construction of larger-scale devices without compromise on resolution and sensitivity, ultimately facilitating a broader range of applications. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. Unlike current hybrid algorithms that may become trapped in local minima, our proposed Trilbert algorithm uses a more efficient search for solutions and can handle larger networks. Through simulations and real-world applications, our approach demonstrates significant improvements in computational efficiency and accuracy. Specifically, our method outperforms state-of-the-art multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks in multiple scenarios and provides a more concise solution set. Trilbert is particularly effective in identifying key nodes in networks with distinct separate components and is particularly applicable to detecting influential spreaders in multi-layered propagation networks. Moreover, our approach is adaptable to various network types, including directed and undirected networks, as demonstrated by the analysis of emerging trends in co-authorship networks. Our method is available as an open-source tool for calculating multi-layer eigenvector centrality. Through our research, we contribute to the advancement of state-of-the-art multi-layer network analysis and are releasing our new method as an open-source framework for the analytical community. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. These stages have been captured in detail through high-speed imaging, and the associated time durations and cavity properties documented, offering valuable insights into the water-entry phenomenon and its underlying physics. Moreover, the analysis of the partial-seal and surface-seal regimes suggests that the amount of water trapped is governed by an as-yet-unconfirmed law of conservation, implying that the total cavity volume at pinch-off represents a minimum water volume for a particular impact velocity, and any further increase in water volume would result from more efficient surface-seal mechanisms. In essence, the surface-seal regime can be optimized for reduced water-trap volumes during sphere impacts. The findings of this research provide a foundation for further exploration into enhancing the efficiency of surface-seal regime through active control methods. The discovered laws and the detailed analysis of the partial-seal and surface-seal regimes can also be applied to other water-entry shapes, contributing to a deeper understanding of the complex water-entry phenomenon. The research is complemented by a new term, "surface-seal velocity", which distinguishes the two major water-entry regimes and highlights the distinct characteristics of the splash dome closure process. The study concludes by highlighting the need for numerical modeling and simulations that can accurately capture the water-entry processes, especially in the surface-seal regime, by resolving the fine details of the pinch-off process and incorporating the observed laws of partial-seal and surface-seal regimes. Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds. 

Finally, we outline possibilities for scaling our concept to other security-sensitive platforms.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results demonstrated that a modest increase in training time allows the FPG algorithm to obtain an optimal policy with a small factor of $0.14\times\epsilon$ for $20\%$ corruption rates. Our work lays the groundwork for further research aimed at enhancing the robustness of reinforcement learning without relying on explicit security assumptions. We have made our code publicly available.

This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. Our approach utilized collocation and Runge-Kutta schemes, demonstrating that both can yield similar results with fewer computation demands, though collocation meets the system's physical constraints more accurately. Our findings show that both methods allow for adequate tidal volume control for both patients, meeting clinical standards, and indicating that both methods have potential for further exploration in this specific medical ventilation problem. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time well logging during drilling. Ultimately, this method can effectively support the geosteering process by providing accurate and timely formation evaluations, thus facilitating data-driven decision making. Additionally, the large dataset outputs from this method can further enhance machine learning models aimed at capturing complex trends and patterns necessary for interpreting wells across different locations. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Additionally, model evaluations and case studies illustrate the benefits of combining flat and nested NER and provide insights into model performance and predictions. All code and data used in this study are available online at the specified repository.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in processing code-mixed language data. We delve into prominent NLP tasks, examining current limitations and shortcomings, as well as potential breakthroughs, using examples from code-mixed language datasets. Additionally, we outline challenges and potential solutions for processing code-mixed language data, including advancements in model architecture and supervised learning approaches. Furthermore, we highlight promising areas for future research, such as semantic-based decoding, loss functions, evaluation metrics, and the lack of standardization in code-mixed language datasets. We also touch on transfer learning from single to multiple languages and vice versa. We conclude by outlining promising areas for future research and potential applications of code-mixed language models in real-world multilingual communication scenarios. These communication scenarios involve government institutions, customer service representatives, the legal profession, and healthcare providers who communicate with citizens/patients who have different linguistic backgrounds. Therefore, code-mixed language models have practical value in enhancing the effectiveness of these communications. We hope this survey will spark further research and advancements in code-mixed language processing, enabling more seamless and efficient communication across linguistic boundaries. We have made all the code and data used in this research publicly available at https://github.com/adithyan457/code-mixedsurvey. We have also released a new code-mixed language processing repository containing relevant datasets, models, and experimental results at https://github.com/adithyan457/code-mixed-language-processing. We look forward to contributing to the growth of the code-mixed language processing community along with other researchers. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. This research has successfully identified the Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure associated with experimental energy loss features and offers a theoretical framework that can be applied to other materials with complex crystalline forms. Additionally, it highlights the value of time-dependent theoretical models in analyzing experimental energy loss spectra and pinpoints the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure as the most likely representation of the material's actual structure. This finding is supported by calculated energy loss spectra, both with and without local field effects, closely mimicking experimental reflection loss spectra and further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure. In conclusion, this study has successfully determined the Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure associated with experimental energy loss features and provides a theoretical framework for analyzing other materials with complex crystalline forms. Moreover, it highlights the effectiveness of time-dependent theoretical models in interpreting experimental energy loss spectra. Based on these results, the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure is confirmed as the most likely representation of the material's actual structure, and its associated features have been correctly identified. Additionally, the study demonstrates the importance of considering local field effects when calculating energy loss spectra, as neglecting them would not accurately match the experimental results

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, only areas exhibiting increased population independence and cultural norm-free living experienced increased dissemination of misinformation. We also explored additional factors and found that misinformation dissemination slowed down user engagement, with no evidence that demand for misinformation influenced its dissemination. Our study highlights the significance of locality in online misinformation dissemination and suggests targeted strategies for combatting its spread. We propose adjusting Reddit's algorithms to prioritize high-quality news content with low circulation volumes in each state and implementing campaigns to foster critical thinking about news consumption in areas where conscientiousness is low. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert-based detection methods by minimizing the time and effort required for review, reducing the risk of human error, and enabling the scaling of large data processing pipelines.

We showcase the performance of HALFADO in two pivotal applications: (1) detecting derogatory language in social media comments and (2) identifying suspicious financial transactions. Experimental results show that our algorithm achieves comparable accuracy to fully supervised machine learning models, achieved this through the use of a small, representative sample size of 1% or less of total data. HALFADO detects anomalies in real-time, defined as a data stream frequency of one observation every 100ms, demonstrating the algorithm's potential for large-scale, real-world implementations. The code is openly accessible, enabling researchers to build upon our work and further develop semi-supervised streaming algorithms.

The proposed method also enables assessment of detection confidence in relation to various gravitational field configurations, offering a more nuanced understanding of the issue than traditional approaches.  In addition, it's demonstrated that a hypothetical  Planet X with the mass of a dwarf planet like Haumea and located at 42 AU could be detected with some degree of certainty, but its shape would likely obscure its detection.  The proposed method may be applied to various detection scenarios involving extended objects.  The method is robust in that it doesn't rely on a specific theoretical model of the gravitational field, but rather focuses on the measurable effects caused by an object of unknown size and shape. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. The code and data will be made available at https://github.com/ghrua/Cross-Memory.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The auxiliary findings provide valuable insights into user preference underlying the real-world datasets, revealing distinct aspect preferences in each domain and significant complementarity between domains. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/hongzheng1993/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. Hypatia's capabilities are showcased through its superior performance in solving a diverse set of test problems across different domains. Furthermore, it highlights strategies for formulating problems that take full advantage of its features, including the implementation of custom exotic cones. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. This study's outcomes can serve as a foundation for future advancements in automated quality control measures and provide valuable insights into the development and application of MRIQC pipelines in multi-center research projects. Additionally, the categorization probabilities derived from this study can be utilized to enhance quality control measures and facilitate more reliable data analysis. To facilitate replication and further exploration, the code and datasets utilized in this study are available for access at https://github.com/braincog/kaggle-mriqc. Nonetheless, despite the progress made, the efficacy of automated quality control measures is heavily dependent on the specific dataset in question, as illustrated by publicly assessable quality control measures, where diverse models produced inconclusive results on a hidden dataset of 300 participants as presented in the extended version of this study. Consequently, replicating research studies utilizing MRI data remains an intricate task until more reliable, automated quality control measures are developed and widely adopted. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Building upon this finding, we hypothesize that this attractor represents a fundamental underlying structure governing the dynamics of the system, and that it is accessible through a set of parameters that includes the interval desired for our original one-dimensional analysis. Furthermore, we anticipate that the existence of this attractor can provide a theoretical basis for understanding cooperative behavior in complex systems. In addition, we outline potential applications and suggest conducting additional research into adapting this framework for modeling interactions in more realistic scenarios. As an integral part of this investigation, we present a novel method for creating a multivariate vector from a given set of autonomous agents, and utilize this approach to create a simplified model that can be solved numerically. Through this exploration, we aim to contribute to a deeper comprehension of the Motivation Dynamics framework and its capabilities when modeling cooperative behavior in multi-agent systems. As a result, we are able to create a sophisticated model featuring a multivariate vector and achieving stable cooperative behavior, and have identified key features of this model that can be applied to complex systems involving multiple autonomous entities. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Moreover, our results show that all compounds possess an indirect bandgap and Cm-doped GdSn3 materials exhibit significant reductions in bandgaps, turning them into semiconductors. In addition, we analyze the lattice constants and magnetic d-band center positions as a function of Cm content and find them to be in line with trends seen in other AxBxC compounds. Lastly, our data on bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials provide a theoretical foundation for further research into their surface state modifications and potential applications in spintronic technology.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. The bilepton model predicts the rates at which neutrinos interact with each other and other particles, the decay widths of mesons, and the possibility of dark matter composition made of ${\cal S}$-quarks, in addition to conventional predictions about particle interactions that have been confirmed by experiments so far. The paper also presents various production and decay scenarios for the novel particles, offering design guidelines for experiments that could verify or refute the bilepton model at existing and future particle accelerators. Specifically, it suggests looking for ${\cal D}$-quarks at the LHC with upgraded detectors or finding ${\cal S}$-quarks at future colliders like CLIC, LEPC, or SPPC. The bilepton model predicts that discovering ${\cal T}$-quarks might be challenging even with 100 TeV colliders due to ${\cal T}$-quark decay into top quarks and bosons, which would make it difficult to distinguish from standard model processes. The paper also presents strategies for distinguishing ${\cal S}$-quark production from standard model backgrounds in experiments, which involves analyzing the properties of quark bonding to each other or light quarks, such as dark matter composition made of ${\cal S}$-quarks, lepton number violating processes, and the decay widths of mesons. The predictions made by the bilepton model could be verified or refuted with experiments that are currently being carried out or are on the drawing board at particle accelerators, which will significantly contribute to our understanding of the fundamental symmetry group governing particle interactions in the standard model. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Our findings also give insight into the complex interrelationship between the ordered generating sequences, descent set, and Coxeter length for the finite classical Coxeter group Bn. This reveals intriguing patterns that could give perspective on the general Coxeter group dynamics. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the standard ordered generating sequences can be used to represent group elements in Bn, which gives a unique understanding of these groups. We explore the notion of standard ordered generating sequences in relation to the standard Coxeter presentation, its connection to the standard reflection representation, the standard length formula, the standard descent set, and the standard definition of left multiplication. Lastly, we establish a standard ordered generating sequences-based algorithm to compute Coxeter length in Bn. This paper's purpose is to introduce the standard ordered generating sequences concept in a general context, giving a thorough explanation of its features and implications within the finite classical Coxeter group Bn. Consequently, many of our discussion points could be distillated into axiomatic properties governing the standard ordered generating sequences, revealing their fundamental nature that applies universally across all non-abelian groups, without necessitating the specific context of Bn. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Still, its utility will depend on the actual distribution of galactic haloes and how they relate to mass density conditions prevalent in the universe today. As such, this new approach needs to be reevaluated in the context of upcoming supernova surveys, such as the Dark Energy Survey and future missions like LSST, Euclid, and WFIRST. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we compared two different measurement setups to determine single-shot readout fidelities of approximately 90% for both methods. Our study provides a foundation for advancing research on T-type damage centers within the SOI platform. As such, we propose the integration of T-type damage centers with horizontal cavity silicon photonic devices, involving a comprehensive analysis of the relevant physics and challenges. Alongside this proposal, we outline potential paths to overcome technical difficulties and address key research questions. Ultimately, we are confident in the T-type damage center's ability to provide a robust photon-spin interface for efficient quantum communication networks. As such, we believe that further investigation into this defect center's properties and the development of its integrated quantum photonics applications are well warranted. As such, we propose the T-type damage center to serve as a reliable foundation for the development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks. MRI technology utilizes radio waves to scan the human body and obtain precise, pain-free diagnostic images. These images enable radiologists to visually assess anatomy and physiological processes within the body, ultimately facilitating early disease diagnosis and treatment. Advanced imaging capabilities, combined with sophisticated processing techniques, enable detection of hard-to-spot tumors. This assignment delves into Automated Tumor Detection by comparing conventional image processing methods, such as morphological analysis and regional growth algorithms, in order to explore their application and effectiveness. A sample automatic detection process is illustrated using a common tumor type, and possible directions for future investigation are also considered. Given the diverse types of tumors, a customized detection approach would be necessary. Consequently, further research is needed to develop personalized automated detection methods for different types of tumors and to address challenges posed by complex MRI images. Additionally, potential uses for automatic detection in regular monitoring scans and real-time MRI need to be examined. Ultimately, a reliable automated tumor detection system would revolutionize the medical industry by making accurate diagnoses more accessible and reducing the risk of human error.

In this research, we explore the properties of a novel algebraic variant of the degenerate Bernoulli polynomial $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$, as well as its corresponding degenerate Bernoulli number. This investigation is grounded in an innovative algebraic framework for generating functions and symbolic evaluation functions, allowing us to derive $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$. Our findings demonstrate intriguing connections with circulant matrices and Galois fields, while showcasing the potential for $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ to be applied in computationally efficient contexts. Specifically, we showcase its efficacy in designing an efficient algorithm for computing Jacobi symbols and quadratic residues within a finite field $GF(q)$, leveraging the benefits of vectorized operations and numpy. This computational approach is not only highly efficient, with execution times measured in nanoseconds, but it also offers significant performance enhancements when compared to established libraries such as mpmath and numpy for large values of input parameters. Furthermore, our innovative use of $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ paves the way for innovative applications in computational finance and physics. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant improvement of up to 5 times in the RV RMS after correcting for binary line shifts, indicating a more effective strategy for minimizing the impact of activity on RV data sets and potentially enhancing the detection of exoplanets. This research paves the way for a more active approach to selecting line lists, allowing for a better detection of exoplanets in low-mass stars.

For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene information in various ways, categorized into
support, relation, and background categories. To effectively utilize background
information in object detection, we introduce a novel approach called Background
Aware Contrastive Object Detector. This model incorporates a contrastive loss
function to close the gap between the background samples of a target object and
other target objects in the same image. By doing so, the model learns to extract
distinct features from target objects regardless of background content. Our
contrastive loss function is designed to minimize background-dependent loss,
enabling the model to pay more attention to object-specific attributes. The
experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our model on the Visual
Relationship and Generalized Image Captioning datasets, achieving superior
performance compared to other context-aware object detectors. Additionally, our
model exhibits robust background robustness and showcases the importance of
considering background information through analysis of hard background samples. The
code is available at: https://github.com/cg1177/BCD.

Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic greater than two, and consider the ring of power series $R$ over the Witt vectors of $k$, expanded in variables $t_1, \dots, t_d$. The main aim of this study is to generalize classical Fontaine-Messing theory to a base ring of the form $R$. Notably, we establish theorems enabling the comparison of crystalline and \'etale cohomologies with torsion coefficients for smooth schemes $X$ over $R$. These results hold when $X$ is projective, leading to a vast extension of the classical Fontaine-Messing theory. Additional contributions include an innovation explaining Fontaine-Messing theory in the context of the ring of formal power series over the p-adic numbers, along with a generalization of Fontaine-Messing theory to a base ring with an inert residue characteristic, such as the ring of power series over the p-adic integers with an inert prime. Notably, these generalizations facilitate the construction of Galois representations attached to families of motives over $R$. Finally, we establish a connection between Fontaine-Messing theory and Kato's expose on the subject, along with an extension of his results to the base ring $R$. These general results on Fontaine-Messing theory over $R$ are complemented by specific computations of coherent sheaves and their de Rham cohomologies, enabling the computation of specific Galois representations, including one linked to Arijn's family of motives. Utilizing this approach, we successfully obtained the associated momentum transformation, which preserves the four-dimensional relationship between momentum and space, p_{\mu} x^{\mu}.  With the deformed algebra in hand, we derive the first Casimir invariant in this paper.  Following first quantization, we utilize the Klein-Gordon equation to show that Fock's spacetime corresponds to the de Sitter universe, whose spacetime radius can be defined by the invariant length representing the de Sitter hypersurface.  This result implies that Fock's spacetime is actually the (3+1)D representation of the four-dimensional de Sitter universe.  Furthermore, we derive the second Casimir invariant and demonstrate that the de Sitter universe's four-dimensional representation can be expressed by a novel, quadratic form, which may be useful for the second quantization of the scalar field.  Finally, we discuss the potential advantages of using this novel form to mitigate the problem of ultraviolet divergence in field theory.  This could potentially achieve a physically meaningful, renormalizable mass parameter for the scalar field.  We also explore the possibility of interpreting the universe's four-dimensional representation as a Klein-Gordon equation's hidden symmetry, which could have significant implications for the understanding of the universe's inflationary phase.  This could establish a connection between the universe's inflationary phase and its late-stage expansion, which may be driven by the Kennedy-Jarlskog inequality-based vacuum energy with a physically meaningful, renormalized mass parameter.  This could essentially provide a new perspective on the universe's cosmological evolution, which we briefly outline in the concluding remarks.  Finally, we anticipate that establishing the relationship between the universe's inflationary phase and its late-stage expansion will lead to further breakthroughs in our understanding of the universe's very early stages, its fundamental laws, and the principles governing the cosmos as a whole.  This, in turn, may result in a comprehensive theory of cosmology, which is also the primary goal of this series of papers.  We look forward to presenting the details of this new perspective in future publications. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Building upon his earlier findings, Springer further demonstrated that the number of conjugacy classes is equivalent to the product of the number of such forms and the number of such systems, along with the number of monic irreducible polynomials and the number of systems of integers from the set {0, 1, …, n/2}, where n represents the dimension of the group Sp_n(K). Alongside this theoretical framework, Springer also explored the practical application of these characteristics to develop a systematic approach to identifying conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K). He illustrated this method through specific examples, including the calculation of the number of conjugacy classes in Sp_4(K) and a detailed analysis of the structure of the centralizer of a particular subgroup within the symplectic group Sp_2(K). Throughout his research, Springer adopted the notation previously established by T.A. Shapiro and himself in their joint paper 'On the Conjugacy Classes of the Symplectic Group', first published in 1950. This translated thesis is now available to provide insights to mathematicians working on related projects, such as Naor and Kantorki in their paper 'Conjugacy Classes of the General Linear Group Over a Finite Field'. Those authors determined the number of classes based on system of polynomials, also exploring the extension of this classification to the finite general linear group, specifically focusing on the group GL_n(Q), where Q is a finite field with a characteristic other than two.
