Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

Our investigation combines active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the context of ImageNet. The evaluation reveals that results on modest, commonly used benchmark datasets do not reflect actual performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet due to an uneven class distribution selected by the active learning method. Existing AL algorithms failed to surpass random sampling among our evaluated benchmarks, including small and large-scale scenarios. In order to address the issue of class imbalance, we developed Balanced Selection (BASE), a straightforward yet scalable AL algorithm capable of selecting more evenly balanced data samples for annotation. Consequently, BASE outperforms random sampling consistently. The code for BASE is publicly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. 

On top of BASE, our results show that combining active learning with self-supervised pretraining results in notable gains of around 3-4% in top-1 accuracy when using compact datasets comprised of carefully selected images, and around 1% when utilizing the entire ImageNet dataset. Nonetheless, BASE alone leads to around 3% gain in top-1 accuracy on the entire ImageNet dataset. Notably, BASE outperforms existing AL algorithms consistently across small and large-scale scenarios, including scenarios where the class distribution is highly imbalanced. 

In conclusion, our investigation into combining active learning and self-supervised pretraining yields notable improvements of around 3-4% in top-1 accuracy when using compact datasets and around 1% when utilizing the entire ImageNet dataset. The code for BASE is publicly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. In addition to BASE, our results highlight the effectiveness of combining active learning with self-supervised pretraining in deep neural networks. Furthermore, BASE outperforms existing AL algorithms consistently across small and large-scale scenarios, including scenarios where the class distribution is highly imbalanced. In future research, possible directions for investigation emerge from the success achieved by BASE, as well as the possibilities for improving BASE through more advanced methods.

We suggest creating bosonic pairs using large numbers of dipoles with complex internal structures, which interact with an isolated optical cavity. A rapid growth of entanglement between these dipoles arises due to the virtual exchange of photons, resulting in two-mode squeezing. We can relate this phenomenon to optical homodyne measurements by applying transformations and observing changes in the electronic states. We propose using this connection to improve the detection of phase shifts between light signals. We present an example based on strontium atoms and show that our approach remains resilient to errors commonly found in this type of system. Our plan offers potential breakthroughs in entanglement research with atoms and could contribute to the development of more precise optical clocks. We assess the requirements for achieving strong two-mode squeezing and demonstrate that our proposed system is highly competitive with existing creations of entangled states. We believe our concept opens new avenues for investigating quantum physics in atom-light interactions and may pave the way for the creation of other complex states of matter. We also explore the possibility of linking multiple pairs of bosonic systems through their shared interactions with a single cavity. Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and one-qubit gate accuracy. To advance further, demonstrating the ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations with a strong coupling between qubits, specifically through exchange interaction, is crucial. To facilitate efficient development of large-scale quantum processors, a computational model of two-electron behavior has been created by applying a configuration interaction approach based on a multi-valley effective mass theory. By utilizing the code's efficiency to handle computational demands, exchange interaction effects, valley distribution, and electron distribution were examined in a range of positions, orientations, and under applied electric fields. The findings are displayed in an interactive format that shows donor placement's impact on the behavior of valley and orbital components. The research yields a practical understanding and accurate prediction of necessary conditions to execute reliable two-qubit operations with silicon-based quantum processors. The development of this computational framework paves the way for investigations of the spin, valley, and orbital properties of multiple electron systems in silicon donors and could enable the effective utilization of donor spin qubits in combined electron and optical experiments. The code is readily available for replication and further electron system calculations upon request. The code can be found at https://github.com/AlirezaLi/Two-Valley Two-Phosphorus Donor. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. Notably, this phenomenon is observed only within a narrow range of electron densities. A specific neutral point, where the resistance displays a significant increase associated with a magnetic field, has been identified and its implications explored in the context of topological insulators and majorana modes found in HgTe structures. This research was conducted in collaboration with the Hahn-Meitner-Institut Berlin. Both theoretical and experimental approaches have been used to study the phenomena observed. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Specifically, in scenarios with high traffic variability, dynamic TDD, in contrast to static TDD, can reduce downlink interference by as much as 50%. Moreover, our dynamic approach achieves similar performance to optimized global solutions, despite being computed locally. Bar-Gad Gil is thanked for helpful discussions. This study involved an in-depth examination of the magnetotransport measurements conducted on BSCCO thin films, as presented in Zhao et al.'s 2019 paper, to confirm a previously suggested theory proposing that the Hall anomaly arises from vacancies moving within pinned fragments of the vortex lattice. This proposed mechanism is validated by analyzing the vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the vortex crystal and by comparing the measured activation energies to the calculated creation energy of the vortex-anti-vortex pair and the vacancy energy in the flux-line lattice. No adjustments were required in the calculations, providing a comprehensive theoretical foundation for the Hall anomaly. Furthermore, our analysis provides a framework for reinterpreting previous experimental findings related to the vortex state, including those involving high magnetic fields and cryogenic temperatures. This new perspective also sheds light on the role of point-like defects in determining the vacancy energy and influencing the vortex state. This study's findings offer a theoretical foundation for understanding the vacancy-mediated transport phenomena observed in the vortex state of type-II superconductors. This includes the Hall anomaly, activation energies in the magnetic field, and the peak in the magnetic field-dependent volume pinning force, all of which are controlled by the vacancy energy in the flux-line lattice. This study's findings provide a framework for investigating the interplay between superconductivity, magnetism, and cryogenic physics, with implications for the development of efficient thermal management systems and the improvement of magnetic performance in superconducting materials. This perspective on the vortex state may also inform the design of novel magnetic materials with unique properties resulting from the interplay between vacuum and material structure. This could potentially lead to the discovery of novel magnetic states and the development of more efficient thermal management systems for magnetic materials operating at cryogenic temperatures. This study's findings may also inform the design of experiments aimed at uncovering the intricacies of the vortex state and could potentially be applied to other systems featuring topological defects in a lattice structure. This study's perspective on the vortex state may also raise fundamental questions about the nature of lattice defects, their interactions with the surrounding medium, and the implications for transport phenomena. A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares of C*-algebras, resulting in hyperfinite type II_1 subfactors of finite index and depth, is provided, utilizing Morita equivalent unitary fusion categories. We extend a prior investigation by N. Sato, generalizing his findings to encompass the broader context of such squares. Additionally, we establish a characterization for such squares yielding a given type II_1 subfactor, and this analysis contributes to a broader understanding of 4-tensors related to matrix product operators in 2-dimensional topological systems. These insights can be applied to identify necessary conditions for certain 2-dimensional systems to exhibit certain properties, such as the emergence of topological phases in cluster update dynamics. We illustrate this concept through the specific example of a kagome lattice system, obtaining conditions for its ground state to display topological order, before discussing implications and potential future directions. Moreover, we introduce the term "commuting picture" to distinguish this characterization, which holds for finite-dimensional systems, from its infinite-dimensional system counterparts. Lastly, we provide a summary of our findings in the context of matrix product operator algebras.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. The key contribution of this work can be represented through optimization problems defined by ordinary differential equations, and we highlight the advantages of our approach while identifying potential challenges to be addressed in future research. Alongside presenting our main findings, we also examine key aspects of this new framework, including how to incorporate parameters and learn update rules. The code for the Hamiltonian Neural Network optimizer and additional related models is available for download at this link.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing overfits and giving weight to diverse data samples; a refinement agent that uses a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and correct errors. These modifications lead to improved performance on both safety and accuracy. Experiments using the GLUE-Safe and SST datasets demonstrate the benefits of this approach, showing that even modest human guidance can significantly enhance both the trustworthiness and accuracy of machine learning models. Furthermore, the system's scalability is showcased through applications involving large datasets, such as the Stanford Natural Language Inferences Dataset, which contains over 20,000 samples. In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. Furthermore, a practical implementation of our method, along with the dataset, is openly available for further research and development. The code can be found at https://github.com/alibaba institute/alibaba-matroid-rod. The dataset is hosted at https://alibaba-institute.github.io/HiXray/index.html.

In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems. The results showed that our approach successfully detected critical control point combinations leading to vehicle deviations, and provided valuable insights into the complex interactions between road design features and the equipped vehicle's performance. Consequently, this research paves the way for conducting comprehensive, efficient, and targeted searches to find optimal road configurations that evaluate the capabilities and limitations of autonomous vehicles. Furthermore, this work establishes a theoretical foundation for multiple search configurations, enabling the development of more advanced optimization strategies. Additionally, our publicly available toolkit enables other researchers to build upon this research and contribute to the development of more advanced testing methodologies. The potential applications of this research extend beyond lane-keeping testing, potentially benefiting other autonomous vehicle subsystems, and may also be adapted for use in physical testing scenarios with appropriately modified methods. To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. Our model first extracts acoustic features from the playlist, then uses these features to generate a descriptive caption. We test our music captioning approach on a dataset consisting of 5,000 tracks spanning 10 genres and evaluate its efficacy by comparing the generated captions to actual album descriptions and assessing their coherence and relevance. The results show that our approach not only outperforms a baseline captioning model but also demonstrates a level of coherence and relevance comparable to human-written descriptions, especially across music genre boundaries. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of audio content on captioning outcomes and find significant differences in style and structure across various genres, along with implicit cues that guide the captioning model's decisions. Our code and data are publicly accessible, marking a significant starting point for the exploration of music captioning and potential applications in information retrieval and music information extraction. Additionally, this work lays the groundwork for comprehensive music captioning, which can summarize an entire playlist, and calls for the creation of larger, more diverse datasets capable of capturing complex audio content and underlying semantic structures. As a result, we release our dataset consisting of 5,000 tracks with acoustic features and corresponding captions, along with code implementing the music captioning approach, to foster research and advancements in this area. As a secondary contribution, we introduce a new dataset called Music21, which comprises 500 piano tracks with annotated rhythmic and tonal features, along with corresponding automatic captions, to facilitate the development of more precise music captioning models capable of capturing complex audio structures in individual tracks. This new dataset is available for public use and may be expanded upon in future research. Our approach to music captioning, aided by audio content analysis and neural captioning models, yields results showing a level of coherence and relevance comparable to human-written descriptions, especially across music genre boundaries. However, our investigation into the influence of audio content on captioning outcomes and style and structure across various genres reveals a lack of explicit cues guiding the captioning model's decisions. Consequently, our approach may benefit from additional components integrating audio features with language models, as well as direction from music experts on implicit rules governing music language and structure. Ultimately, our code and data, along with the newly introduced Music21 dataset, are made publicly accessible to facilitate research

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN. Visualize our method's performance on ActivityNet v1.3 at https://activity-net.com/challenge/2020?eval=video.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. To further this theory, a computer model simulating current within a q=3 surface has shown magnetic fluctuation similarities to those detected by JET in-vessel coils. This implies that the manifestation of a PTM is closely linked to capturing 'holes' on such a surface post-ELM, producing corresponding signatures in magnetic field readings. Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of IRS-provided virtual links in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. Furthermore, our research indicates that when the LOS link strength is higher than $~10^{-1}$, the performance gains from IRS are minimal. We also explore various IRS reflective surface configurations to identify the optimal arrangement that yields the highest gain in target parameter estimation. Our findings also reveal that when the LOS link strength is an order of magnitude more robust than the NLOS link, an optimized IRS design can deliver performance gains of up to $10^{8}$ times improvement in target parameter estimation. Additionally, our research shows that IRS design optimization under different scenarios and target parameters can be achieved using evolutionary algorithms such as the differential evolution (DE) method. We present results from a real-world experiment conducted in a college campus environment, involving a complex scenario with multiple interacting radar signals and targets. Our data demonstrates the capability of IRS technology to create virtual links in real-world scenarios, thereby enhancing target parameter estimation. We also highlight the potential of IRS technology to revolutionize radar systems, enabling the detection of smaller targets and improving accuracy in parameter estimation. We conclude by highlighting potential research paths for further investigation, such as the integration of IRS technology with other radar enhancement techniques and exploring the feasibility of IRS in active radar systems. We also propose the development of new channel modeling that accounts for IRS interactions and integrates new virtual links into existing radar scenarios. We also suggest the utilization of IRS technology in multi-static radar scenarios and the investigation of new signal processing methods for optimal target parameter estimation. Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a category of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games where each player's payoff function is influenced by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz rate in response to other players' actions. Their work demonstrated that these types of games have the capacity for achieving $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$ settings. Despite their findings, they left unanswered the question regarding the complexity of obtaining such equilibrium points. Our work contributes a query-efficient conversion from broader classes of games to those defined as Lipschitz games, thereby allowing us to derive a lower-bound restriction for the efficiency of randomized algorithms in finding $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player games with binary actions and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties, with an exponential relationship between the complexity and the ratio of $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of 'Multi-Lipschitz games' that incorporate distinct Lipschitz rates for each player, followed by a transformation from equilibrium-finding tasks within this broader class to similar tasks within the domain of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, with implications on the sum of individual $\lambda$-Lipschitz parameters. Finally, we establish a lower-bound restriction indicating that deterministic algorithms experience an exponential increase in complexity in finding $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibria in $n$-player games with multiple action options and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties for particularly restrictive $\epsilon$-value settings, thereby advocating the utilization of randomized algorithms in our previous analysis and further contributing to our methodological simplifications over prior work yielding comparable results. These contributions yield an understanding that the complexity of finding approximate Nash equilibria can exhibit an exponential increase in proportion to the product of the number of players and individual games' $\lambda$-Lipschitz parameters, thereby providing a query-efficient representation of complex multi-player games through conversion from simpler games, introducing the concept of Multi-Lipschitz games and deriving implications on its sub-classes, along with a novel lower-bound restriction on the complexity of finding approximate correlated equilibria in multi-player games. These results contribute an analysis of complex multi-player games' complexity to approximating equilibrium points, thereby providing implications on the efficiency of randomized algorithms in finding such points.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Our study shows that j=10 fold CV achieves notable variance reduction, resulting in more reliable parameter adjustments that are consistent across different random initializations, thereby facilitating better generalization performance. Furthermore, our study highlights the reduced variance j-k CV method's applicability to popular optimization algorithms including stochastic gradient descent (SGD), Adam and Tensorflow's default optimizer, as well as the impact of estimation variance on network architecture, revealing that reduced variance can lead to unexpected generalization improvements following the Kermany healthcare dataset's architecture adjustments. Our research also illustrates the challenges of reproducibility in machine learning, as well as the difficulties of achieving robust parameter adjustments despite the issues mentioned above. In conclusion, our study presents the concept of reduced variance j-k fold CV and showcases its utility in facilitating effective parameter tuning, as well as the associated generalization improvements, across a range of NLP tasks and models. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Additionally, as both theories for frictionless and anisotropic jamming involve strain hardening and share a universal viscosity curve, it is suggested that shear jamming may be more accurately described as "shear hardening." This concept is supported by studies using cornstarch in glycerol, where viscosity was found to increase with the number of hard spheres, indicating that shear hardening is a powerful tool for exploring the physics of jamming through shear. By combining these results with previous findings on shear jamming, researchers present a unified framework that explains the physics governing the shear thickening transition, offering a vision for revitalizing the field through the study of nonequilibrium phenomena at the borders of shear jamming. This vision is set to be put to the test by proposed experiments using an extended set of materials and targets. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be viewed as a discrete version of the maximum entropy loss function. A penalized predictive control approach is presented as a way to incorporate MEF into the strategy, and key aspects of the solution, including distinguishability and variational equality constraints, are leveraged to develop an efficient numerical solution based on projected gradient methods. The benefits of this approach, referred to as MEF-aware penalized control (MPCP), include reduced communication demands from operators, lower computational burdens for aggregators, and lower overall costs due to the minimization of MEF. Simulations validate the performance of MPCP, particularly its ability to balance current efficiency with future gains. Furthermore, MPCP is deemed a suitable architecture for multi-agent systems and there are opportunities for further improvement through the use of adaptive feeds back and learning algorithms. This work provides a foundation for the development of real-time coordination architectures that optimize controllable loads within future complex energy systems. Those architectures should be robust to various feedback mechanisms, adaptable to different energy sources, capable to handle high penetrations of controllable loads and be scalable to accommodate the growing number of load participants. Finally, the research on this topic can be extended to explore the application of similar coordination architectures to other type of load participants and non-cooperative game theory approaches. 

This work is a extension of our conference paper presented at the 2022 American Control Conference. It provides an updated analysis, including the examination of maximum entropy feedback (MEF) and a deeper investigation of the MEF-aware penalized control (MPCP) approach. Additionally, this paper examines the performance of MPCPC both with central controller and multi-agent systems, and it inquires about the potential of adaptive feedback and learning algorithms to enhance the MEF-aware penalized control (MPCP) approach. Lastly, it inquires about the possibility of applying the proposed MEF-aware architecture to other type of load participants and non-cooperative game theory approaches.

One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. Our findings indicate that CLIC has the capability to directly constrain the two dominant HEFT coefficients, whereas ILC can set limits on these parameters through indirect searches for the HH $\to b \bar b b \bar b$ decay mode with varying kinematic assumptions, and that the predicted rates for the two colliders lie within the reachable sensitivity of the ILC's small-radius calorimeter system. Finally, we demonstrate that despite the more challenging detection environment at CLIC, the predicted rates for the two colliders lie within the reachable sensitivity of the ILC's small-radius calorimeter system. The study highlights the unique capability of the CLIC detector to directly constrain the two dominant HEFT coefficients, whereas ILC can set limits on these parameters through indirect searches for the HH $\to b \bar b b \bar b$ decay mode with varying kinematic assumptions. The study also demonstrates the efficacy of the small-radius calorimeter system of the ILC in detecting the predicted rates for the two colliders. The study's findings will inform the optimization of search strategies and detector sensitivity in forthcoming analyses of double Higgs production at CLIC and ILC.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. A simple model that takes this into account was able to explain our findings reasonably well. Interestingly, when the cylinder moved quickly enough for air to have an impact, the anisotropy decreased significantly, and we found that the drag experienced by the cylinder was essentially the same whether it was oriented perpendicular or parallel to its long axis, likely due to the formation of vortices on either side of it. This led to the cylinder experiencing a significant amount of drag as it moved, especially through beds with high friction, and this, in turn, caused the grains to lift off the surface below it, resulting in the cylinder being suspended and experiencing drag as if it were moving through a fluid with a much higher viscosity than water. This effect led to further anisotropy, but only when the cylinder moved quickly enough for air to have an impact and when it was moving slowly enough for its long axis to have an impact, but not when it was moving quickly enough for its ends to have an impact. This led to the phenomenon of preferential flow, where the cylinder flows easier through beds with high friction due to the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends, and we found that the threshold for this phenomenon to occur is when the cylinder's velocity is such that its Reynolds number, based on its diameter, is less than 1. This has significant implications for the study of sediment transport, particularly when it comes to the movement of long solids through granular materials. This could also have an impact on our understanding of other complex systems that involve the interaction of solids moving through a layer of grains and may also have applications in fields such as medicine and engineering. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. By modeling a system as a probabilistic graph, BoAnon's framework is expected to benefit other optimization domains that involve complex, structured parameters. Additionally, the methodology employed by BoAnon is expected to be useful in other problems related to system analysis, debugging, and security. While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking. This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies. When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models. The benefits of minimum density power divergence estimators are illustrated through simulations and real-data applications in the analysis of life times and gene expression levels. The associated R software allows users to easily apply this estimation method to various stochastic processes. 

Keywords: Incomplete data; Minimum density power divergence; Model uncertainty; Robust estimation; Time series process.

This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. Shock models also explain the diversity in ionization conditions within one kiloparsec of these galaxies. The position of the shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 suggests they could be caused by the collapse of a massive galaxy disk during a major merger, which is also indicated by concentrated starbursts and far-infrared luminosity. This may be the case for Mrk 607 as well, with far-infrared luminosity however below detection limits. These findings highlight the significance of ionization and shock patterns in powering the optical emission in close-to-nuclear regions of active galaxies. They also suggest that narrow ionization cones are likely the result of shock patterns, which could lead to a reevaluation of their physical mechanisms in active galaxies near starburst regions. Lastly, the ability to observe variations in electron temperatures in Seyfert galaxies will allow for a better understanding of the mechanisms powering their optical emission and may provide insights into the energy that is consumed or absorbed within these systems. This study showcases the capabilities of using spatially-integrated spectra to measure electron temperatures in active galaxies, which can be further enhanced with even higher spatial and spectral sensitivity by upcoming generation of optical integral field units. Consequently, a large survey of a significant sample of Seyfert galaxies, conducted with a current state-of-the-art equipment, is proposed to explore the relationship between the mechanisms that sustain the optical emission in these galaxies and the merger-induced massive starbursts, shocks, and gas flows, specifically by investigating the ionization, shock patterns, gas velocities, and chemical abundances within one kiloparsec of these galaxies. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations. Furthermore, Frisbee includes a set of innovative testing techniques, such as the automated creation of fault injection scenarios and a logic-based approach to testing depending components, which together boost the detection rate of critical bugs by over 3 times in our performance metrics. The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art traffic scenario models and shows considerable promise for contributing to the development of autonomous vehicle technology. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, by combining this new iterative method with an explicit Runge-Kutta scheme, we can achieve both high-order accuracy and preservation of the underlying system's properties. We illustrate the method's effectiveness through several numerical examples involving scalar advection, Navier-Stokes, and the incompressible Boussinesq equations. Specifically, our results improve upon key existing bounds in the literature. We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located within low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) molecular clouds.
Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect superbubble dynamics and dust grain formation. Our goals were to
understand dust grain growth within clumps orbiting the superbubble, as well as
dust survival from supernovae in a highly distorted and expanding supershell.
The model accounted for cluster self-gravity and star cluster potential, while
considering cooling effects and dust influences, using a sophisticated cluster
synthesis model. Similar to previous research, clumpy media cause superbubbles
to become irregularly shaped and driven mostly by expanding hot gas through low
density pathways. Our findings show that in large ($\sim 10^7M_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds hosting large ($\sim 5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot}$) superclusters, dust grain
growth contributes $4.8\times 10^{-5}M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ to dust accumulation
over 2.5 million years. However, pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
increase dust supplies up to $\sim 1200M_{\odot} (M_{SC}/5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot})$, 
with $M_{SC}$ denoting the stellar mass of the supercluster. Consequently, dust
production by both grain growth and supernovae could lead to considerable dust
accumulation within low-metallicity molecular clouds, a process compatible with
galactic dust formation patterns during early cosmic reionization phases.

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of 3D detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. The code for our research is available at https://github.com/yunusbetil/Far-Field-3D-Detection. Our work lays the groundwork for reevaluating detection performance in three dimensions and highlighting the significance of far-field object detection in autonomous driving. It also provides the code necessary to achieve the best results on this challenging task. Software available at https://github.com/yunusbetil/Far-Field-3D-Detection.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. Our study involves determining the E2F status for the following non-bipartite cubic graphs: the 2-regular cover of the complete graph on 5 vertices ($x_5$), the 2-regular cover of the Clebsch graph ($x_2$), and the Gosper polyhedron ($x_4$). Our findings show that $x_5$, $x_2$, and $x_4$ do not possess the PMH-property, whereas $x_5$ and $x_4$ satisfy the E2F condition, as their structures solely comprise the union of the three required colors. This implies that a cubic graph satisfies the E2F condition if, and only if, it contains no $x_2$-subgraph and no $x_4$-subgraph. Furthermore, our research involves presenting an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs, derived from the Davis-Higman polyhedron, as well as providing a new proof that even-2-factorable graphs correspond to 3-edge-colourable graphs. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. In the future, we believe Timeloops could serve as a model for other system call filtering architectures. This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. Building upon this proof, we further show that sensitivity analysis can be employed to obtain explicit upper and lower bounds governing the population's decline rate. Ultimately, our findings establish the optimality of the obtained control action in relation to its magnitude. Additionally, we develop a bilevel control strategy that minimizes costs associated with applying control, with the cost function dependent on the population's size. A numerical example is implemented to illustrate the effectiveness of this approach. Notably, our research involves introducing a novel method for establishing a Carleman estimate in a setting that involves multiple systems of partial differential equations. This innovative approach may provide a framework for exploring similar controllability questions in other population dynamics models. Lastly, our work highlights the advantage of employing sensitivity analysis to obtain precise estimates of action costs, a benefit that can be derived from analyzing the basic population model alone. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. The model's performance is impressive, given the complexity of soccer and the diversity of its environments, and it highlights the potential for strategic policy optimization in similar multi-agent domains. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields.  Ultimately, both WRI and ESI are evaluated through synthetic numerical examples, and it is demonstrated that both can successfully improve seismic models by converging to a more accurate velocity model, with the main difference being that WRI favors frequencies with larger amplitudes, while ESI focuses on matching source time histories.  Additionally, both methods outperform classical FWI, and further, it is shown that WRI with sparse frequency-domain wavefields has the advantage of significantly reducing storage requirements while yielding comparable results.  Hence, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion is seen as a valuable seismic imaging tool, capable of handling complex seismic data with increased spatial sampling.

Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods. This work introduces the program's concept, references historical sundials found in existing literature, and suggests potential methods for collecting data and engaging the public in this research. Further development of this concept hinges on technological advancements in mobile applications and online platforms capable of managing large datasets and facilitating public participation in research. The proposed approach could also be applied to similar research projects involving historical artifacts found throughout Indonesia. This work also includes references to previously unknown sundials discovered through public participation and existing literature, along with historical information compiled from various sources. Ultimately, this work highlights the potential of the Suryakala-Nusantara program to advance research on Indonesian sundials while promoting citizen science initiatives within the country. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Furthermore, we investigate the performance of such a phase plate 
under real-world conditions by simulating its interaction with the electron source, 
resulting in a probe size of 0.67 Angstrom. Additionally, we explore design 
flexibility by creating a pair of binary phase plates able to operate in both 
outer- and inner- ring configurations, both of which yield acceptable results. To 
facilitate experimental implementation, we also present manufacturing guidelines 
for these designs. To provide a foundation for future research, we also examine 
designs capable of combining the functions of a phase plate and a beam constrictor. 
For this, we present over-doable designs that simultaneously achieve high 
resolution and large probe current, also capable of operating under both 
scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and electron energy-loss 
spectroscopy (EELS) conditions. These designs could significantly enhance the 
TEM's imaging and spectroscopic capabilities.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. This study's evaluations and experiments provide valuable insights into the encoder representations of fundamental dialogue language models and suggests areas for further improvement and research in this field. We have made our evaluation codes and datasets available for download at https://github.com/ghrua/eval-dialog-encoder.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state. Furthermore, we establish the conditions under which the spectrum contains only stable or neutral modes, demonstrating that this circumstance is realized when the quadratic term in the anharmonic oscillator has a negative value in certain intervals. We validate our analytical findings through numerical simulations, demonstrating the emergence of unstable modes despite stable orbital conditions in the anharmonic oscillator when the quadratic term becomes positively definite in small enough intervals, even in the absence of energy reservoirs. This phenomenon is illustrated through plots of the spectrum and the corresponding solitary wave dynamics. We also establish that increasing the anharmonic oscillator's quadratic term's magnitude results in a shift from localized to non-localized traveling wave solutions, which exhibit the same speed as the original solitary wave state. Q-ball studies in a single symmetry theory are common, yet the field can be more expansive, allowing for the examination of theories featuring multiple symmetries in a more general context. In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a more detailed investigation into its implications will be addressed in a subsequent study. 

In the realm of effective potentials characterized by multiple symmetries, we observe that the most basic form of such systems can be represented by the Linde-softly broken natural inflation model. We analyze this model numerically and both theoretically within a multiple-symmetry scenario, revealing that the most basic form of this type of system can produce both standard and advanced type of Q-ball objects. We also find that more complex form of this type of scenario may produce both standard and advanced type of Q-ball objects, as well as a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored'. This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend a word's meaning and
context, hindering the distinction between syncretic words with identical
forms but different meanings, such as get(V) and get(N). To facilitate
further research, we make available the difficult cases identified, along
with relevant data and model implementations on GitHub. The paper is
previously published in the proceedings of the 2021 Conference of the
International Organization for Standardization in Computational Linguistics. 
https://www.isco-conferences.org/proceedings2021/P18.pdf will be made available
upon standardization approval. 

This work is enabled by publicly available datasets, models, and tools, 
namely SemAntic, Historical Common Sense Knowledge Graph, Hypernyms, 
Synonyms, Wikipedia, ConceptNet, the Google Multilingual Universal Sentence
Encoder, and the Spacy English model, respectively. We also cite earlier
research on diachronic word meaning analysis and contextualized language models. 
In addition, we outline newly raised queries and offer previously used scores
for evaluation in this domain.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$). These limits can be viewed as minimum values, as multiple species of such particles would increase their total mass fraction. This research can be expanded upon, as future observations will yield more precise measurements, capable of addressing a broader range of fundamental physics questions. This will be achievable as a result of distinguishing between the general relativistic and Newtonian descriptions of AGNs' behavior, which will become possible due to the improvement in luminosity and radio luminosity accuracy, as well as the reduction of system variability. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, we utilize mathematical modeling to
show that the unequal distribution of nuclei is a result of a diffusive process exacerbated by surface tension, and that
this phenomenon is robust against various parameters including retinal growth rates and diffusion coefficients. We also

stochastic effect on cell fate choice. Consequently, our study suggests that the random cell fate selection observed in
the retina may be an intrinsic outcome of IKNM rather than a separate process. Moreover, our findings indicate that the
retina offers a valuable system in which to study the interplay between migration, cell fate choice, and tissue growth.
