In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images. This code optimization problem is effectively viewed as a generalization of the minimum-cut problem in graph theory, allowing for the construction of customized code patterns that match specific capture device capabilities and can adapt to varying image sizes with only minor adjustments, leading to enhanced reconstruction results compared to the traditional uniformly spaced codes. Experimental evaluations confirm the code patterns proposed in this research yield superior reconstruction results and outperform traditional methods, especially for narrow borders. Additionally, these custom-designed code patterns offer considerable advantages over uniformly spaced codes in terms of compressed sensing coherence, leading to reduced reconstruction artifacts and better overall performance. Consequently, customized code patterns are seen as an essential component in the development of specialized video compressed sensing systems and hold significant potential for other applications involving structured sensing, such as color image demosaicing. This research provides code patterns that can be directly integrated into popular image processing libraries, such as OpenCV, for immediate utilization in video compressed sensing and other applications requiring structured sensing. Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity, where a strong 
electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions. 
We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional 
van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations. 
Furthermore, we anticipate that this singularity will be observable in 
electron spectral functions, offering a viable method for detecting the 
exceptional van Hove singularity in experiments. 
Additionally, we explore possible routes to triggering this singularity 
experimentally, including through pressure application or chemical doping. 
Finally, we discuss the implications of this concept for our understanding 
of the normal state of materials exhibiting pseudogap behavior. 
In this context, we propose that the normal state is characterized by 
coexistence of both doped and van Hove electrons, separated by a Fermi 
hole pocket, and that this picture applies to all materials exhibiting 
pseudogap, including cuprates, pnictides, and dichalcogenides. 
We predict that this normal state can give rise to diverse physics resulting 
from the interplay between doped and van Hove electrons, including 
topological phases and other exotic states of matter. 
Thus, we propose that this concept of exceptional van Hove singularity 
will serve as a unifying framework for understanding a broad range of 
electron systems exhibiting pseudogap behavior. 
In addition to cuprates, this concept may also be applicable to 
other strongly interacting electron systems, such as pnictides and dichalcogenides, 
and could have implications for our understanding of these materials. 
Furthermore, we anticipate that this concept will not only provide a 
unifying framework for these materials, but will also offer a promising 
approach to identifying new applications for materials exhibiting 
exceptional van Hove singularity.

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. During testing, it revealed a significantly increased count rate of neutron scatters, likely caused by neutrons produced in the tunnel's surrounding rock. The apparatus also demonstrated the capability to correlate neutron events with cosmic-ray muons. Furthermore, we present results from a demonstration experiment where the apparatus was used to measure the neutron flux produced by muons at the laboratory location. The measurement shows a marked increase in neutron flux rates, likely due to neutrons produced in the surrounding rock as muons pass through it. The apparatus has already provided valuable insights into the rock surrounding the laboratory and has significant potential to contribute to scientific research in this field. The design and performance characteristics of the apparatus make it an innovative solution that can effectively measure the production of spallation neutrons in deep, rocky environments using cosmic-ray muons. The apparatus has the capability to monitor various rock properties, such as neutron flux and energy spectrum, which can be utilized to study water infiltration and rock composition changes over time. Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The algorithms used to rank the targets can be executed in a time-efficient manner on a standard computational platform. The outcome of the TKS is a unique dataset of 103 validated planets, offering numerous opportunities for further scientific investigation. The approach presented here is equally applicable to future missions such as PLATO and LVSCO, and the algorithms developed for this survey are freely accessible to facilitate the comparison of theoretical models of the extraplanetary population with observational data. The TKS is also the largest dataset to date of small planets detected through transit methods, and is featured in the 14th edition of the TESS Guest Investigator Manual as GI-20190. The survey is carried out with a grant from the TESS Guest Investigator Program. The authors would like to extend their appreciation to A. Chontos and C. Johnston for contributing to the target selection algorithm

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, the extracted text was further corrected using Natural Language Processing.  When tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images, the F-score achieved was 0.78, and the extraction process for each ID card took approximately 4510 milliseconds.  To verify accounts associated with the ID cards, the proposed system was integrated with the existing account management system of one popular Indonesian E-commerce Company.  The existing account management system was modified to link accounts with IDs, allowing for easy verification.  The proposed system successfully prevented at least five fraudulent account-related transactions.  The ease of data entry and verification enabled by the proposed system also led to at least 30 new online account verifications daily.  The proposed system's ability to extract ID information was compared to an automated ID card extraction service, and the results showed that the proposed system's extraction accuracy was higher than the service's.  The proposed system's accuracy and effectiveness in preventing fraudulent transactions make it suitable for use in similar applications.  The proposed system's source code is available for replication and further development.  Several variations of the proposed system's extraction approach were tested and compared, and it was found that the combination of OCR and NLP yielded the highest accuracy.  The proposed system's extraction time can be further optimized using techniques such as image pre-processing and compression.  The integration of the proposed system with various account management systems requires modification of the existing code, and its applicability to different types of ID cards requires adjustment of the text correction rules.  The proposed system's accuracy on ID cards with poor image quality can be improved using techniques such as image enhancement and noise reduction.  The proposed system's applicability to different languages requires development of language-specific text correction rules.  The proposed system's effectiveness in preventing fraudulent transactions can be further improved using more advanced verification methods.  The proposed system's extraction time can be further optimized using multi-threading or distributed computing, and its applicability to different types of ID cards can be further improved using machine learning models.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations. The simulations showed excellent agreement with analytical results for both scenarios, paving the way for studying oscillators interacting with environments using this method. Furthermore, this study highlights the effectiveness of using the lattice algorithm to compute the ground state of quantum systems when the number of oscillations is relatively small. However, larger systems may require larger lattices, necessitating more sophisticated sampling methods to achieve accurate results. Consequently, this study demonstrates the capability to employ big data sampling techniques, such as stochastic optimization, for such quantum ground state calculations. In addition, this method can be modified to include driving forces that change over time by treating the displacement operator as a classical variable during the simulation. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. This finding counteracts a false hypothesis proposed by Ju. T. Shmidt and confirmed by Kechen Wang in a specific context. Furthermore, we derive an analogous result for homeomorphisms that act on the surface's boundary, and provide an additional proof of compactness for a specific type of homeomorphism subgroup within the surface's interior. Alongside these outcomes, we explore the topological compactness properties of homeomorphism groups across all compact surfaces, establishing conditions under which these groups are topologically compact. Lastly, we establish an equivalence between the homeomorphism group's compactness and the surface's genus in a particular topological context. This research is based on cutting-edge techniques involving topological dynamics, in addition to earlier methods used to study these spaces. It provides a comprehensive framework for understanding topological dynamics on compact surfaces with boundaries.

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. This new concept, titled 'quasi-continuity', is defined by slightly relaxing the original conditions for continuity and is also assignable to Turing machines with infinite input. The ability to decide quasi-continuity is also established and takes the same $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ requirement. 

Finally, the theoretical possibilities and limitations of this approach are further examined and potential applications discussed, including its implications for handling streaming data streams and the potential to enhance the functionality of existing systems that handle infinite inputs. 

Keywords: infinite string functions, computability, continuity, quasi-continuity, MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, two-way transducers, decision-making, log space complexity, property preservation, rational and regular functions, $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ requirement, quasi-continuity decision-making, possible and impossible cases, time complexity, system enhancement, streaming data streams, infinite input streams, formal language theory, mathematical theory.

By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. For integers y that are much smaller, the issue becomes whether the estimated count of y-friable integers can still be expressed in a similar form involving the Dickman function. By improving an earlier upper estimate of the count of y-friable integers from our previous paper and further analyzing the results under the condition that RH is true, we are able to determine that the estimated count of y-friable integers can indeed be expressed in a similar form involving the Dickman function even for very small integers y. In particular, we had found that the estimated count of y-friable integers up to x, where $\left(\log x\right)/y$ is greater than some extremely small quantity, is equal to x times the Dickman function of $(\log x)/y$ times a factor that is close to 1. Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and several cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework. The experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of Bayesian optimization and evolutionary algorithms over traditional methods, with all algorithms outperforming the manual selection method in terms of balance achievement. The results also reveal that the MOEA/D algorithm is the most effective evolutionary algorithm for hyperparameter tuning in the private setting, and the Kneser-Ney style model performs best among Bayesian optimization methods. The research findings can serve as guidelines for selecting hyperparameters in private machine learning applications. The paper further presents the application of the developed framework to the private deep neural network, achieving notable improvements following the integration of optimized algorithms. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our findings provide valuable insights into the propagation mechanics of online rumors and may contribute to the development of more effective counter-measures. Furthermore, the data collected can be utilized for self-monitoring and public service purposes, such as creating warning systems and promoting fact-checking information. To facilitate future research, we made the data set and the code publicly available. Through the mitigation protocols implemented by major social media platforms during the pandemic, we observed significant reductions in the peak and attenuation coefficients, indicating a positive response to these measures. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. The definition is then applied to a particular curve called the helicoidal curve, resulting in an analysis of its properties and demonstrations of both left and right Bertrand curves within a four-dimensional space. Finally, the paper explores the distinction between curves that are both Bertrand and Chaprat curves, providing examples in the form of a helicoidal curve in (1,3) and Chaprat curves in (2,2) space. The paper also includes an analysis of a curve's behavior when it transitions from being a Bertrand curve to a Chaprat curve. The research is conducted within the context of (n,p)-Bertrand and (n,p)-Chaprat curves, defined as curves in an n-dimensional Euclidean space described by the following equations: x(s) = a(s) + b(s), x(s) = a(s) + b(s)/p, a(s+b) = a(s) + b(s), and a(s+b) = a(s) + b(s)p, respectively. The research provides various examples of these curves, including the helicoidal curve, in (1,3) space and Chaprat curves in (2,2) space, offering insights into the characteristics of these curves and their relationships. The paper also discusses the challenges associated with distinguishing between curves that are both Bertrand and Chaprat curves. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization. We introduce a novel, efficient algorithm to minimize a wide range of loss functions, including non-differentiable ones, by leveraging the properties of the subgradient in an Adam-like framework. We further showcase the benefits of our method through a series of classification experiments, highlighting the advantages of exploring less common loss functions. To facilitate further research, we have made our dataset generators and code publicly available.

A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation. By transforming the underlying problem into a similar system of equations with altered boundary conditions, we achieve the desired control outcome. Subsequent analysis demonstrates that this modified system satisfies the conditions required for a classical Lopitaitskii theory application, thereby yielding a stabilizable solution. Consequently, we establish the existence of an optimal control that minimizes a related cost function within a specified time frame. Furthermore, our discussion includes the numerical implementation of the proposed control strategy, successfully demonstrated through a computational example involving flow control in a rectangular channel. The numerical results, obtained by implementing a finite-element method with a dual-domain approach, showcase the efficacy of the proposed control scheme. Specifically, we present results for both two-dimensional Taylor-Gortler modes and three-dimensional curved vortices in a rectangular channel, highlighting the successful attenuation of these instabilities through the application of the boundary feedback controller. Finally, we examine the sensitivity of the optimal control solution to vortical structures with varying swirl numbers. The findings provided valuable insights into the feasibility of flow reversal using optimal boundary control, successfully achieved in a limited domain but indicating the potential for future investigation. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. Advantages of delayed conventional differential detection include lower computational requirements and comparable performance to its non-delayed counterpart, demonstrating relevant applicability. Moreover, an interesting phenomenon is observed where CPM formats with smaller delay periods outperform those with larger delay periods due to increased metric noise. As a result, conventional differential detection with short delay periods can be viewed as a method that opposes the effects of frequency shift. This opposition leads to reduced uncertainty in the trellis structure, resulting in improved performance. Furthermore, this technique can be viewed as an alternative to frequency shift compensation methods. As expected, increased delay periods result in performance improvement for many CPM formats; nevertheless, unusual cases like square-root raised cosine (SRCR) CPM demonstrate counterintuitive behavior where performance actually decreases with larger delay periods due to increased metric noise, resulting in reduced performance. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques.  The code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/DisRain. Meanwhile, the developed rain simulation module can independently produce realistic rain images directly from clear backgrounds. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Moreover, we demonstrate that high precision labels are not necessarily prerequisite for significant improvements in the agents' performance. Human-provided labels with only 25% precision are sufficient to achieve improved performance compared to learning from scratch, highlighting the potential of our method for scaling reward learning with human input. Finally, we explore the potential benefits of our approach in other scenarios, such as improving agents with existing human data and learning human preferences in complex scenarios. Overall, our work presents an efficient and effective way to enhance the performance of reward learning agents via human input, addressing one of the key challenges facing the field. We are sharing our code and data visuals with the community to facilitate further research. We invite you to watch our work in progress at https://yuanminliu.com/hrc20_demo and explore our code at https://yuanminliu.com/hrc20_code. Our final paper presentation will take place at the Virtual Press Room of NeurIPS 2020.

Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial, and online surveys have proven effective for gathering relevant data. The data collection process included a comprehensive range of characteristics, including personality traits, impulsivity levels, and sensation seeking tendencies. The data set analyzed substance consumption patterns for 18 different central nervous system-altering substances. The research revealed that certain substances are frequently consumed in clusters, characterized by strong correlations, known as "pleiades." Notable clusters were identified around the substances ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. By exploring various classification techniques and features, a data-driven approach identified the most effective methods to categorize individuals as users or non-users for each specific substance or cluster. Among the techniques examined, including tree models and probability estimations, a top-performing classifier was chosen for each drug. The accuracy of these classifications exceeded 70 percent for nearly all substances when using a rigorous evaluation method. The best performance was seen for the substances cannabis, crack, ecstasy, legal highs, LSD, and volatile substance abuse, achieving a high classification accuracy of above 75 percent. The research utilized a large and diverse data set, gathered from over 1 million active users of a German online survey platform, with data collected over a period of 12 years. The study demonstrated the value of employing machine learning methods and multidimensional data sets in identifying the complex patterns of drug consumption. The techniques developed can potentially contribute to personalized interventions aimed at reducing drug misuse. However, the approach has its limitations, primarily stemming from the reliance on self-reported data, which is prone to inaccuracy. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  Our work presents a foundation for creating theories of how the human mind represents logical rules governing daily life and also presents methods for assessing the degree to which these rules are embedded within the mind.  This is highlighted by our evaluation of the difficulty level of each type of relationship as determined by the frequency with which they appear in language.  Ultimately, we believe that broad access to a framework like ATOMIC is crucial for propelling the development of next-generation artificial intelligence through the integration of its components with systems of machine learning.  This is to create machines that are capable of applying the vast array of knowledge that humans possess in relation to their environment and the consequences of their actions.  Along with the dataset, we have established a knowledge-based search engine that is incorporated into our user interface demo, in which users can enter conditions and receive effects that are derived from ATOMIC, as well as contribute their own reasoning rules that are reviewed by our annotation team and incorporated into the dataset. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This technique also improves ASR models' robustness to noisy input conditions and enables them to adapt to new domains with limited paired data available. Furthermore, this multi-modal attention mechanism can be incorporated into existing encoder-compressor decoding frameworks without a loss of performance. In our experiments, this technique resulted in a 14.59% error reduction when using unpaired text data with the Transformer transcription model. This technique is deemed versatile as it can be applied to other speech recognition architectures, such as the Transformer and Monotonic Transformer, with similar performance improvements. This paper's proposed multi-modal attention technique provides a viable solution for effectively leveraging unpaired text data in end-to-end ASR models. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. For $n$ large, the conditioned random walk approximation yields remarkably accurate estimates, demonstrating that the desired asymptotic distributions can be closely approximated by specific normal or geometric distributions. These estimates provide superior precision over related previous estimates. These normal or geometric approximations can be particularly useful in their own right, especially in relation to recent work by Birkner et al. on random walk parking systems. Some of our results are robust enough to be applied in a broader context. Additionally, our research includes an novel proof of the identically distributed system $\pi_n$, which is an open problem mentioned by Diaconis and Hicks. Our proof involves showing the invariance of $\pi_n$ by demonstrating the uniqueness of the stationary distribution for a specific random walk system. Alongside, we discuss an interesting connection between the parking distribution and the uniform distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ in relation to permutation statistics. Some of our results also include specific limit theorems for certain meshed or spaced locations within $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(n)$. Ultimately, our work provides an comprehensive framework that can be applied to various types of parking distributions generated by different random walk systems. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. Moreover, observations suggest that quantum phase slips can be induced by a source of dc bias at frequencies comparable to those of microwave pulses, enabling the possibility of controlling phase slips and, in turn, the superconducting state itself. This could enable the development of sensitive sensors capable of detecting tiny changes in a device's environment. Furthermore, the quantization of quantum phase slips may provide a means to measure the fine structure of Fermi's distribution function. The complex interplay between quantum interference and capacitance in these nanowires presents an intriguing phenomenon that awaits a comprehensive theoretical explanation. This finding highlights the diverse range of quantum phase slip behaviors waiting to be understood and exploited in research involving superconducting nanowires. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, requiring further examination due to their implications for intermediate population object formation processes. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, GJ 229B exists near the boundary between the planetary and stellar domains, offering an opportunity for its atmospheric analysis to shed light on formation mechanisms. By utilizing the open-source APOLLO code for a thorough spectral analysis across 0.5-5.1 ${\rm \mu m}$, we derived a precise mass estimate of $41.6\pm3.3\, M_J$ and an accurate temperature assessment of $869_{-7}^{+5}$ K that corresponds with evolutionary models, indicating the system to be older than 1 billion years, and also identified high CO molecular abundance replicating earlier observations, which provide implications for this object's formation and evolution, further contributing to the knowledge of analyzing brown dwarfs and planets through new-generation telescopes. Furthermore, a re-examination of the radial velocity data revealed minimal variability, which could be attributed to the cooling of the dwarf's rotational kinetic energy over time, also observable in similar objects like LHS 2924B, HS 1723B, and VHS 1256-129B, which might have larger masses but exhibit similar low-velocity variations, suggesting a possible decline in their internal heat and possibility of synchronization with their cooling rates. Additionally, a analysis of the near-infrared flux excess in GJ 229AB indicated the presence of a large horizontal convective zone in GJ 229A, also present in other late G-type dwarfs, also highlighting the need for evaluating convective flux multiplicative parameters in larger G-type main sequence stars through spectral analysis. Lastly, we discovered the system to be moving towards the Milky Way's center, accompanied by increased velocity along the line of sight, which, combined with its unique intermediate nature, positions GJ 229B well for further analysis of its development through repeated spectroscopic examinations, ultimately contributing to a deeper comprehension of its formation and evolution within our galaxy.

Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views. Additionally, we leverage the algorithm to construct an infinite series of polyhedra in two-dimensional Euclidean space, along with a distinct polyhedron in four-dimensional Euclidean space. Consequently, the possibility of applying the algorithm to other spaces is explored. Finally, the potential benefits and limitations of the algorithm in this context are discussed.

Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
the star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can
lead to detectable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets. It also discusses recent space missions and future
satellites that will allow for a better understanding of these phenomena. Specifically,
it highlights the capabilities of the Alexei team's proposal for the Solar Express
satellite, which will be launched in 2025. This satellite will focus on studying the
Sun's magnetospheric field and the surrounding interplanetary medium. It will also
be capable of simultaneously observing the Sun's magnetic reconnection sites and
mass loss areas in extreme ultraviolet, X-rays, and radio waves. This will enable
scientists to investigate the relationship between the locations of reconnection, X-ray
flares, radio bursts, and mass loss, as well as the reconnection sites themselves. 
It will also study how the Sun's magnetic field changes over time and how they 
affect the magnetospheric field. Furthermore, it will be able to observe the Solar 
System's magnetic field lines reconnecting in the Earth's magnetosphere and provide
earth-based validation for global magnetic field models. This satellite will thus
provide fundamental insights into the shared magnetic physics governing the interactions
between stars and planets. It will offer a unique opportunity to compare the magnetospheric
physics of the Sun and other stars, as well as to gain a deeper understanding of how
magnetic reconnection and mass loss are linked in our Sun and other celestial bodies. 
This knowledge will be achieved through multi-wavelength, multi-body space astronomy 
combined with sophisticated computer simulations of magnetic fields in stars and planets.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. This could result in an increase in Spin-Orbit Coupling within a few Angstroms of the interface, contributing to the observed resistivity and Hall resistance changes. Further research is needed to fully understand the spin-orbit proximity effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers. This study may also spark interest in exploring other ferromagnetic/skew-scattering materials with varied spin-orbit coupling strengths.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations. Computational models vary depending on the specific values of $\alpha$ and $N$. As an example, when $\alpha=1$ and $N=3$, potential parameters are chosen to model a Na$_2$ molecule, yielding five distinct bound states, and when $\alpha=1/2$ and $N=2$, the Harrie-Schrieffer model is modeled to calculate one bound state eigenvalue and corresponding wave function. 

Keywords: Fractional Schrödinger equation, Mie-type potential, Bound state, Mittag-Leffler function, Confluent hypergeometric function, Diatomic molecule.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We observed improved generalisation performance, assessed through the use of a simple reliability metric, for multiple benchmark datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and MNIST. We believe our findings offer a clear case for the use of constrained training methods over alternative regularisation techniques.

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models. 
The code and data used in this research are available online. 
Keywords: neural network language models, agreement prediction, Basque, 
hierarchical sentence structures, language learning.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. Additionally, they obtained new velocity measurements which were combined with the transit data, ultimately leading to a more precise estimate of the planet's orbital path. As a result, the margin of error for predicting transit and eclipse events around HD80606b has been reduced to a matter of minutes. This new level of accuracy may allow researchers to detect subtle irregularities in the planet's orbit when combined with upcoming observations using the James Webb Space Telescope. Furthermore, this new data may also be used to refine the estimates for other planets with similar orbits, such as HD189733b and XO-1b, by accounting for the effects of their hosts' stars on their orbital paths. Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation; nevertheless, developing adjustments that cater to both therapy and enjoyment objectives poses a challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose an approach where an initial statistical model of game performance identifies specific settings that mirror players' typical behavior, even in the face of diminished control. This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller for the Pac-Man game. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the identification of two key factors that affect the gameplay experience and influence rehabilitation adjustments. Experimental measurements of the participants' interaction with the modified game revealed that our low-latency statistical model accurately identifies optimal parameter values that reproduce baseline gameplay under controlled conditions. This methodology holds potential for addressing balance problems related to the design of gamified systems, particularly those involving conflicting requirements for physical involvement and subjectively enjoyable experiences. To facilitate replication and further exploration of this research, we are providing the associated software and data in an open-source package available for download. Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks. This approximation involves minimizing a functional that combines data and regularization terms to achieve a piecewise smooth configuration for the solid, consistent with given displacement bounds. Specifically, the data term penalizes configuration deviations from the prescribed reference state, while the regularization term promotes piecewise continuity across potential fracture locations. To demonstrate the model's efficacy, we show it includes established models such as the Griffith criterion and the Amor-Horsington model as distinct linearised elasticity cases. Furthermore, the approximation can be formulated as a stable and solvable problem via the Bregman distance and Lagrange multipliers. Finally, we illustrate the model's performance through a numerical simulation of a nonlinear fracture problem in a critically stressed plate subjected to bi-axial tension. This simulation employs a non-linear UEL formulation and a mixed-form finite element method with rotational DOF for modelling plate fractures. The results highlight the model's capability to accurately capture the fracture location, depth and branch morphology. This leads to the conclusion that the proposed model provides a robust and effective framework for modelling brittle fractures in piecewise-rigid solids within both linearised and nonlinear elasticity contexts. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Furthermore, this code can be adapted to generate predictions for other processes involving vector leptoquarks. By exploring the most probable scenarios for the existence of vector leptoquarks, we can anticipate the mass range and strength of interaction required for these particles to account for the observed discrepancy in certain B-meson decay processes, specifically in the R$_{K^{*}}$ parameter. According to lattice quantum chromodynamics simulations, the most likely mass range for these particles falls within the range of approximately 1000 to 1500 GeV, although this range is still somewhat inconclusive. As a result, our code can be utilized to anticipate the most likely outcomes for ditau production within this mass range, and can be refined to accommodate potential discoveries of vector leptoquarks, including their production mechanisms and properties. By integrating our code with publicly accessible tools for simulating the behavior of particles at the LHC, we can visualize the expected outcomes for ditau production within various mass ranges for these particles, providing a comprehensive overview of their likely existence and characteristics. Ultimately, our code is poised to enhance the ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, as well as shape the outlook for these particles in light of the observed discrepancy in certain B-meson decay processes. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. The proposed revision is then applied to model the coherence of the text and the results indicate an improvement in the coherence model but only to a limited extent. The study's findings suggest that modern computer systems already consider the necessary coherence information required to recognize connections and that these systems already model the connections within the text to some extent. Consequently, the study proposes a simpler revision of CT and posits that the core concepts underlying these computer systems are responsible for modeling the connections within the text, thus making CT's contribution limited. The study's results have implications for research aimed at understanding the coherence of the text through connections, especially when conducted in isolation, and highlights the importance of considering the underlying computer systems' architecture when analyzing their capabilities. The proposed revision of CT is available for public review and the study's results may spark further debate on the relationship between computer systems that identify connections within the text and the principles of CT. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Our new results are matched by a previous study regarding the treewidth parameter but outperform that study in terms of running time. Moreover, our new results improve the previous best known times for the treedepth parameter by a factor of n. Our research was inspired by an open problem posed in a previous research paper. Our methods involve the systematic application of parameterized techniques to graph decomposition methods associated with SPQR trees, resulting in highly efficient algorithms. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations while revealing underlying patterns that underpin the operator growth phenomenon. By distilling the essential principles governing operator growth within these systems, we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in tackling more intricate systems like Lie-symmetric Causal Dynamical Triangulation. Lastly, we highlight the potential for exploring operator growth patterns in other fundamental theories that exhibit Lie symmetry, such as certain variants of General Relativity.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The research utilized K-Fold Cross-Validation to ensure the reliability of the model across different settings and situations. The evaluation of the proposed approach showed that a universal model could effectively estimate the geospatial distance between WiFi fingerprints with a median error rate of 2.48 meters when folding cross-validation was applied. To facilitate replication and advancement of this research, the associated data and algorithms are freely available online. This research paves the way for a deeper exploration of machine learning techniques to enhance WiFi fingerprint processing, in addition to empowering the development of more precise indoor location awareness platforms that can fold cross-validation into their methodology. For nearly 60 years, researchers have been searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through SETI initiatives, with a Dyson Sphere as a primary target - an advanced megastructure capable of harnessing a star's energy for an advanced civilization. A study explores whether constructing such a structure around a black hole would be feasible and efficient in powering a civilization. Considering six potential energy sources, researchers found that an accretion disk, which can produce $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$ of energy, would be sufficient for an advanced civilization. Additionally, a Dyson Sphere could potentially collect energy from relativistic jets and increase its overall energy output fivefold. Calculations indicate that a Dyson Sphere constructed around a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way could be detectable with current telescopes using waste heat radiation in the ultraviolet to mid-infrared spectrum. Analyzing spectral energy distributions and radial velocity variations could aid in identifying possible artificial structures, such as Dyson Spheres. With many black hole candidates with suitable conditions waiting to be studied, searching for artificial structures around them may offer a more effective strategy than focusing on stars and planets. Leveraging advancements in observational capabilities and machine learning, searching for Dyson Spheres constructed around black holes holds significant potential to contribute to the search for extraterrestrial intelligence. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. In fact, with properly chosen filling patterns, beam breakup instability effects can be minimized to a level where other limitations, such as collective effects and RF power deposition, become the more constraining factors. This implies that multi-pass energy recovery linacs can effectively utilize beam recirculation, potentially enhancing the efficiency of these accelerators by a factor of 10 compared to single-pass designs. This report also includes specific design recommendations for reducing beam breakup threshold currents, such as filling all functions in one fill cycle, giving low charge beams priority, giving moderate charge beams priority when co-existing with low charge ones, and carefully selecting beam positions for re-circulation. This report provides a comprehensive foundation for further investigation into beam breakup threshold currents and offers valuable design guidelines for the effective operation of multi-pass energy recovery linacs. In addition, the beam breakup model developed here can be applied to various other accelerator scenarios, such as proton accelerators or those making multiple passes in different types of accelerators, by modifying the beam characteristics to match those of the specific application in question. This report was inspired by the framework for Multi-Pass Linac Research developed by the Global Zero-Waste Strategy Group. To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems rely heavily on the development of detailed models describing the interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei. The intricacy of these models is significant, partly because existing detectors have been incapable of observing final state neutrons, which has led to significant systematic uncertainties. The implementation of 3D scintillator tracking technology in next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments has improved detection capabilities by enabling event-by-event measurement of neutron kinetic energy resulting from neutrino interactions, thus providing valuable information for refining neutrino interaction models and reconstructing neutrino energies. The primary goal was to demonstrate the ability of neutron detection by comparing the total cross-sectional area of neutrons and scintillator interaction at 98-688 MeV, which was measured at 0.36±0.05 barn, in accordance with established external measurement standards. The implemented 3D tracking algorithm employed for this calculation utilized ring and shower shapes in addition to conventional 2D techniques. The significant achievement of this experiment was the detection of neutrons produced through exclusive deep-inelastic scattering, specifically at 157-688 MeV, with cross-sectional areas ranging from 1.15 to 8.04 barns, exhibiting substantial agreement with theoretical models and readjusting the scale of neutrino total cross-section by a margin of (0.04±0.05) x 10^-28 cm^2. In conclusion, the successful outcome of this research paves the way for implementing precision neutron detection in long-baseline neutrino experiments and will contribute significantly to the scientific community's ongoing quest to comprehend the nature and properties of neutrinos. In the present investigation, we shift focus to the effect of surface moisture on the grains under normal lab conditions, which involves having multiple water layers. In the case of the cooler protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only hold one water layer. Since this water layer would evaporate in the warmer sections of the discs as dust moves inward, we decided to examine how two alternative methods for dust cleaning up affect stickiness in the intermediate temperature range. In the first method, hot dust is scattered into the cooler sections by massive planets, resulting in water recondensing and dust sticking together with increased force. In the second method, dust is heated to the point where water turns to gas, which allows it to escape, reducing the force of attraction between the dust particles and allowing smaller particles to escape more easily due to their higher vapor pressure. In the lab, we simulated both scenarios by examining dry grains at moderate temperatures and under more extreme temperatures with minimal water supply, and compared our findings with theoretical models, which showed strong agreement. The outcome supports a two-tiered dust aggregation process, where large particles form through weak van der Waals forces in the cooler sections, and smaller particles are held together by stronger forces caused by water recondensing in the hotter sections. This could result in the growth of differentiated dust cores as they move into the hotter sections. Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools. Additionally, the package includes metrics for evaluating the accuracy of reduced data and supports loading data from CSV, XLS, and SDC files. The package was created adhering to CRAN guidelines, and the source code is openly accessible on GitHub. The package further includes a comprehensive tutorial (LFDA_v2_0.pdf) detailing its features and data formats. The package is compatible with R 3.5.0 and subsequent versions. The source code and tutorial are freely accessible online.

Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our research offers a versatile skill learning framework that can serve as a foundation for future works aiming to capture the temporal nature of human skills. The code for our project is available at: https://github.com/ethan-jin/EKMP. Our research also includes video demonstrations, which can be accessed at: https://ethan-jin.com/project/ekmp.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. Additionally, it has been demonstrated that the conformally invariant cross ratios can be used to derive a soft function for six-gluon processes, providing a novel connection between the BFKL equation and the conformal bootstrap, and offering further evidence for the significance of such ratios in understanding the dynamics of the BFKL equation. As a byproduct of this analysis, the known CEV functions for single-emission processes have been re-expressed using a basis of conformally invariant operators defined by low-twist representations of conformal group, highlighting the role of conformal symmetry in understanding CEV functions. Consequently, it becomes apparent that further research is needed to fully comprehend the nature of conformally invariant cross ratios, which are anticipated to hold significant implications for our understanding of the BFKL equation and its connection with the conformal bootstrap and the dynamics of gauge-gravity duality.
