A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface.

By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. 

This study, conducted on samples with varying lengths of 0.5 mm and cooling times of a few seconds to several hours, utilized specific sound measurements to directly examine the effects of magnetic fields on the material's crystal structure and determine the activation energy of the vortex state, which varies in a non-linear manner with magnetic field but remains relatively consistent across temperatures from 1.5 K to 1.8 K. The results of these experiments, combined with magnetic field absorption and local density of states measurements, reveal the rotational state transition and the associated energy barrier that vortices must overcome to move within the material. This finding has significant implications for the understanding of magnetic field effects on highly doped La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ and may have a major impact on the development of high critical current materials for magnetic fields higher than 30 T.

However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. Some well-known graphs like a straight line, a cycle, a tree and a complete graph have their beta_k values well documented but there is a gap in the literature regarding the metric dimension of cyclical graphs that connect every two vertices with two edges (especially those that are not trees) up to a certain large enough number. This paper fills that gap for cyclical graphs that connect every two vertices with two edges especially those that are not trees for k=3 and shows a general formula for cyclical graphs that connect every two vertices with more than one edge for any k greater than or equal to 2. This paper also discusses some related ideas and presents some open questions. Additionally it introduces a new lower bound technique and uses it to find a higher bound for beta_k of such graphs for any k greater than or equal to 3. This is an initial look at the topic as the field of identifying sets in graphs is a rich and highly developed one with many interesting open questions. Thus the paper hopes to contribute meaningfully to this area by offering new techniques and a fresh perspective on the topic. The paper specifically addresses the version of the problem where the distances between points are limited to some number k and calls it beta_k of the graph. It discusses the version of this property where the distances between points are not limited and calls it gamma_k of the graph. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Furthermore, this method allows for more realistic simulations of the telescope, which can reveal how changes in the detector's settings affect the detection of these sources and phenomena. This work paves the way for enhanced analysis and simulation of gamma-ray images and spectra, which can be applied to other imaging satellites like e-ASTROG and future Fermi missions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We conclude that action sequences produce high-quality solutions for various combinatorial optimization challenges despite lacking optimal performance in theoretical terms. Moreover, we find actionable insights can be derived from pricing serial dictatorship in terms of its implications for efficiency and fairness. Additionally, we provide a framework and results for pricing specific combinatorial optimization tasks that may contribute to the development of general methods for pricing serial dictatorship in other domains. This paper analyzes the performance of complex MIMO systems that utilize spatial modulation and multiuser detection with a least-squares method, and derives rate and distortion metrics for this setup. By applying an asymptotic characterization, we evaluate specific detector methods, including an optimal Bayesian detector, and develop a simplified approach for optimizing a related detection method, before supporting our findings with numerical simulations. Notably, using an optimized version of the detection method results in significant performance improvements over conventional approaches, with gains of up to $10.4$ bits per channel use in ideal scenarios, and near-capacity-compliance in non-ideal scenarios. Interestingly, using an optimal detection method for SM systems yields performance comparable to that of systems that utilize full-dimension MIMO transmission. Additionally, we observe that using an optimal detection method enables the efficient use of MIMO dimensions, and that the optimal detection method outperforms other detection methods even in the presence of channel estimation errors. Furthermore, we investigate the performance gains attainable through the use of MIMO transmission, and find that for large MIMO systems, the performance gain from MIMO transmission diminishes. Lastly, we examine various design options for the transmission precoder, and find that using a precoder optimized for minimum MIMO dimension usage results in performance near-optimal. Lastly, we present results showing the potential applicability of our findings to popular wireless communication standards, including 5G NR.

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  It led to unusual patterns observed in seismic data, and helped forecast salt basin finders in unexplored areas of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  It also enabled improved reconstruction of paleo-altitudes of the West African conjugent margin.  This allowed for modeling of the primary hydrological evolution of the S~ao Paulo High during the Jurassic period.  It indicates the high experienced paleo-altitudes of around 1500 meters around 126 Ma, and how they gradually decreased to sea level over 20 million years as the rift basin expanded.  This multi-velocity, multi-directional history of the conjugate Brazilian and West African margins helped explain the unique features observed in the S~ao Paulo High, and its role as a domal upwelling focused on hydrothermal activity related to a large mantle plume.  This led to a modified model for the S~ao Paulo High during the Jurassic period, which this study hopes will be adopted by other researchers. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Additionally, we uncover that simply anticipating the players' responses to dialogue proves more crucial than delivering those responses itself, which surpasses baseline conditions that ignore the players' identities and world context. Our experiments provide initial insights into D4C, examining how the interactions are affected when the goal of the authority figure is shared among the players, as well as when the players' identities are manipulated within the framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/hahnfrt/dotproduct-dnd. Our work paves the way for further studies on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, evaluations rooted within the context of role-playing games, and the integration of theory-of-mind-inspired components with reinforcement learning. Our D4C framework also presents a unique role-playing game challenge that encourages the development of novel methods to tackle these issues. As a result, we release the code for our experiments in open-source form, along with the D4C framework, to support the growth of this area of research. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. Our analysis also reveals that proteins with trefoil knots have a higher tendency to get stuck at intermediate stages of folding and that this tendency is linked to their core residue resistance during folding. By examining specific examples, our research highlights the challenges that proteins with trefoil knots face during folding and how these challenges are reflected in the unique folding patterns of these proteins. Ultimately, this study suggests that the peculiar folding patterns of proteins with trefoil knots may be attributed to their intrinsic properties rather than being influenced by co-folding with other proteins or factors. The methods developed in this research can be applied to analyzing the folding processes of proteins with other types of knots and also to understanding the folding processes of other topologically complex proteins. By providing a focus on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, this study offers novel insights into their folding processes. Additionally, this research establishes a framework for comparing the geometry of these proteins based on their spatial arrangements, their folding pathways, and their co-folding behaviors. To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension. Additionally, we investigated the impact of varying assumptions in modeling structure formation and found that EDE's effect on the matter density parameter and the Hubble constant is minimal, supporting the idea that EDE is necessary to resolve the Hubble tension. Consequently, we derived a more precise prediction for the Hubble constant at the present time to be $68.9\pm 2.5$ ($68\%$ C.L.), significantly reducing the tension with observations of redshift. Our findings validate the existence of EDE and its ability to resolve the Hubble tension. To validate our analysis, we developed a publicly accessible code called EDEnorm and make it available for further investigation of EDE. Ultimately, our research highlights the value of structure formation data in conjunction with cosmic microwave background constraints in determining EDE parameters. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Ultimately, we observe that incorporating these counterfactual data into the instructor model itself leads to a small improvement in performance, albeit with room for enhancement. Alongside our primary findings, we also examine various components of the DISCO framework and counterfactual data quality, in addition to presenting techniques for refining the methodology. The code and data developed through our research are available at https://github.com/google-research-data/disco.

neighborhood sum distinguishing counterparts for specific types of circulant graphs. Moreover,
we established upper and lower limits for these chromatic numbers compared to general circulant
graphs. Additionally, some unsolved conjectures were proposed to further explore total chromatic
number properties within this class of graphs. Our investigation employed a novel method using
the structure of remainders from integer multiplication, combined with techniques from total
graph theory and circulant graph theory. This research was initially presented as part of the
firstoretical Computer Science Honors Project at the University of Hawaii at Manoa.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. A comprehensive theoretical analysis offered a surface energy model that can distinguish between remote epitaxy and other growth mechanisms, and predicted that the rotation domain percentage should increase at lower growth temperatures due to changed surface diffusion behaviors. This study highlights the potential for growing high-quality Heusler compounds with controlled electronic and magnetic properties through the precise manipulation of remote epitaxy. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to models trained using comprehensive datasets.  The technique developed in this paper provides a groundbreaking solution to the long-standing challenge of creating high-quality multi-label data while drastically reducing the need for extensive annotation. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  In addition to hadronic radiation, other processes must also contribute to gamma-rays in radio galaxies and the Milky Way's center.  Using this model, constraints can be placed on the conditions necessary for gamma-rays to occur and it can be applied to other radio sources and systems.  Furthermore, it is proposed that a search for gamma-rays occurring in relation to magnetic reconnection in our galaxy can inform us about the galaxy's overall radiation history. This study seeks to create advanced mathematical methods and computational tools to model portfolio returns, establishing essential formulas and efficient algorithms using techniques from computational geometry and splines. By leveraging these methods, our approach can efficiently handle large portfolios and accurately compute moments of the probability function within seconds. We primarily focus on the long-only strategy and develop an adaptable method for this type of investment. By representing the stock market as a geometric space, our cumulative distribution function enables a score for each portfolio based on the percentage of its returns exceeding a certain threshold. We derived closed-form equations for the first four moments and an innovative algorithm for computing all other moments, demonstrating a direct connection between the cross-sectional returns and the moments of the distribution. All of our methods are highly versatile, covering scenarios including when asset returns are equal. We used our score-based approach to design new performance metrics and found the portfolios it produced less concentrated and less prone to high risks than those from the mean-variance model. Our method and data are now available online at {https://quantfinance.github.io/PortfolioSDF/}. We plan to extend this work to other investment strategies and explore its applications in other fields. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.  The proposed method's performance, with an overall f-score of 0.75, serves as a benchmark for future research in this area.  The authors also highlight the potential applications of this technique to other sound-based diagnosis tasks and offer suggestions for improving the method's robustness through the use of transfer learning techniques.  The data collected and methods proposed can be useful for developing cardiac diagnosis systems, especially those based on machine learning, and the study's findings on noise effects can guide the design of more robust recording devices.  The author suggests that the method's use of multiple feature combinations and deep neural networks can facilitate the development of similar systems for diagnosing other medical conditions.  The author makes the proposed model's code and data set available for the benefit of the research community.  Future studies can build upon this work by investigating other noise reduction techniques and analyzing the effects of recording devices on cardiac auscultation sounds.  Additionally, extending this research to other sound-based diagnosis scenarios is also worthwhile.  The author also suggests using transfer learning with deep neural networks, which could enable the development of cardiac diagnosis systems using low-cost devices in different acoustic environments.  The author concludes by highlighting the potential for creating cardiac diagnosis systems that can accurately detect conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The code includes data preparations, evaluation protocols, and customization guidelines for healthcare datasets. The presented strategies can serve as a starting point for the development of active hedge fund strategies. In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional grid mapping for temporal sequences. If these vector bosons are substantially heavier, around $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ or above, a problem arises, as we then encounter difficulty in resolving the $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ anomaly consistently with the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ mixing constraints. However, the proposed framework is compatible with the given data within the one-sigma confidence threshold for each anomaly, with the parameter space to be examined by experiments such as NA62 and KOTO and through direct searches at the Large Hadron Collider. This concept also offers a possible explanation for the matter-antimatter asymmetry present in the universe. Furthermore, we find the framework capable of addressing, albeit marginally, the $B^0_\mathrm{s}\rightarrow\mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0\rightarrow\mu^+\mu^-$ anomalies; nevertheless, additional contributions will likely be needed to fully resolve the discrepancies seen in the latter decay. The introduction of these vector bosons results in an novel $pp\rightarrow \mu\nu$ signal that can be examined at the Large Hadron Collider, offering a possibility to verify our framework through direct observation. The proposed framework also facilitates the exploration of additional flavor-anomaly puzzles, such as the $D^0\rightarrow \mu\nu$ and $D^0\rightarrow \mu e$ decays, as well as the $B^0_\mathrm{s}\rightarrow D^0 K^-$ decay, within the context of the $B^0_\mathrm{s}\rightarrow D^0 K^-$ mode set to be examined by the LHCb experiment at an energy of $\sim 1.4\,\mathrm{TeV}$. It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
This research also involves an efficient approach for checking whether a given

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This is evident from the results on the new Music21 dataset, a recently created dataset dedicated to the classification of musical instruments. This dataset is now available for public use and may be suited to addressing other challenges related to the classification of instruments. Our proposed project paves the way for the expansion of existing models to tackle new categories of instruments with minimal shots required. Furthermore, the code and model have been deployed on a web app allowing users to upload sound files and get the classification results. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. You can access the dataset at which https://qasper-semantics.nlp.ucla.edu/ where you will also find instructions to use the proposed benchmark. Additionally, we present baseline models that can utilize the entire paper for answer generation, but these models fall short of human performance even when aided by document context, prompting us to propose new metrics that focus on answer quality within the extracted context. We anticipate these proposed metrics, along with the challenges they address, will spark enhanced research into document-grounded question answering that considers not just answer quality but also answer relevance within the document context. We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. Additionally, we develop the speed process for TASEP on a torus, the speed process for TASEP with jump parameter $s$, and the speed process for ASEP with jump parameter $p$. These developments are possible due to the deep connection established between the ASEP speed process and the stationary version of the speed process for TASEP, which is shown to be an orderly permutation process whose type is determined by the initial conditions, further illustrating the intricate relationship between these two systems. Moreover, we prove that the ASEP speed process can be represented by the stationary speed process for TASEP, whose order is determined by the initial data, and we discuss how this relationship provides a foundation for future exploration of the interconnection between these two systems. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our discovery for the TASEP speed process, the ASEP speed process, the stationary speed process for TASEP, and the speed process for ASEP, and we present an alternative proof for the convergence of the ASEP speed process, which is analogous to the proof for the TASEP speed process. This alternative proof is offered in an attempt to further clarify the underlying principles governing these systems. Consequently, our analysis offers a richer understanding of the dynamics governing these systems, which is complemented by the visualization of our findings in the accompanying figure. This visualization illustrates the trajectory of the ASEP speed process for systems with step initial data and various parameters $p$ and $s$. It is our hope that this visualization will stimulate additional exploration of the interplay between the ASEP and TASEP systems. To this end, we also propose an open question concerning the behavior of the ASEP speed process for systems with non-step initial conditions. Lastly, we present our results in a form that is accessible to a broad audience and includes relevant visualizations. These findings have a theoretical foundation but are also intended to stimulate further mathematical exploration and validation of our conjectures through rigorous proof. In particular, we propose an open question concerning the behavior of the ASEP speed process for systems with non-step initial conditions. This question represents a starting point for additional research

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. Additionally, along with the system, we was able to gather and present a comprehensive acronym dataset comprising over 300k unique expressions, encompassing phrases from over 11 million academic papers and extending beyond the existing Roster theory-based classification model. Within this dataset, we have been able to accurately identify acronyms in 75% of cases and successfully resolve ambiguities in 50% of situations where multiple definitions existed for a single acronym. Consequently, this system represents a significant step towards overcoming the challenges posed by acronym usage in written communication. It is also hoped that the data collected will prove useful for advancing related machine learning topics, such as word sense induction and distributed representation of words and concepts. Ultimately, this system is an open-source platform available for public access, along with the acquired acronym dataset, at no cost. Consequently, it is hoped that it will be of value to any researcher interested in the topic. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. This review also outlines potential applications of topological nodal lines, including their potential use in high sensitivity measurements of electric fields, temperatures, and strain, as well as their potential to enhance nonlinear optical effects and quantum phenomena in artificial materials. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Experimental results show the model's excellence in tumor classification and segmentation, exceeding the accuracy of radiologists in some cases. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Moreover, we show that shading-related losses can be learned through implicit models, such as neural networks, without relying on ground truth annotations. We demonstrate the versatility of our approach by applying it to various image-based problems, including shadow removal, illumination recovery, monaural stereo, non-lineare rigid pose estimation, and model-enhanced single-image 3D reconstruction and decomposition. Our method outperforms the best previous results or significantly improves upon them in tasks like shadow removal, monaural stereo, and single-image 3D reconstruction and decomposition. Our code and data are available at https://virtuals.org/projects/spherevision. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. Notably, our flow velocity predictions exhibit lower errors than previous studies, with a mean absolute error of 0.43 meters per second across all test points. The associated source code is publicly accessible for further modification and application to similar problems. Overall, our hybrid approach offers a balanced solution that balances predictive accuracy with computational efficiency, making it suitable for real-time flood risk management applications. In addition to its use in modeling river flows, this hybrid approach has the potential to be adapted to other complex problems characterized by uncertain data sets. In this research, we provide a thorough evaluation of the compared models and discuss their potential applications and future directions. Specifically, we explore the potential benefits of integrating this approach with other techniques, such as data augmentation and model ensemble methods, to further enhance its performance. Ultimately, we believe that our hybrid solution represents an important milestone in the development of efficient and accurate solutions for modeling complex phenomena from noisy data sets. Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions. For each comparison section, the authors include a method map, a summary of findings, and suggested future directions in the field. As an initial test, the authors include a comparison of methods within the context of the counterfactual prediction challenge. The framework, along with the associated code and results, is available for download at this link: https://github.com/ghfrick/CausalDeepLearningFrameworks. The field of causal deep learning is continually evolving, and the authors invite the research community to contribute to and utilize this framework for further comparisons and discussions. The current version of the framework is focused on counterfactual prediction but may be extended to cover other topics within the field. The authors hope that this initiative will facilitate open scientific discussions, encourage comparative studies, and provide a resource for method comparisons in the field of causal deep learning. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. By incorporating a model that takes into account the diversity of individual diffusion characteristics and their correlations, we derive a scaling law governing the population's mean squared displacements. Alternatively, individuals with similar diffusion characteristics can also be analyzed using an alternative model. We demonstrate the practical utility of our theory by analyzing the spread of a population utilizing a vision-based barium labeling method and observe the diversity of individual diffusion speeds within a sample population of 5 micron rods suspended in water over a temperature range of 5 to 37 degrees Celsius. Our research indicates that even in highly turbulent fluids, individual diffusivity can play a significant role in the spread of a population over time scales that are much longer than the individual's correlation time. Our research provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to any self-similar diffusion process, utilizing a general approach that is applicable to diverse correlation functions. Our study challenges the conventional notion that diffusion spreads uniformly over time and instead suggests that the spread can be nonlinear, influenced by the diversity of individual characteristics and their correlations. A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling an examination of mode coupling and phase modulation. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to study the nonlinear dynamics of twin modes born from mode coupling, revealing the emergence of an equilibrium state, period doubling, and an oscillating equilibrium due to Kerr nonlinearity. The validity of the derived trigonometric equation is verified through direct numerical simulation of the full PDE model. The developed framework provides a theoretical foundation for investigating the combined effects of linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity in optical systems, enabling the in-depth study of nonlinear mode coupling phenomena. Additionally, we discuss the feasibility of adapting discrete-time control methods when the system dynamics involve delays. It subsequently derives a non-radiative condition across inertial frames, consistent with the stability requirements of an atom, and establishes that this condition is analogous to certain relationships between charge, current, and the wave equations. The paper then demonstrates that these relationships lead to quantised electromagnetic field energy displaying the characteristics of the Balmer series. This implies that the quantisation of electric charge results from the restriction of possible solutions of the wave equation by the non-radiative condition, and is therefore a fundamental property of any stable atom. The paper also discusses the converse proposition - that any stable atom must have quantised energy. While this is mathematically valid, it is argued that it lacks physical significance due to its circular dependence on the non-radiative condition, which itself requires justification. The paper further explores the implications of these findings for the special theory of relativity and discusses the role of the non-radiative condition in atomic energy level structure. The quantisation condition is shown to apply beyond atomic physics, arising from the interaction between matter and the non-radiative electromagnetic field. The paper also analyses the energy spectrum of the hydrogen atom in a strong magnetic field, revealing that the quantisation condition holds across all energy levels, including those with orbital angular momentum. The paper also derives an explicit formula for the energy shift of the 2p orbital in a strong magnetic field, consistent with existing literature. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. This is reflected in lower calibration errors across various datasets and evaluation metrics. Additionally, EBOS exhibits superior performance in complex open-world scenarios, showcasing its effectiveness in real-world applications. The source code and data are freely available for download at: https://github.com/ghrua/EBOS. Our paper's findings also highlight the inherent advantages of open-world assumptions in modeling uncertainty. This research provides a novel, unified approach to both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling, demonstrating that machine learning models can achieve high accuracy while simultaneously capturing true uncertainty. This is particularly significant, as models are now equipped to tackle tasks that were previously considered the exclusive domain of uncertainty modeling, such as outlier detection and likelihood estimation. This research is a significant step towards developing machine learning models that are not only highly accurate but also robust in handling uncertainty. This is particularly important, as real-world machine learning tasks inevitably involve dealing with unknown data, unknown tasks, or unknown inputs, making uncertainty modeling an integral component of any machine learning model. This, in turn, enables them to excel in situations where a static world model would result in the learner being trapped in suboptimal loops. The model also achieves remarkable performance in more realistic settings, as illustrated by its success in a relatively simple gridworld environment. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. Our findings indicate that SPADE of this type can achieve higher precision in super-resolving the separation than what is achievable through coincidence measurement following the projection onto a Gaussian mode, and also reveal that the optimal SPADE state corresponds to an equal distribution among the lateral split photons as per the original SPADE proposal by Igumenshchev et al. Our experiment involves using a partially coherent source and two single-photon detectors to collect a total of $10^5$ events, resulting in a resolution improvement of 1.4 times the classical limit. This represents the largest improvement reported to date. Our work demonstrates the capability to super-resolve the Rayleigh criterion in optical imaging based on the SPADE principle. While our approach utilizes a quantum entangled source, its potential applications may still be accessible through classical imaging techniques that mimic quantum SPADE states. Consequently, our findings suggest the possibility of developing novel super-resolution optical imaging technologies. Although our research focuses on spatial resolution, the associated discussion on frequency entanglement and the construction of sources with desired properties may be applicable to other imaging scenarios based on time or frequency domain imaging. Consequently, our work has the potential to initiate a broader investigation on quantum-related aspects of super-resolution imaging. This, in turn, may lead to the development of more efficient sources and novel imaging technologies. Ultimately, our experiment paves the way for a range of quantum-related aspects of super-resolution imaging, encompassing both the study of sources with desired properties and the construction of actual imaging devices. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. Additionally, the requirements for the model's MMO behavior can be met in scenarios where the prey population experiences a moderate-level oscillation before the model transitions to its equilibrium. This finding is particularly relevant in analyses of the model's dynamics with variable prey movement rates. The model exhibits a complex, fragile environment that is sensitive to parameter adjustments, demonstrating the interplay between smooth, chaotic, and concatenated oscillations in a nonlinear system subject to selective filtering. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This implies that bulge growth is the primary driver of the mass-star formation rate relation behavior at these massive galaxy scales. Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The outcome shows substantial performance gains, attaining speeds up to 3.9 times faster than the original programs. Furthermore, when comparing programs concerning safety criteria, our method proves capable of finding correct programs where other methods fail. The counter-example driven fence insertion procedure's complexity prevents it from being suitable for real-world applications. However, the study still highlights the potential advantages of coherence-through-invalidation protocols, as optimal fence placement could significantly enhance program performance. In coexistence with traditional coherence protocols, fence-based methods may provide a balance between efficient cache management and ordering requirements of different program components. Ultimately, the research suggests the value of exploring fence-based coherence protocols for multi-core systems, Multi-Processors Systems-on-Chip, and distributed memory systems. The associated costs of fence insertion need to be balanced against the benefits of efficient cache management, especially when dealing with programs prone to data corruption. The potential for optimal fence placement to significantly improve program performance also presents an interesting research direction. The work introduced a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, an algorithm for optimal fence set insertion, and a prototype implementation to further investigate the efficacy of coherence-through-invalidation protocols. The study highlights the potential benefits of such approaches, offering a balance between efficient cache management and ordering requirements of different program components, especially in multi-core systems, Multi-Processors Systems-on-Chip, and distributed memory systems. The research also sets the stage for exploring fence-based coherence protocols in relation to traditional coherence methods. The

In this paper, we aim to enhance this by limiting the number of possible summands available from subset B. It's shown that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every four-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. It's also established that this Freiman's 3k-4 theorem holds if subsets A and B are composed solely of prime numbers. Furthermore, we establish a higher-dimensional analogue of this theorem along with a higher-dimensional analogue of a theorem attributed to Yang. It's also proven that if subsets A and B, of size k, meet the criterion that for every two-element subset of B, the sumset A plus that subset doesn't exceed 2k, it follows that A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. It's also shown that this Freiman's 3k-4 theorem holds if subsets A and B are composed solely of odd prime numbers. Using Dirac's time-dependent variational principle, we establish a simple H\'enon-Heiles model based on semiclassical mechanics. A two-body trial wavefunction in the form of Hatree-type is applied, leading to the derivation of an effective Hamiltonian in the context of Jackiw-Kerman theory. The calculations yield results indicating that quantum fluctuations can provoke chaotic behavior in regions of the H\'enon-Heiles system that classically remain stable. This finding is corroborated by both Lyapunov exponent and quantum correlation function analyses. Notably, we demonstrate that the quantum phase transition associated with the breakdown of classical stability shares the same eigenenergy as the starting point. This implies that the quantum transition is a result of the onset of correlations driven by the Jackiw-Kerman interaction, regardless of whether the classical system is chaotic or stable. Consequently, we propose that this type of transition represents a universal hallmark of quantum chaos in classical stable systems. Finally, we discuss the potential for generalizing these findings to additional stable classical systems. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Through this novel combination of techniques and insights gained, this work lays the groundwork for further exploration of using imaging characteristics to predict clinical outcomes in COVID-19 patients. As a broader contribution, this study demonstrates the value of using interpretable models to extract quantitative features from datasets with outcome labels in low-data settings, thus opening new avenues for additional medical applications. As such, this work is shared with the medical community to spark replication and additional investigations. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/SABRA.

This study offers a supervised action recognition solution that's effective even in the absence of light. We've obtained promising results by testing our approach on the ARID dataset, a significantly smaller and darker collection of video data. Notably, previous action recognition methods typically relied on well-lit datasets such as Kinetics and HMDB51. Our results indicate that our technique achieves remarkable accuracy despite being trained on a much reduced and poorly lit dataset of video sequences. We've experimented with multiple training and prediction methods including cross-domain techniques, as well as introducing an efficient yet straightforward approach for frame selection. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses existing benchmark models with a significant margin of 11% improvement. Additionally, our study shows that our technique performs frame selection efficiently and effectively, with results indicating that just 20% of frames hold valuable information for action recognition. Our code and dataset are available for public access. We've also initiated the release of a larger darker action recognition dataset called HeavyDish, consisting of 2000 classes of video sequences available for download. This dataset consists of rough, crowded real-world scenarios that are 5 times larger and darker than the ARID dataset, with challenging conditions that resemble everyday scenarios that our model should be capable of handling. We've established a competitive benchmark model that achieved a margin of 5% improvement on our proposed method, however it was trained on a much larger dataset with more light. We believe this study represents an important step towards developing a real-world action recognition model that's capable of functioning effectively in the absence of light and rough conditions. We plan to build upon this work by collecting more data, developing more advanced cross-domain techniques and refining our model to handle everyday situations that require action recognition. We've initiated the release of our code, dataset (ARID) and models for public access with the hope that it will spark further innovation in this field. We've received the code but not the new dataset HeavyDish yet.
