By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in the material structure, we employ two-scale convergence methods, while novel results are established for addressing the linear differential constraints via existence proofs for potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators. Ultimately, our investigations lead to an explicit formulation of the limit functional for a given problem. This formulation involves separating the energy contributions from the matrix and the fillings, or alternatively, an abstract formulation that directly considers the differential constraints. Consequently, our work paves the way for the systematic study of homogenization problems governed by differential constraints. To illustrate the effectiveness of these theories, we consider a specific application involving an electromagnetism problem. In this context, we derive a precise homogenized model, demonstrating the emergence of a principal part that represents the conductivity of the material, alongside a non-local part that reflects the impact of the fillings on energy storage. Notably, the stored energy within the fillings exhibits distinct variations across different components of the material structure. Consequently, the material structure's contrast plays a significant role in determining the energy's distribution between the matrix and the fillings. Ultimately, our analysis demonstrates the convergence of minimizers with respect to the $H^{1}$ norm under dimensional reduction scenarios. The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. To showcase its capabilities, we apply our software to the LCLS-II photo-injector laser, an example of a complex CPA-NLO system requiring high power and precise control. The model expedites innovative concept validation, allows for a comparison with experimental data, and facilitates the inverse design of new laser systems, paving the way for future CPA-NLO systems that integrate multi-petawatt amplifiers and compact dye lasers and enrich the scientific capabilities of future light sources. Moreover, this software is available online at https://github.com/linacsim/ampds and can be accessed through https://ampds.web.cern.edu for collaborative development and to support the community's modeling efforts.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual research, such as power spectrum calculations and foreground removal methods. As an example, we showcase how's4cmb' can be utilized to evaluate the impact of instrumental systematic effects on temperature and polarisation power spectrum estimates. Furthermore, we highlight the benefits of utilizing this type of simulated data in research, specifically in research related to next-generation CMB experiments such as CCAT-p and SPT-3G. The's4cmb' package is highly adaptable and simple to use; it comprises approximately 3000 lines of Python code and is openly accessible on GitHub at the stated URL. In addition to the package itself, we are providing the simulated data used in this study, along with the research described in this paper, in order for it to be reproducible and for other researchers to utilise it for their own research. In fact, the field of cosmic microwave background research stands to gain a maximum amount of $10,000 from the simulation of actual research conducted with's4cmb', in order for it to be thoroughly assessed in an actual experimental setting. In addition, the paper also includes an evaluation of the simulation's accuracy in replicating actual detector data, along with a demonstration of its flexibility in simulating various types of instrumental systematic effects and the performance of different foreground removal techniques on simulated data. In conclusion,'s4cmb' is a highly adaptable and simple to use Python tool that generates realistic raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments, along with a variety of instrumental systematic effects, in order to facilitate a deeper assessment of the impact of such effects on actual research. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. BART's ability to capture such structural information is a key factor in its success. Additionally, our findings suggest that BART's ordering capabilities can be attributed to the combination of the model's pre-trained language knowledge and its automatic acquisition of structural information during training on massive corpora. Building upon this insight, we propose an enhanced model that incorporates a auxiliary tree structure decoding task to further explore the potential of BART in this area. Our results show that models similar to BART that incorporate auxiliary tasks while transferring knowledge from the training set to new instances outperform baseline models and yield significant improvements, exceeding 90% accuracy in the test set for the first time in this field. Moreover, this improvement is achieved without the need for complex decoding algorithms or tree structures, simplifying the ordering process while surpassing previous performance benchmarks. Our work lays the groundwork for examining the capabilities of modern language models in word ordering tasks and provides preliminary evidence that models pre-trained on massive corpora possess a innate ability to recognize structural information that is leveraged through simple transfer learning. Alongside our code and data, our study is also accompanied by an extensive evaluation of BART's structural knowledge using probing, as well as an in-depth analysis of the model's performance on partial tree linearization. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Furthermore, our proposed method excels in robustness and is less prone to overfitting, as validated by experiments conducted with different dataset splits. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/NJU-Deepfake-Detection-Code.

In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. However, our results also indicate that positive degree-degree correlations may result in performance degradation or even ineffectiveness of certain coding modes. Interestingly, certain positive degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles can still achieve excellent error rates, albeit requiring careful optimization of degree-degree correlations at specific error tolerance levels. In particular, our experiments demonstrate that LDPC codes adapted to 10^-3 error tolerance can achieve substantially improved performance, with further increases yielding only marginal improvements. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical basis for the design of unequal error protection codes that adapt to varying error rates, as well as the construction of correlated LDPC codes with enhanced performance. Furthermore, we propose using our model in conjunction with general loss channels, and outline strategies for optimizing degree-degree correlations via iterative decoding performance metrics. Lastly, we describe the potential advantages of extending our findings to other coding schemes, such as polar codes, and outline the scope for future research in this area. The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide ideal environments for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse and the streaming instability. Observational data on exoplanets supports this process and creates favorable conditions for planetary system formation. This model may explain the origins of ring systems in our solar system and account for the absence of large dust formations in mature disks. It also provides a possible solution to the planetary migration mystery, allowing planets to migrate without destroying the disks they form from. This process of viscous ring-instability may be a crucial step in planetary system formation, leading to the creation of planetary building blocks and eventually, planets. This may occur not just in our solar system but also in other systems, as suggested by similarities between our solar system's disk structures and those observed in advanced disks. This theory requires further experimentation in laboratory settings that mimic protoplanetary disks to be fully tested. It offers a possible solution to several planetary formation-related puzzles and lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive understanding of planetary system development. This research also highlights the value of collaborating between theoretical astronomers and the developers of astrophysical simulation software. It also highlights the potential of GPU-based simulations, which can handle complex interactions in protoplanetary disks, making it possible to study these systems in greater detail. This study paves the way for a series of follow-up simulations that can model the development of planetary systems and inform upcoming telescopes that will study these systems up close. A specific setup involving a path that only includes neutral modes, essential for an electric current from the source to the drain, is examined here. When a source is biased in this circuit, it is observed that an electric current can be measured at the drain, provided that backscattering between opposing modes at the contact locations is present. The result shows that neutral modes hold relevant information and can be used for a nonlocal reconstruction of a dc charge current. The described protocol may be employed to detect any neutral mode that counter-propagates with respect to charge modes, and this detection approach is applicable not only to the edge modes of quantum Hall systems but also to systems possessing neutral modes that do not originate from quantum Hall effects. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also outperforming other decentralized distributionally robust learning algorithms, specifically obtaining an improvement of up to $30\%$ over DecENT-D2PAI. Our work provides a comprehensive solution to the distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks, addressing model uncertainty and data skewness issues. Our research code can be found at: https://github.com/linguicai/Distributionally-Robust-Decentralized-Optimization. Our work is also featured in the proceedings of the 33rd International Conference on Algorithmic Learning Theory (ICALP 2021).

Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. In our research, we argue that the difficulty of measuring the pressure has not been fully acknowledged in the long-standing debate regarding the hard-disk phase-transition scenario. Our paper provides the fundamental principles of the hard-disk model, defines the concept of pressure and presents new, unbiased methods of estimating it. Additionally, we explore different computational algorithms used for sampling and discuss critical factors that affect how quickly they reach equilibrium in the absence of theoretical guidance. Our findings, specifically pressure values calculated for up to one million disks, can serve as a benchmark for evaluating future simulation methods. This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with perturbative scales, nuclear PDFs, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated through Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored. Finally, the sensitivity of jet modifications to nuclear PDFs is quantified in terms of $R_{AA}$ at 2 TeV, and the importance of considering multiple nuclear PDF options is highlighted.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. In conclusion, our research demonstrates the value of combining manual and automated code analysis with social media data in examining complex, hidden networks of deception. Furthermore, this research is a call to action for a more unified set of terminology and classification frameworks for the study of pyramid schemes and other hidden networks of deception. This is essential for facilitating interdisciplinary research in this field. This is the first empirical analysis of a blockchain-based pyramid scheme built by thousands of participants, offering unique insights into the inner workings and user behavior of this kind of investment deception. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We included a list of suggested new globular clusters for external verification. We also analyzed the distribution of a RR0 type star found within the VVV survey and concluded that they could be part of two distinct movements within the galaxy's bulge, also highlighting the need for follow-up studies in the Eclipsing Binary category due to their important role in measuring the galaxy's bulge's rotation speed. We stressed the significance of solving the mystery surrounding the galaxy's bulge's rotation speed, especially with the upcoming survey known as VHS. We ended by highlighting the scientific value that could be obtained from the VVV survey, especially with its unique infrared perspective, and suggested using its database to analyze other interesting objects such as dark globules, planetary nebulas, and white dwarf stars. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We further established that the difference between these models arises solely from the interband effects, whereas the single-band approximation is gauge-invariant by definition. Finally, we employed our findings to improve the simulation of pump-probe spectroscopy. By incorporating interband effects, our modified velocity-based model accurately replicates the outcomes of the dipole-based model, ensuring proper description of optical excitations while adhering to gauge invariance. This improved approach offers a straightforward solution to mitigate the discrepancies often observed in velocity-based TB models and facilitates a deeper comprehension of the limitations and successes of these models in relation to first-principle theory. The formulated rules are universally applicable to any TB model constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions in two-dimensional paradigm materials. The strategies outlined in this study can be extended to other simulation methods for light-matter interactions, such as strong-field simulations, and serve as a crucial reference for the simulation of light-matter interactions utilizing TB models. Furthermore, the steady-state quantum yield was shown to be exquisitely sensitive to minor adjustments in system parameters, in stark contrast to the relative insensitivity of transient dynamics. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing suggests that quantum chaos might underlie this phenomenon, and potential avenues for experimental validation along with implications in complex light-sensitive systems are explored. Moreover, the sensitivity of quantum yields to temperatures and energy barriers surrounding the reaction path is also considered. Ultimately, this study proposes that rhodopsin's ability to control quantum yields could be an adaptation to minimize heat loss due to non-radiative decay in complex environments. In doing so, this research frames quantum coherence in complex systems as worthy of further empirical investigation in an experimental context. Although this study focuses on visual receptor rhodopsin, similar considerations may apply to other sensitive systems that respond to light, such as cryptophores. Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Furthermore, our findings pave the way for further
research into the behavior of deep learning models in complex processes by
incorporating event quantities and case completion times in assessments. The
associated data and methods are openly available for replication of our studies.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare on AD Leo during its peak phases. This model employs line broadening factors that closely mirror those seen in the observed flare spectra, and it demonstrates how near-ultraviolet continuum flux can be accurately estimated through the use of semi-empirical formulas that take into account the radius of the flare peak and the spectral energy distribution. In addition, this study finds that the two largest flares observed so far, including the massive one on EV Lac (R=4.16R$_{\odot}$, E=42.8$10^{31}$ erg) and the superflare on AD Leo (R=1.71R$_{\odot}$, E=8.8$10^{33}$ erg), with energies that significantly exceed those of the largest X-ray flares observed on our Sun, have radii that are comparable to those of the largest solar white-light flares, and imply that similar amounts of energy could also be released in future large flares on these stars, with a substantial portion likely being absorbed by the surrounding planets, which could have important implications for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures. Lastly, this study suggests that extreme UV flux increases of as much as 10$^4$ times above normal levels in low-m mass stars, which can persist for several hours following a stellar flare, may provide a suitable opportunity for life on planets in these systems to be exposed to increased levels of energetic radiation. Consequently, assessing the potential for biosignatures in these planets should take into account the presence of recent stellar flare activity. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems. Additionally, we find that using Bogoliubov quasiparticle energies instead of original particle energies yields a more efficient matrix filling scheme. By leveraging these compact formulas, various physical properties of complex nuclei can be computed with enhanced speed and accuracy. Available upon request are Python scripts that implement these concise mathematical formulas, along with specific Bogoliubov-de Gennes Hamiltonian parameters for the nuclides $^{140}$Ba, $^{142}$Ba, $^{144}$Ba, $^{146}$Ba, $^{148}$Ba, $^{150}$Ba, $^{152}$Ba, $^{154}$Ba, $^{156}$Ba, $^{158}$Ba, $^{160}$Ba, $^{162}$Ba, and $^{164}$Ba. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing. Lastly, we include an analytical technique for the complexity of compositionally indirect transformations in 3D geometry. This research paves the way for trustworthy operation of point cloud models in critical applications.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics. We
also provide visualizations highlighting time-encoded information and demonstrate
our code's flexibility by applying Time-LowFER to inference tasks and multi-task
learning. The code is available at https://github.com/hubersb/Time-LowFER.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. Moreover, calculations indicate that the real part of one of the poles located at 10.8 MeV is only 5.1 MeV, which is significantly lower than the average energy of the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance. Additionally, research has shown that the width of this resonance can be explained by the resonance fluctuating towards the 110 lying state at a energy of 24.7 MeV due to the interaction with it, which is characterized by a large width of 7.5 MeV. This finding highlights the importance of considering the effects of long-lived states that lie far above the main resonance in question. It is hoped that further exploration of this approach will lead to a deeper understanding of the complex excited states of nuclei. In addition, it is hoped that this research will pave the way for investigating the complex excited states of stable and unstable nuclei, as well as studies of electron-scattered nuclei in other reactions, such as quasi-free scattering, fragmentation reactions, and photo-nuclear reactions, using world-leading experimental facilities such as the AMBER experiment at the FAIR facility. Research is also planned to be carried out in collaboration with leading research centers around the world. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. In all scenarios, our method showcases the systems' dynamic nature captured in cluster structure, also incorporating temporal information to improve accuracy and reliability. Furthermore, our approach is found to be robust to parameter settings and outperforms established clustering algorithms using dynamic data. Additionally, our technique facilitates meaningful labels by integrating expert knowledge and the structural properties of clusters, which is illustrated through the analysis of cluster results in the three mentioned applications. This research is part of a broader framework that aims to investigate fundamental properties of complex dynamic systems through clustering and dimensionality reduction techniques. Specifically, this paper focuses on detecting communities in dynamic systems, while future work will explore more advanced techniques to analyze the temporal dimension and system dynamics. Alongside this work, an open-source repository is available for reproducibility and future advancements in this area. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. The gained linguistic efficiency and purity also lead to better performance on unsupervised and low-resource settings. Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted at redshift z=0.5, comparing these to the performance that can be expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys. The impact of removing foregrounds using methods that rely on simulations is accounted for in the analysis, which shows how it affects the accuracy of the parameter estimation. The 10 parameters that we vary during the analysis consist of 3 cosmological and 7 non-cosmological parameters. The 4 most relevant parameters are the cold dark matter density, the Hubble constant, the primordial power spectrum amplitude and the linear HI bias. When assuming that foregrounds can be effectively removed, our best case scenario finds that the estimated parameters are accurate with less than a 3% error. When including the impact of foregrounds however, all parameters are estimated inaccurately by more than 5 sigma, indicating that foregrounds removal has to be more accurately handled to avoid biases. Scale cuts, specifically a minimum k-value of about 0.03 h/Mpc, need to be imposed in order to get an accurate estimation of the two most relevant cosmological parameters. The price for this accuracy, however, is a loss of precision, while two of the other parameters still end up biased in their estimates. The implications of these findings are relevant to the ongoing analysis of actual data and will be relevant in forthcoming data analysis. The code that is used for these analysis is publicly available and can be used to derive power spectrum constraints for any experiment that maps the sky in the same way as the ones that we study here. The code can therefore be a useful tool for any experiment that is planning to conduct an analysis of its own data or is preparing for upcoming data analysis. The code can be used to derive power spectrum multipoles, power spectrum covariance matrices, foregrounds power spectra and maps of the sky, all of which are essential for any analysis of HI intensity mapping data. The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest. The vacuum's initial spontaneous symmetry breaking can give dark matter its present-day relic density. The implementation of this concept in quantum field theory is examined, including the effects of vacuum fluctuations and the potential for the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry. The interplay between dark matter and the antimatter universe is explored, offering the possibility of predicting the universe's matter content based on its dark matter content. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Our proposed method addresses this issue by factoring in the biase's adjustment to provide more accurate density estimates.  Moreover, using resource selection models in capture-recapture enhances the understanding of animals' spatial behavior, providing valuable information for research on animal population ecology.  We apply our method to data involving the movements of bobcats and their prey in the southeastern United States.  Our analysis highlights the value of combining capture data from multiple sources, resource selection data from telemetry, and the advantages of using capture-recapture models that account for space usage, as well as the benefits of using telemetry data alone to investigate space usage.  We also provide a comprehensive description of our method's components, model parameters, and the associated R code.  Ultimately, our study emphasizes the significance of integrating biological knowledge about animals' movements and space usage, incorporating data from multiple sources, and using appropriate statistical models to conduct in-depth research on animal population ecology.  We conclude that our proposed method opens up fresh avenues for conducting groundbreaking research in this field.  We conclude by outlining potential applications and future research directions for combining capture-recapture and resource selection data, including new methods for analyzing multi-season data, exploring new capture-recapture models, and developing new models for analyzing encounter probability. This study proposes a technique for the autonomous planning of swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles within a predefined environment. When the swarm detects changes, such as the movement of a target, within a designated area, the command center recalculates and adjusts the swarm's flight path. Key algorithms employed in this research are A* pathfinding and Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli for target tracking. The approach is adaptable to scenarios where the swarm's configuration and sensing capabilities vary. Implementing the proposed method on a simulator built with PySN, we investigate how A* path planning is affected by different A* parameters, target movement, and camera field of view. Furthermore, we examine the impact of target tracking on swarm planning through simulated experiments. Despite not being feasible for real-world implementation due to its synthetic nature, the research provides valuable insights into the behavior of A* path planning in dynamic scenarios. In addition, it sets the stage for exploring more advanced planning methods, such as time-dependent A*, in future related studies. The implemented algorithm and experiment data are available for replication through an accompanying GitHub repository. Alongside this paper, a companion video illustrates the swarm's planning and adjustment processes in response to moving targets.

This study tackles this issue by measuring nodal activity to quantify localization in networks undergoing dynamic changes. The proposed method is widely applicable and can be employed with theoretical models, simulated data, and real-world observations. The researchers analyze spreading processes on various networks, demonstrating that nodal activity can display intricate patterns depending on the network's architecture. The findings indicate that localized and widespread patterns are not mutually exclusive features in a spreading process. Additionally, the prevalence of an epidemic near a critical transition is influenced by the delocalized component of the network. Furthermore, different critical exponents can coexist with similar localization patterns. The study also reveals a more intricate behavior in quenched networks, influenced by the type of activation and degree exponent. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive players. Furthermore, our approach enabled us to provide insights into the superior defensive performances of finalist teams in the 2020 European Football Championship, and our methodology may also be applied to location data from other broadcast football matches. By combining player location data and game data, our approach can facilitate a deeper understanding of the relationship between game events and their underlying causes. Alongside its accuracy, our approach stands out from previous research through its robust prediction of rare game events and consideration of diversity factors. The code for our approach is available online at https://github.com/marcosouza/evaluating-defensive-teams, along with additional details about our methods. The code incorporates metrics for assessing the importance of individual players in specific game circumstances, such as situations leading to goals or concessions, and offers insights into the effect of player diversity on game events. Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwriting, and their relationships. Our technique excels in handling imperfect form images, unlike previous approaches designed for well-organized images. To test its effectiveness, we created a database of deteriorated forms from the late 1800s and early 1900s. Our model uses a neural network to identify both types of text, after which we classify their relationships through the analysis of the detected text features. Our research indicates that our relationship-determination technique performs better than rule-based methods and confirms that visual features play a key role in achieving high accuracy in these situations. Our technology has the potential to make significant contributions to the analysis of historical documents. Our relationship-determination technique is particularly relevant to other fields that deal with complex documents, such as scientific articles and web pages. Our model achieves the best results in our "Wild": a random subset of deteriorated forms that were not included in the database. Our results demonstrate accuracy rates of 83.6% for identifying pre-printed text, 83.9% for identifying handwriting, and 47.5% for determining their relationships. Our technique has the potential to assist other document analysis algorithms with the interpretation of output, thereby enhancing the overall performance in applications like database updating and form-based data collection. Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed a state-space model called the Gaussian Embedding Recurrent State-space Model (GERSM), which uses an embedding similar to word2vec to capture these types of connections within a dynamic system. By modeling the temporal relationships between these embedded states, GERSM can accurately forecast multiple interconnected time series at a single underlying state variable. Through various applications, including forecasting financial indicators and electrophysiological signals, we demonstrated that our model performs exceptionally well when compared to other methods, such as feedforward neural networks and traditional state-space models. Furthermore, to tackle the challenge of non-linear observations, we also explored a variation of the model and found it to be a powerful tool for analyzing and visualizing state space data. Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of asymptotic conditional freeness. Specifically, we demonstrate the empirical spectral distribution of randomly rotated matrices converges towards a conditionally free convolution. We've also identified new relationships between infinitesimal freeness, type $B$ freeness, conditional freeness, cyclic monotonicity, and monotone independence. Moreover, we show that the BBP phase transition in an additive rank-one perturbation of a GUE matrix is a consequence of asymptotic conditional freeness. This line of reasoning applies as well to an analysis of outlier eigenvalues in various unitarily invariant ensembles. Lastly, we present an direct proof of asymptotic conditional freeness for very large matrices, and an indirect proof of the same condition for matrices of the same size. The indirect proof relies on an argument involving asymptotic type $B$ freeness, and thus is valid only for matrices of relatively small size. In contrast, our direct proof is valid only in the "very large" case. In this case, one of the matrices can be shown to be relatively free from the other with an error of $O(N^\delta)$ where $\delta$ is an arbitrarily small positive number. This fact alone seems worthy of note. In particular, the freeness error for two $N\times N$ matrices would be $O(N^{1/3})$ according to a known lower bound by Edelman. However, our new analysis yields an even more significant improvement. In fact, we've proven that the error can be further reduced to $O(N\log N)$ by using an inequality from Taagera (2000). In turn, this improvement results from our primary finding of asymptotic type $B$ freeness for unitarily invariant matrices. We construct a genus-2 curve X, such that its Jacobian is connected to a product of the Jacobian of D and X's Jacobian, the Jacobian of C being an isogeny. Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and notably, the choice of measurement method became significantly less crucial, with most methods surpassing the previous best performance following normalization. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough evaluation and comparison of different structural polarization measurement methods. Additionally, we provide a suite of simulated networks that can be utilized for further study and are compatible with the widely employed Multiplex Perspective, thereby enriching the set of available reference networks. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. Additionally, attempting to parameterize the Einstein operator leads to the Bianchi operator, which is a bridge to further research on the Einstein operator's deeper symmetries and potential connections to the Einstein field equations. By extending the Einstein operator to an $n$-dimensional manifold and designating a differential module with differential rank zero, the paper proves that the original differential operator can be expressed solely by the Einstein operator, which is analogous to how the Einstein operator can be defined solely by the Cauchy operator for a one-dimensional manifold. This discovery paves the way for exploring deeper symmetry properties of the Einstein operator and may provide new insights into the Einstein field equations. Lastly, the paper mentions a related interesting problem concerning the N-dimensional Einstein operator and discusses the Eisen operator's symmetry properties in relation to the Bianchi operator. The discussion is extended to the Einstein operator in the presence of gravitation's multiplicative symmetries, linked to the Eisen operator's Galois module structure, which is governed by the Bianchi operator. This work also raises the inquiry as to whether new fundamental deep symmetries of gravity might be identifiable through the Einstein operator's deeper properties, which would then be reflected in the structure of its generating compatibility operator, the Bianchi operator. The discussion on this topic is expanded to consider whether there may exist an intricate web of dyadic relationships between the Einstein operator, the Bianchi operator, and the Eisen operator, all of which would be codified within the framework of the Eisen operator's Galois module architecture. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. Once changes are made, the tool can display the modified code's reliability as a vector pointing out necessary steps to verify the fix. To illustrate this concept, we created a prototype using a data structure called dependency graphs, whose nodes represent pieces of code and whose edges indicate data flow between them. To test this prototype, we created a sample program that incorporates various programming principles and tested it with different types of errors, including both program bugs and intentional flaws. The results showed that the prototype can effectively pinpoint the root cause of each mistake, understand the implications of proposed fixes, and gauge the reliability of the modified code. To take this verification and testing process to the next level, we also developed a way to visualize the code's reliability as a path leading to a goal state represented by trustworthy code. To demonstrate this, we created a prototype that uses a technique called metric vector visualization, whose advantages include the ability to show the distance each proposed fix needs to travel to reach the goal state and highlight areas of the code that need adjustment. However, this technique has a significant drawback where the number of lines of code that can be displayed at once is limited to only a few dozen. To address this issue, we created another way to visualize the code's reliability, where the underlying causes of each mistake are presented as a causal chain of events leading to the error, whose advantages include the ability to display hundreds of lines of code at once. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on diverse models and benchmarks, such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks for Natural Language Understanding, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning approaches like Prompt-Tuning, HyperFormer++ and T5. The code and models are openly accessible at https://github.com/acghuang/HyperPrompt. With HyperPrompt, prompt-based multi-task learning has achieved performance parity with heavy finetuning baselines. Furthermore, HyperPrompt has achieved remarkable success in Natural Language Generation, specifically on the CausalLM dataset, surpassing sequence-to-sequence models that utilize additional support. We also present an in-depth analysis of HyperPrompt's architecture, encompassing a detailed exploration of the learned global task memories, demonstrations of robust performance under data augmentation, as well as a comparative study of prompt types. Ultimately, HyperPrompt represents a landmark model that showcases the capability of prompt-based multi-task learning to attain high-performance parity with heavyweight baselines. Additionally, its success in Natural Language Generation solidifies the foundation for further exploration of prompt-based methods in this domain. With its open availability, HyperPrompt offers a valuable resource for researchers to advance prompt-based multi-task learning and Natural Language Generation. Let $\Phi$ be a root system belonging to type $A_l$ or $D_l$. Let $K$ be a field whose characteristic is not $2$. Let $\delta$ be the maximal root in the root system $\Phi$ and define the set $\Phi_0$ as consisting of the roots $\alpha$ in $\Phi$ for which $\alpha$ is orthogonal to $\delta$. In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena. Furthermore, it paves the way for applying symmetry protection principles to other phenomena of non-classical photon emissions, such as those related to quantum chaos and entanglement. This finding is further illustrated by an emission spectrum that exhibits an increased visibility of events like anti-Stokes processes and the formation of sidebands, all of which would typically be obscured by strong single-photon emissions. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. In theory, the algorithm's performance is optimal in a broad sense, as it attains the highest possible ratio of network size estimation accuracy to round complexity, to the power of 1/delta, where delta is any arbitrarily small positive constant. In addition, our implementation in a simulated environment demonstrates the algorithm's effectiveness. The algorithm complements other well-known algorithms for detecting a small number of malicious nodes in complex networks. The algorithm's novelty lies in focusing on estimating the network's size rather than detecting malicious nodes, and it is an uncoordinated decentralized solution, as contrasted with existing centralized and coordinated approaches. The algorithm addresses a critical challenge in designing complex networks and the fundamental protocols that underpin them, facilitating further research in this area. The algorithm is applicable to various types of networks in which node estimation can be adequately characterized by counting node connections, such as distributed hash tables, where estimating the network's size is equivalent to estimating the number of entries in the hash map. The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. The effectiveness of this approach is further highlighted by a comparison with standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition methods involving the momentum constraint. The novel approach also preserves the same gauge choices and symmetry properties inherent in earlier methods. The code developed through these experiments is now publicly available for the community to use in future related research projects. The algorithms discussed here have significant implications for extending the scope of existing numerical relativity codes to include fundamental fields. The review also includes an examination of the fundamental aspects of the technique, along with a detailed exploration of its practical applications and potential future directions. The code developed in this project can be found at https://github.com/zhangzhongtao/Lax-Wendroff-Shapiro-Solver. The features of this code include an iterative algorithm for solving the Hamiltonian constraint, a wave collapse solver for the Einstein equations, and a monopole treatment for boundary value problems. The code represents a significant step towards improving the flexibility and capability of current numerical relativity codes, making it suitable for inclusion in publicly available general relativistic simulations of binary neutron star mergers. The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra. Upper limits on the decay rate of $\Sigma^+$ to $p$ and muon pairs are set at 0.016 $10^{-6}$ ps$^{-1}$ and 0.017 $10^{-6}$ ps$^{-1}$ for branching ratios respectively, significantly reducing previous limits and providing the most stringent upper limits on this decay type to date. Additionally, observed events' characteristics are consistent with expectations of scalar quark pair production theories that predict $\Sigma^+$ decaying to muon pairs to occur at a rate of $0.33$ $10^{-6}$ ps$^{-1}$. 

This study's results, coupled with previous findings from BaBar and DELPHI, enhance the case for $\Sigma^+$ decaying into muon pairs, a phenomenon that could be examined in depth by upcoming experiments such as NA62/ANGEL and LHCb's upcoming upgrade, particularly when considering the sensitivity of NA62/ANGEL to discover or confirm $\Sigma^+$ decaying into muon pairs, a phenomenon anticipated to occur at a rate of $0.33$ $10^{-6}$ ps$^{-1}$. 

This research, published in Phys. Lett. B 775 (2019) 429-438, offers the most competitive upper limit on $\Sigma^+\to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ until more precise experiments like NA62/ANGEL can provide conclusive evidence or validation of this decay type.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity share a linear relationship, exhibiting direct proportionality, and can be interpreted as a manifestation of the spin-dependent thermal diffusion and the influence of local magnetic field on thermal diffusion. Notably, our study offers a perspective that the anomalous Nernst effect can be understood in relation to the anomalous Hall effect, and both are controllable via magnetic manipulation. Moreover, our research implies that the anomalous Nernst effect could serve as a viable measure for assessing the local magnetic state in materials with hidden magnetization. Lastly, our results may contribute to the development of more accurate thermal transport theories in these complex materials.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. Notably, PILE's efficiency in model compression is remarkable, achieving a 25x model compression ratio with minimal performance degradation in online settings. This pioneering work is now available as an open-source repository.

This lecture will provide an elementary overview of both transverse and longitudinal beam dynamics, in addition to key beam loss phenomena in circular accelerators, catering to attendees with minimal to no prior understanding of this topic. It's intended for individuals not directly involved in beam work, such as administrative staff, engineers responsible for infrastructure, and those in financial roles, although anyone interested in learning about beam dynamics is welcome to attend. Presentations covering specific topics like straggling, nuclear interactions, and additional loss mechanisms will be kept brief and illustrated with simple diagrams. Estimates of global and local beam loss rates, as well as their impact on machine performance and availability, will be highlighted using real-world data from the Large Hadron Collider. It's hoped that by the end of the lecture, attendees will have a fundamental grasp of beam loss concepts and their effects, as well as the importance they hold for ensuring the effective functioning of particle accelerators. Presentation slides can be found in the 2019 beam loss conference proceedings available at https://doi.org/10.1088/1742-6596/1378/1/012004. Further information on future relevant training opportunities can be found at https://edms.cern/chapter/1817314. It's anticipated that discussions following the lecture will explore potential collaborations to develop computational tools illustrating beam loss phenomena, which could be made accessible to the particle physics community via the Community Grid Computing project. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. As demonstrated with data from the ID32 beamline at NSLS-II, this framework allows users to develop modular, robust, and easily deployable machine learning models that can be used for real-time classification, regularization, and enhancement. By incorporating these models into their experiments, users can obtain high-quality data more efficiently, thereby opening up new possibilities for scientific research. To facilitate collaboration and streamline development, the source code for these machine learning models has been made publicly accessible on GitHub. By providing a modular machine learning framework that runs on top of Blueky, this work aims to inspire further innovation in machine learning for functional materials research and encourage more users to contribute their own models. As a result, a broader community can benefit from this framework and help develop machine learning models that can be executed across multiple beamlines at user facilities. Ultimately, this work represents a significant step towards creating a community-driven machine learning library that can be executed across different user facilities, empowering the machine learning community to contribute models developed at other facilities and fostering greater collaboration among researchers. By doing so, it will accelerate the adoption of machine learning across the materials science community and fuel the development of novel machine learning models for other applications in this field.
