This work revisits linear gyrokinetic theory for geodesic acoustic modes and develops a general dispersion relation applicable to various ion distribution functions. A specific bi-Maxwellian ion distribution is analyzed to determine the impact of temperature anisotropy on mode frequency and growth rate, which shows significant increases due to anisotropy, heavily influenced by the electron-to-ion temperature ratio. Additionally, a condition is identified for the mode to be unstable and dominated by a driving instability. Growth rates and frequencies from linear gyrokinetic theory are compared to empirical mode energy and fluctuation density observations found in the Tore-Supra and J-ET-PT-U experiments. Findings suggest that high frequency GAMs could be explained by ion temperature anisotropy, while lower frequency modes might result from anisotropy alone or in combination with electron responses. A parameter anisotropy ratio is proposed to classify modes into distinct regimes. Nonlinear effects are examined in a simplified model, revealing that the ion response can lead to mode amplitude saturation, while the electron response can induce mode amplitude growth. As ions play a crucial role in supporting the mode energy, further research is recommended to fully understand ion dynamics in this context. Finally, this work is supplemented by a detailed review of linear GAM theory.

A promising technique known as quantum annealing has the potential to efficiently solve complex optimization problems by leveraging the unique properties of quantum systems under gradual change. However, a significant challenge lies in creating and controlling quantum devices that closely mimic the described physics. A new approach proposed here divides large optimization problems into more manageable components by representing their minimization as magnetization transitions within Ising models and applies this transformation to a driver spin connected to multiple "problem" spins. As a result, any two spins with interaction become interchangeable. Furthermore, this driver spin allows us to implement "history-based" and "avalanche" types of quantum annealing. Experimental demonstration of these protocols has been performed using a quantum annealing platform based on superconducting quantum circuits, resulting in the successful solution of an avalanche-like minimum-finding for a problem of of 16 variables. Furthermore, this study also investigates the performance of these protocols on "valley-free" and "avalanche-like" types of Hamiltonians, indicating that the "avalanche" type has a higher success rate than "history-based" for "valley-free" and the opposite for "avalanche-like". This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. In addition, some autobiographical elements are incorporated as the author is one of three directors serving the lab since van Rhijn's tenure. In reviewing van Rhijn's contributions and the circumstances surrounding his leadership, this study hopes to provide insight into the events that triggered the lab's revival and ultimately resulted in the formation of the Kapteyn Astrophysical Laboratory at the University of Groningen. In doing so, it sets the stage for the lab's future role in the ongoing global scientific quest. In 2009, the European Astronomical Agency selected the lab as the site for the formation of the Dark Energy Survey and subsequently the Square Kilometre Array's Optical Survey, positioning the lab at the forefront of the next generation of groundbreaking surveys in the field. In this context, the legacy of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn and the evolution of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory during his tenure hold significant lessons for the lab's current direction and future ambitions. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training. The paper's figures and additional results can be found in the accompanying supplemental document.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.

This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. As such designs should also be susceptible to enhancement by data from modules, ours represents a pioneering effort in this realm and paves the way for further research into optimizing instructional design with data, particularly in physics education. As students faced significant challenges adapting to remote learning, our data may be viewed as'stress data'. Consequently, our study provides valuable insights for designers of online learning modules in high-stress conditions and serves as a starting point for investigating best practices that emerge from modules in such circumstances. In this context, ours is the first study to examine the effects of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on university students' ability to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. As such, our findings are likely relevant to other STEM courses with similar instructional designs. Given the temporary nature of the COVID pandemic as a stressor, our data is unlikely to be useful for guiding long-term instructional design decisions. We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures. Furthermore, we prove that Coxeter groups are oriented total uniform lattices. Combining these findings with recent work, we achieve a complete classification of the oriented total uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings, encompassing all Coxeter groups and their superrigid counterparts. Our classification enables the resolution of direction-faithfulness conjectures for various algebraic representations, including those associated with tree lattices, complex hyperbolic lattices, and Finsler geometry. Additionally, our results extend the Birkhoff-Tarski theorem and its counterparts for Dirichlet uniform lattices. Moreover, we establish the existence of orientation-preserving uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings, resolving a conjecture of Ballamy and Razafimandimby. Alongside these outcomes, we also present results on the biautomatic properties of these lattices. Lastly, we discuss implications of our work on the dynamics of Coxeter groups and uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass and charge configuration. The outcome of scattering when this relationship is not met is that the near-extremal black hole is overcharged, resulting in its transformation into two separate particles. The study also confirms that the horizon radius of these black holes plays a critical role in determining whether they have singularities or not. Specifically, when the horizon radius is greater than the critical value, these black holes have singularities, whereas when the horizon radius is less than the critical value, they do not have singularities. The investigation into the cosmic censorship conjecture in these black holes reveals that overcharging causes the destruction of these black holes, leading to the emergence of a naked singularity. The study further reveals that the big bang cosmology could have resulted from the collision of two overcharged near-extremal black holes, leading to the creation of a naked singularity. The subsequent collapse of this singularity led to the formation of two separate universes, each containing a black hole with negative electric charge. The study also reveals that the entropy of these black holes is proportional to their horizon area, confirming the validity of the holographic principle. The investigation into the temperature of these black holes shows that their temperature is inversely proportional to their horizon radius. The study further reveals that the specific heat capacity of these black holes is negative, confirming that they can undergo phase transitions. The investigation into the adiabatic invariant of these black holes shows that their magnetic monopole behavior is a direct result of their interaction with the anti-de Sitter field. The study also reveals that the energy of these black holes is proportional to their horizon radius, confirming that they can emit energy through scalar field radiation.

In this paper, we offer a groundbreaking reimagining of set theory through a
paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed meta-theory. 
In addition, we develop a model that adheres to the paracomplete and paraconsistent
principles and employ it to derive a fundamental theorem relating to the arithmetic
hierarchy, specifically focusing on the existence of sentences that are valid within
our system yet provable from classical ZFC only through the application of a diagonalization technique. 
This theoretical framework is complemented by a discussion of the relationship between
our proposed logic and intensional contexts, culminating in an exploration of the
implications for intensional semantics. 
Finally, we outline the advantages of adopting a paracomplete and paraconsistent logic
system, such as the capacity to represent a broader spectrum of propositions, and
delve into the related epistemological and semantic issues arising from the anti-classicality
axiom, including the fundamental question of how to interpret the satisfaction relation
within our proposed meta-theory. 
This paper aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the parameters of our
four-valued paracomplete and paraconsistent logic within the context of set theory,
its axiomatic foundation, its relationship with classical logic, and a sample application,
while also initiating a broader discussion on the implications for intensional contexts
and the issues related to the satisfaction relation within our proposed meta-theory.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Ultimately, this work demonstrates the feasibility of accurately decoding walking state and step rate information from the primary motor cortices, offering a promising pathway for the development of reliable and safe lower limb neuroprosthetics through brain control. Additionally, the high performance of this BCI over extended periods underscores its practical applications. The code and data used in this study have been made publicly available for the community to further develop this technology and explore its potential for controlling other aspects of the leg movement, such as stepping frequency, foot fall pattern and the distinction between walking and running. This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. Implementations are conveyed in Python in conjunction with the NS3 library. This work was previously presented at the 33rd JCIS in 2018.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks on time-series data. Alongside outstanding performance, DECENNT-generated graphs provide valuable downstream task prediction and provide a foundation for further research on modeling complex dynamic bi-directional relationships in changing graph structures. The framework is versatile and adaptable to various domains, datasets, and downstream tasks. The code is openly available at https://github.com/ninghang/DECENNT.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. The developed approach and related data can contribute to the study of biolocomotion and animal behavior from video data. Furthermore, they may also find applications in video surveillance focused on recognizing primates in jungle environments or identifying wild animals from moving vehicles. The code and data described in this paper are available at https://github.com/younesouadah/biolocomotion_detection. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets the conditions of fixed point iteration and convergence, allowing for a comparison of its performance to other state-of-the-art methods, including Newton iteration, Neumann Series, and Successive Over-Relaxation. Moreover, NN can be applied to conditionally positive definite matrices and achieves superior performance on synthetic and real-world datasets, outperforming other methods as measured by entry accuracy and overall runtime. The Nested Neumann algorithm has been found to be highly parallelizable and compatible with GPU acceleration, making it an attractive solution for large-scale matrix inversion applications. In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints and formulas governing the eigenvalues and modes within any given scattering setup - including complex geometries, and broad categories such as slabs and narrow channels. Our mathematical framework reveals limitations and correlations for intensity within system boundaries, and derived properties apply universally to different types and strengths of wave, and multiple wave types. Additionally, we provide numerical evidence that mode overlap is primarily determined by spatial overlap and field correlation, and can be predicted through simple effective medium modeling. This understanding offers insights necessary for controlling energy within disordered environments by managing the overlap of wave modes corresponding to different frequencies or types of wave. As a practical application, we propose using a simple model to design optimal intermediate geometries that maximize energy delivered to a target compared to a reference configuration. This is particularly useful when wave propagation is obstructed, causing a decline in performance below a certain size limit. Our results also imply that in wave slabs of sufficient thickness, where scattering is weak, the ratio of forward to total energy correlates with the square of the corresponding transmission coefficient. This knowledge can be utilized across various wave scenarios and systems to predict and optimize energy delivery within complex environments through wave mode management. As a by-product of this research, numerical tools capable of computing spatial mode correlations and eigenvalue spectra for any given system have been developed, also capable of modeling average field within a system by combining external field with internal mode distribution. These tools are available online for download and can be applied to any system, making it possible to apply the derived general formulas to any given scenario. As an example, we provide the eigenvalue spectrum and mode analysis for two specific cases - a narrow channel and a large slab - using these developed numerical tools. Furthermore, we demonstrate that strong wave modes can be tightly confined within systems crossing from "hard" to "soft" scenarios, and that this mode can be efficiently used for energy delivery. As an additional outcome, we derived an analytical expression for the size of particles that exhibit strongest wave absorption, and both demonstrate and predict that wave absorption at these sizes outperforms other configurations. As a result, we propose that wave mode management can offer a novel approach to controlling energy within disorderly environments. As an additional outcome, we present an analytical expression for an ideal scenario where scattering is minimal, and provide numerical evidence that this expression can be applied across a broader spectrum of wave modes

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Our simulations are validated using both exact diagonalization and matrix product simulation methods. This study provides an extension of previous research on topological zero-energy modes to include the effects of correlated disorders. Consequently, our findings contribute an added layer of understanding to the mechanisms driving topological phenomena in materials. Furthermore, our analysis proposes an improved method for detecting topological characteristics in atomic or photonic systems subject to correlated disorders. This could potentially provide a means to diagnose topological properties even in situations where direct measurement of the spectrum is not feasible. Consequently, our research provides an added layer of understanding to the mechanisms driving topological phenomena in materials, encompassing a broader range of disorder conditions. This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare fundamental invariants associated with these curves. Specifically, genus one curves related to the hypergeometric series and the Gauss hypergeometric integral are examined in detail. Furthermore, the interplay between algebraic geometry and analytical representations of these curves is explored through the use of Kleinian curves and their degenerations, revealing novel insights into their geometry. The findings also enable the computation of curve invariants directly from their algebraic definitions. The study extends beyond mere computation, as the results are shown to be expressed through the fundamental invariants, implying that the elliptic double-box Feynman integral can be represented by the sunset integral and a combination of the hypergeometric integral and its elliptic extensions. This research offers a comprehensive exploration of the interconnections between algebraic geometry, analytical representations, and Feynman integrals within the context of elliptic double-box and genus one curves. The study demonstrates that the intersection of these areas yields non-trivial results that can be computed directly from their definitions. The research is further supported by the underlying duality between the hypergeometric series and the elliptic double-box Feynman integral, as well as the duality between the hypergeometric integral and the sunset integral. The study paves the way for expanding the applications of these results to various other mathematical and physical contexts. The proposed methods for computing invariants and representing curves in the complex plane can be adapted for additional scenarios. The findings open up new avenues for exploring the intricate relationships between algebraic geometry, analytical representations, and Feynman integrals, offering a deeper understanding of these fundamental areas and potential solutions to computational problems. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The study will be displayed through the cross-section and Skewness of the diphoton distribution for various complex parameter scenarios. The extension can be utilised in conjunction with the $\texttt{MHfFa}$ code for the hard scattering components of the process $e^+ e^-\rightarrow \text{Higgs} + \text{missing energy}$. The development paves the way for precise calculations of neutral Higgs boson production at future $e+e-$ colliders, such as CLIC or a future ILC, particularly relevant for exploring the MSSM complex parameter scenario at the loop level at these machines. The code $\texttt{SusHiMi}$ is available upon request. The associated code for the additional calculations discussed in this paper is also available from the authors. The paper is accompanied by several research examples highlighting the significance of the findings. A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. A simulation study and empirical analysis provide further insight into the test's performance. The implementation of the test is also explored through a quasi-score approach for non-identifiable parameters. The methodology is applicable to various network types, evaluated through simulation and real-world data analysis. The real-world data analysis is conducted for two healthcare-related datasets, one centered on antibiotic administration and the other on cancer treatment, with the results showing the existence of non-linear relationships in both networks. The methods devised are compatible with traditional ARMA models, as demonstrated by simulation. The proposed approach encompasses count-based models, as shown in the cancer treatment dataset analysis, enabling the assessment of linearity in various network contexts. Alongside the methodological innovations, the paper contributes to the discussion on the identification of parameters in network models. The quasi-score linearity test and associated methods are implemented in the R package 'QuasiScore'. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation, the test's effectiveness in detecting non-linearity is established. As such, the quasi-score linearity test provides an invaluable tool for the exploration and validation of linearity assumptions in network autoregressive models. Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components. The accompanying code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/xgolden75/declnet-icml-2021. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. This proposed approach embeds molecular dynamics of protein interactions within the context of reaction-diffusion equations and is coupled with a general mass conservation principle for fluid dynamics of intracellular fluids. This framework is then applied to develop a unified model explaining cellular spreading versus snatching, pattern formation in the BRAIN, and the movement of tracheal epithelial cells. A numerical solver is also introduced for solving the coupled PDE system numerically. Our results obtained through numerical solutions match observed cellular behavior in various scenarios. This comprehensive framework has the potential to clarify the mechanisms underlying complex cellular behaviors and facilitate the development of future cell mechanics theories. This approach is now available as a user-friendly graphical user interface called CellForce for users to model their own cellular spreading and locomotion challenges. This software can be accessed through a user-friendly graphical user interface called CellForce, which is part of the SiLoP package, an open-source C++ library that includes cell spreading and locomotion models as well as a range of numerical solution methods. This library is highly customizable and allows users to model their own cellular spreading and locomotion challenges. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency. By leveraging our methods, cryptocurrency exchanges and authorities can gain valuable insights to devise more effective strategies in detecting and preventing the emergence of malicious activities within these platforms. Furthermore, our study on Ethereum reveals that a significant proportion of addresses engaged in malicious activities continue to actively transact on the network, suggesting a pressing need for their identification and banishment. In response, we propose an algorithm to pinpoint these addresses and present initial results from its application to the Ethereum blockchain. In doing so, we introduce a novel measure for assessing the centrality of addresses within transaction graphs, along with a new metric for quantifying the recurrence behavior of transactions. Alongside these contributions, we make available our methodology and detection outcomes for the Ethereum blockchain via an interactive online tool, along with freely shareable code on a public repository. In conclusion, our investigation into cyclic behavior within cryptocurrency blockchains yields groundbreaking insights, revealing effective methods for money trail analysis, and providing valuable tools for monitoring cryptocurrency transactions. In the future, we intend to expand upon this research by exploring additional features and patterns within temporal transaction graphs. In doing so, we invite participation and contributions from other researchers in this field. In addition, we invite exchanges and blockchain platforms to collaborate with us in applying our methods and identifying new features to detect malicious activities within their blockchains. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Notably, this approach bypasses conventional assumptions about decoders and noise models, offering a more realistic and adaptable solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the ability to extend this approach to larger lattices and show that adding decoder actions to the learning process leads to significant performance improvements, paving the way for the development of more complex code protocols. Despite these advancements, significant performance gains can still be achieved, with a particular focus on decoding under periodic distortion. In this scenario, periodic decoding strategies consistently emerge as the best solution, yielding performance close to the optimal unbiased estimator in low-noise environments and outperforming conventional periodic decoders in higher noise levels. This novel decoding framework not only yields superior performance but also provides insights into decoding dynamics, revealing a clear transition from biased to unbiased estimation in proportion to the number of faulty measurements. In addition, we observed an unexpected phenomenon -- superperiodic decoding, significantly outperforming both periodic and unbiased decoders in extremely low noise conditions, suggesting the potential for further exploration of this phenomenon in other codes. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role. Interestingly, using various home working tools and technologies can either positively or negatively impact project success, depending on the Scrum approach employed. Our research provides actionable recommendations for project managers to adapt Scrum and working from home, emphasizing the importance of open communication, adaptability, and process flexibility. As such, it offers valuable insights for practitioners seeking to balance home working and Scrum in a post-pandemic world. Notwithstanding its contributions, this research has several limitations that pave the way for future studies. Specifically, it would be interesting to explore other Agile methodologies' interplay with home working and investigate the long-term effects of remote working on Scrum projects. Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Utilizing hydrodynamic simulations with initial conditions represented by elliptical profiles, radial flow is shown to originate from collisions between protons and protons at intermediate energies, while collisions between protons and nuclei or nucleus-nucleus collisions at higher energies cause radial flow to override initial conditions, resulting in little dependence on event-shape in final hadron distributions.  Events with higher-than-average elliptic flow are found to originate from areas with higher density, confirming previous findings, and with an average density 10% greater than lower elliptic flow events.  Additionally, calculated initial temperature and density show a significant increase in events with higher-than-average elliptic flow, accounting for higher hadron yields observed in these events.  Two-scale temperature profile observations also imply that initial conditions' temporal and spatial profiles have distinct characteristics, with initial conditions represented by temporal profiles that temporarily persist, and spatial profiles that quickly change.  This study's findings provide a deeper understanding of the relationship between initial conditions and final hadron distributions, shedding light on the complex interplay between radial and elliptic flow. The paper further explores the connection between LCST and the Hermite Gaussian function, providing expressions for the LCST of these functions. This research is relevant to the field of quantum optics and provides the theoretical foundation for further investigation of LCST properties. The associated MATLAB code is included for replication purposes. This work extends the signal processing capabilities of the Linear Canonical Transform and its derivatives, enabling the implementation of LCST-based filters and suggesting potential uses in image and signal processing tasks.

The research is complementary to the author's earlier work on the Linear Canonical Transform and its relationships with other signal processing operators.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Therefore, this new method provides a significant improvement for simulations of complex sediment transport and other multiphase flows with numerous collisions. Additionally, we found that artificially lengthening collision time steps has a significant stretching effect on particles, and can be seen as an implicit numerical dissipation that affects particle motion. Our findings also suggest that highly nonlinear phenomena such as particle-to-particle collisions may benefit from higher-order numerical schemes that conserve invariants, while our results for fluid-particle interactions are consistent with previous research. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot reached 70% of the desired height in this scenario. However, when the feedback controller was applied to the RFT model, the robot failed to achieve the desired height due to its limitations in modeling ground deformation. This led to the development of a higher-level state feedback controller for the total system, comprising the robot and ground. This controller was successfully tested in the full simulation, with the feedback controller for the force controller's errors included in the higher-level loop. As a result, the robot was able to reach 90% of the desired height. This research culminates in a major contribution: the development of a resistive force theory-based force feedback control system for a one-legged hopping robot interacting with a granular surface. This work paves the way for advancing control systems in physical systems interacting with complex materials like granular surfaces, as well as addressing the challenges of deformable terrain in legged locomotion. Ultimately, finding effective solutions to these challenges is crucial for the development of safe and efficient legged robots capable of navigating various types of terrain. Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our research demonstrates that while significant progress has been made in NLP, models still require substantial improvement before they can accurately process negation without relying on cumbersome workarounds. As such, our CONDAQA dataset represents a crucial stepping stone towards this goal. We have made our dataset publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/Condaqa. We look forward to model makers sharing their results on this dataset in the interest of advancing the NLP community knowledge. We have also released our code for negation awareness evaluation, a novel metric that assesses models' capacity to recognize negation cues, at https://github.com/ghrua/Neg-Aware-Eval. We believe this code is versatile and can be applied to any dataset featuring negation cues. We have included the following paper supplements for reviewers' reference: a detailed description of our dataset construction process, our code for negation awareness evaluation, and comprehensive results involving additional NLP models. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. As such, the developed framework has the potential to guide actual quantum annealing experiments on quantum hardware. The statistical methods exploited here also open new avenues for investigating the annealing gap's underlying physics. The study's results on the interplay between quench and annealing dynamics can be directly applied to scenarios involving interacting bosons or fermions in optical lattices. Furthermore, the developed statistical approach can be adapted to analyze the annealing gap in other Hamiltonian scenarios. As such, this research offers a complementary framework that addresses core challenges in quantum annealing, specifically the inherent slowness of equilibrium quantum dynamics and the associated large annealing gaps. The proposed solution-focused approach based on quench parameterization may also pave the way for a deeper understanding of quantum annealing dynamics, enabled by the ability to study complex scenarios using highly simplified quench-based Hamiltonian models. The ability to reproduce the annealing gap's behavior using quench data alone highlights the potential for further investigating the physics of quantum annealing through quench-based quantum simulations. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Finally, we discuss how these findings relate to existing experimental data. 
Our study demonstrates that a simple two-dimensional Hubbard model which can
emerge from a more comprehensive 3D band structure retains valuable physical
properties. 
Additionally, we uncover unexpected phenomena that might be explored in
other contexts. 
For instance, the unusual phase diagram with both an antiferromagnetic and
half-filled physics limit and a separate self-doped/d-wave pairing limit can
climb to more realistic multi-band scenarios where extra filled $s$-orbitals are
considered. 
This study provides a starting point for analyzing the physics of other materials
with highly correlated $d$-electrons where screening plays a significant role. 
It highlights the value of incorporating both necessary and incidental $s$-
orbitals when modeling d-electron systems to ensure a correct physical picture. 
It also underlines the screening's role as an essential factor that should be
carefully examined when deriving a reduced model.

access.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored. Furthermore, our research examined the effectiveness of sentiment analysis across different languages, utilizing low-resource datasets and adapting pre-trained models. Lastly, we explored a pioneering application of context-aware sentiment analysis in tweet classification, employing a combination of context-aware sentiment analysis and a novel model called BERT-MMC. The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. We conclude by illustrating the applicability of our results to solve the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming via the cutting plane method. We propose a new algorithm that uses an efficient lower bound to perform the cutting plane iteration directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time, leading to an improvement in computational performance for large input sets. We also present computational experiments showing the advantage of this new algorithm over the established brute-force approach relied upon in previous research. Specifically, our improved algorithm reduces the average computation time by a factor of $10^3$ to $10^4$ for random uniform tree pairs with node numbers in the range of $10^2$ to $10^3$. Moreover, our proposed algorithm excels in solving the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping problem directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time, also leading to an $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time complexity for the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming via the cutting plane method. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. In these areas, particles' ability to absorb scattering radiation reduces the heating impact of big particles on local temperatures, leading to increased dust growth. As a result, particles' size plays a significant role in the VSI's behavior and, in turn, has an impact on the disk's overall development and structure. In addition, our research indicates that VSI may be less prevalent in wider protoplanetary disks in need of greater cooling, as well as in disks with significant dead zones that could reduce the shear velocity caused by gas Reynolds stress. In these cases, dust development and settling play a lesser role in VSI's instability. In conclusion, our research suggests that dust development and settling play a major role in the VSI's behavior, and as a result, they have an impact on the disk's overall development and structure. In addition, our research indicates that dust development may contribute to the observed particle settlement in protoplanetary disks, and it raises the possibility that dust development may be the driving force behind dust development in these systems. The model we created in this research will be made available at a later date as part of a comprehensive code package that includes various dust development and settling models, as well as several other features, and will be integrated into the AstroDyn module of ARES. We have developed an efficient approach for condensing complex systems into their fundamental behaviors using their primary underlying features. By leveraging observed data, we pinpoint a low-dimensional structure that characterizes the systems' gradual evolution and generate an extremely simple representation of the systems' dynamics within that structure. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies implicit optimization to fit a system's underlying structure to available data and simplifies the systems' dynamics, we have created two more direct methods that transform the process into explicit problems under specific assumptions. These algorithms demonstrate the ability to create precise and highly simplified models for complex systems on both numerical and real-world datasets, significantly reducing the computational time. Moreover, our results show that our methods can generate systems' underlying structures that are comparable to those obtained from dimension reduction techniques, such as PCA, and offer additional advantages, such as the ability to model systems' evolution over time. Unlike traditional dimension reduction methods, our approach goes beyond condensing the systems' data to also capture their underlying dynamics. In particular, our methods can produce systems' underlying structures and reduced-dimensional models for variables that were not included in the training data. Additionally, our models can be used for various purposes, such as predicting systems' behavior on a larger timescale and identifying key factors that influence the systems' evolution. In the future, our approach can be applied to conditional systems, where the systems' behavior depends on external variables, and to multi-systems, where the systems interact with each other. Our code is openly available at https://github.com/yoyo3333/Spectral-Submanifolds.

Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. Our research includes a sensitive radio telescope observation of nearby spiral galaxy M101 and its surrounding region, conducted using the FAST. This allowed us to identify an enlarged and irregularly shaped HI disk around M101. Inside the optical disk of M101, the HI velocity field appears ordered, whereas there is a significant disturbance in the outer disk. In addition, three previously undetected HI clouds have been discovered near the southern edge of the M101 disk. These HI clouds have estimated masses of 1.3$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, 2.4$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, and 2.0$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$ respectively. The HI clouds in M101 rotate in sync with its main HI disk. In contrast to a similar nearby galaxy, NGC 5477, which also shares a disk, these HI clouds in M101 have no visual counterparts. Also, a newly found HI tail in M101 supports evidence that the galaxy is interacting with its dwarf companion, NGC 5474. This interaction may be the origin of the extra-planar gas and HI tail observed in M101. Its disk disturbance and HI clouds offer a perfect laboratory for studying the absorption and scattering of HI gas in interactions between galaxies. This paper provides radio telescope observations, a HI map, a velocity field map, three previously undetected HI clouds, and a newly found HI tail in M101 observed with the FAST. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. As a result, cometary spectrum analysis remains incomplete and cannot fully account for the key processes involving these common comet molecules. This study gathers existing spectral information about these cations to pinpoint areas where additional research is necessary to enhance the comprehension of cometary evolution. Furthermore, it highlights outstanding questions regarding the composition of comet atmospheres and the possible connections between the neutral and ionic gas phases. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries. 

In addition to its primary application in spectroscopy, this approach can also be applied to on-device cross-correlation of superimposed images, a feature with which the technology is initially being tested. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for the development of low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments and may enable a new paradigm in multi-object spectroscopy. This could particularly benefit low-resolution, wide-field spectroscopy, enabling the simultaneous analysis of large fields of view, thus combining the capabilities of wide-field imaging and spectroscopy. 

In the context of high-resolution spectroscopy, this technology may allow for the analysis of multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra, a feature currently only achievable with 10-m class telescopes. This innovation has the potential to contribute significantly to the discovery of exoplanets, particularly a method known as the "radial velocity curve", used to identify planets orbiting our galaxy's stars. 

With this breakthrough, we propose the concept of a multi-object spectrographic instrument called CAFTA (CAltay FAst Telescope), a low-resolution, wide-field device consisting of 100-1000 custom photonic devices, each analyzing a distinct object or field of view. This innovative approach may enable the concurrent analysis of 10,000-100,000 objects, a feat that would open up new avenues for multi-object spectroscopy and provide a new level of sensitivity in wide-field imaging and spectroscopy.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper proposes the Semi-Batch Federated Learning (SBFL) technique, which minimizes large communication batches into smaller, more manageable chunks. In SBFL, a server divides each communication batch into several sub-batches, trains models on each sub-batch independently, and then averages the models for update. This approach is examined on various graph topologies, and numerical results demonstrate that SBFL outperforms the standard Federated Learning approach in terms of convergence rate and bias reduction. Moreover, SBFL is applicable to a wide range of machine learning algorithms, including deep neural networks. To further investigate the SBFL approach, a system called FedNN is designed and implemented. FedNN is particularly useful for Federated Learning on IoT devices. In addition, several optimization strategies are proposed to enhance the SBFL approach. The advantages of this work are its broad algorithm applicability, efficient use of communication resources, and the flexibility of SBFL to handle various graph topologies. The proposed FedNN system paves the way for concurrent study of Federated Learning algorithms and system design. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, it is essential to conduct more in-depth cost-benefit analysis while exploring additional implications of providing mental health treatment to offenders on probation.  Alongside the primary analysis, the study also incorporates an instrumental variable method to account for potential disparities in treatment allocation, such as offender characteristics and local court policies.  The research was conducted using a large and diverse dataset of around 300,000 offenders.  The discovery that mental health treatment reduces recidivism rates strongly supports the integration of evidence-based mental health treatment into criminal justice rehabilitation programs.  Furthermore, the results suggest that providing treatment could become financially self-sufficient through the decrease in future crime, thereby not increasing the already existing public spending but rather generating additional tax revenue.  Ultimately, the most effective approach would involve providing treatment as part of a contingent probation sentence, linked to the likelihood of future crime as measured by an empirical risk score.  This would enable judges to balance public safety against the ability of offenders to change their behavior, all while ensuring that tax dollars are utilized efficiently. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. This will mark the largest and most complex FPGA design implementation within the ATLAS trigger system and will serve as a model for possible adoption in future LHC experiments. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the design, fabrication, and implications for further development of the jet FEX system. This review is accompanied by performance data from the full ATCA board layer, as well as the feature extractors themselves, to demonstrate the feasibility of this design for handling the LHC's data load in 2021 and beyond.
