Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions, alongside an analysis of how these methods impact the reliable classification of images. Experimental results on multiple image classification tasks showcase the effectiveness of this approach in mitigating both silent errors and data corruptions, alongside an exploration of the optimal balance between error reduction and precise classification performance. Furthermore, we provide a practical example of this technique's efficacy using a real-world automotive vision system. We also provide the code for our method at https://github.com/andresayala/RangeControlErrorDetection. By relying solely on runtime data, range control offers a appealing error detection and prevention solution for classifier CNNs that is easy to implement across various deep learning frameworks. Additionally, it offers an efficient error mitigation strategy that finds a balance between error reduction and precise classification performance, making it suitable for the reliable deployment of classifier CNNs in safety-critical applications prone to hardware errors. Finally, we highlight future research directions for extending this method to other types of neural networks.

The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting transactions and business-to-business interactions. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively. In addition to proposing a suite of graph algorithms, we also address the common pitfalls of netting scenario representation and offer possible solutions. Notably, our study offers an antithesis to commonly held opinions that graph algorithms become impractically slow for large-scale applications or are unsuitable for modern use cases. Our findings prove that appropriate algorithm selection and optimization techniques allow conventional graph algorithms to handle substantial real-world challenges efficiently. As such, we believe that our research can serve as an ideal foundation for further large-scale clearing infrastructure projects. As such, we are making the Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data used in this analysis publicly available to facilitate future research in this domain. This data set is particularly noteworthy because it lacks the anonymization commonly applied to similar financial data sets, ensuring maximum usefulness for clearing-related research. In addition to presenting our algorithm suite, we also explore various graph representation approaches commonly employed in clearing contexts, highlighting their implications and often overlooked drawbacks. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our work paves the way for further research on multilingual distributional semantics and provides a resource for other researchers to build upon, with the code and models available at https://github.com/zhujinyaolong/MultiSpace.git. Our paper is also accompanied by a live demo accessible at https://aueb.github.io/multispace_demo/.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. The proposed framework does not incur additional data or computational costs, enhancing the delivery of high-quality dialogue state tracking. Furthermore, we introduce a novel metric named selectivity to quantify the degree to which a dataset supports various dialogue state tracking goals. Ultimately, we employ the proposed framework to rectify the labels of the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset, leading to a 5.33% boost in joint goal accuracy. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. A tentative proposal is made to rectify this shortcoming by introducing a new model component, drawing from research on Santiago's transportation systems, which could potentially be applied to similar urban environments. However, further data is necessary to test and refine this modified model. The results presented showcase the challenges associated with modeling the spread of unrest in Santiago, and offer a starting point for ongoing research aimed at contributing to the scientific study of urban epidemics. By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. With a dust attenuation of $A_{V} = 0.5$, we find a moderate correlation between observed and predicted values of this line, although it is reduced by dust and therefore less effective as a proxy for star formation rates. However, in more heavily obscured galaxies, the line becomes too weak to be detected reliably with current near-infrared detectors. Despite this limitation, we anticipate that observing this line along with the $\lambda$1.64 $\mu$m Brackett-$\alpha$ line could provide a more accurate understanding of dust attenuation in these galaxies. Using a set of 15 galaxies with low to moderate dust attenuation, we develop a simple empirical formula to estimate dust attenuation at $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m in terms of the line flux ratio between $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m and $\lambda$1.64 $\mu$m. This formula holds significant potential for future observations of galaxies with low to moderate dust attenuation in this wavelength range. Using these results, we reexamine earlier studies indicating a potential relationship between star formation rates and the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m line, finding a moderate correlation hold true when considering a larger dataset, but finding that the relationship is influenced by dust attenuation. Consequently, observing this line alone may not provide an accurate understanding of star formation rates, but combining it with other observations, particularly those related to dust attenuation, may yield a more accurate understanding of galaxy physics. Ultimately, the ability to monitor changes in star formation rates within individual galaxies over time may be possible with this approach, using this line in conjunction with other features, although more research is needed to determine the best approach. We are studying a critical boundary that involves breaking down real polynomials into the sum of squares of other real polynomials, specifically those that don't equal zero. This specific boundary overlaps with another critical boundary that involves nonnegative polynomials and is characterized by polynomials that become zero at at least one point. Our focus lies on a separate part of the boundary that involves positive polynomials and we have already successfully identified the complete description for some specific cases with low degrees in a small number of variables. However, more complex cases with more variables or higher degree polynomials remain to be fully understood and there is currently very limited knowledge on them. Using an assumption from D. Eisenbud, M. Green, and J. Harris, we have obtained new restrictions for the number of decomposed polynomials and the matrix dimensions in this context. These new restrictions particularly improve our understanding for homogeneous quartic polynomials in 5 variables and they match a recent confirmed case in this context. Lastly, combining both theoretical calculations and computational techniques, we have obtained specific examples and counterexamples to further analyze the general applicability of G. Blekherman's findings and we have proven that the established bounds are indeed reachable. In high-scale theories involving extra neutrino states, the standard low-energy matrix used to describe neutrino interactions may be invalid. We reevaluate how much is currently known about individual components of this matrix, making no assumption about its unitarity. We establish two fundamental sets of experimental limitations - direct plus inherent constraints, and indirect ones. We examine the effects of each set on the possible deviation of neutrino behavior from expected unitarity. We also provide a clearer understanding of predictions related to flux and cross-sections, taking into consideration any contamination from new physics affecting hadronic measurements. We focus on the currently operating FASER$\nu$ experiment to show that certain neutrino experiments have sensitivity to this issue. We discovered that certain constraints can limit deviation from expected neutrino behavior to below $10^{-3}$, exceeding current limits on a similar problem related to other subatomic particles. However, if we consider only certain other constraints, large unitarity violations can occur and be confirmed or disproven with the currently operating FASER$\nu$ experiment in a significant margin of error. We propose that future experiments should incorporate novel methods to directly measure neutrino unitarity, potentially involving secondary particles such as muons or hadronic components of showers. Finally, we outline how such experiments could provide significant insight into neutrino physics, potentially paving the way for a deeper understanding of the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry. This could involve providing valuable input to a future, more comprehensive theory of extra neutrino states and their interactions. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Notably, we also find SHOWS can be electrically switched by a nearby junction of charge-degenerate Dirac points, providing a potential means to control the exotic states through electric manipulation. This discovery opens up possibilities for further investigation of showy topological phenomena in 3D electronic materials.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. All implementations utilize the free open-source platform FusionForge and can be found at https://gforge.inria.fr/gso/project?id=1855. In particular, the results include the solution to an electromagnetic imaging problem with incomplete Cauchy data on a boundary with a complex geometry, featuring a cavity filled with air and occupied by dielectric materials. Further development of this research is discussed and forms the basis for potential future extensions to this approach. This research was conducted with funding from CNPq and FAPESP. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model trained on data from multiple protected client datasets. The FedSA challenge aims to address the challenge of limited sample size in client-side data by incorporating multiple client datasets. The FedSA approach builds upon traditional federated learning by selectively aggregating data from various sources, creating a stronger educational effect that accelerates model learning. The FedSA challenge also enhances data protection by limiting the transfer of data to minimal features only. The paper further investigates the FedSA approach through various comparisons, including baseline federated learning, aggregation without federation, and merge-only strategies. The results show that the FedSA approach yields superior performance, achieving a 10.17% improvement in accuracy compared to traditional federated learning. The paper also explores the selective aggregation technique in detail, demonstrating its positive impact on model learning. The code and benchmarks used in the paper are available open-source on GitHub. The paper also includes additional related techniques, such as federated learning and dataset augmentation, and highlights the FedSA challenge as the most distantly distributed dataset scenario reported to date. The paper also anticipates the FedSA challenge to contribute to further research in federated learning, inspired by the successful application of superconducting materials. Approximately a decade ago, the existence of grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as a spatial metric. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations. Furthermore, we explore and evaluate various models and theories pertaining to grid cells, discussing their capacity for generating grid cells through mechanisms like self-organization, pathway interactions within the temporal loopy circuit, and the integration of directional signals and spatial information. As the field of grid cell research continues to evolve, it is likely that future studies will uncover even more substantial aspects of grid cells' complex functionalities. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

Ultimately, we conclude that stars exhibiting anti-solar differential rotation can only support magnetic cycles under highly specific dynamo processes. Consequently, we suggest that the presence of magnetic cycles be used as an indicator to distinguish between normal and reversed differential rotation in slowly rotating solar-type stars. Conditions for this to hold are that the star must be rotating slowly enough and have an $\alpha$-effect that acts independently across different regions of the star. If these conditions are met, we anticipate finding magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases, providing a clear signature for further identification of this rotation regime. The first potential example of such a case is presented in this research, applicable to the Sun. Although our analysis focuses on global magnetic cycles, local cycles in regions like active regions or magnetic polar spots may also occur independently. Consequently, observing and studying these local cycles will provide valuable insights into the dynamics of these regions and how they relate to the star's global magnetic cycle. Notably, under specific conditions, we establish the existence of an infinite number of $S_4$ quartic extensions where the rank of an elliptic curve doesn't increase compared to its rank over the rational numbers. This achievement is made possible by our development of methods to manage the 2-Selmer rank of elliptic curves within certain quadratic fields, enabling control of the rank in families of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. In particular, we utilize class field theory and the Shafarevich-Tate conjecture to devise strategies to rank 2 Selmer groups and 2-descent methods for rank 1 cases. By combining computational approaches to 2-descent and analytic rank predictions along with highly optimized computer programs, we gather data to predict the behavior of rank for a specific elliptic curve under various $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions, mirroring findings previously observed in cubic extensions with Galois group $A_4$. In addition, we present several instances of our predictions alongside computational evidence. Notably, some of these cases illustrate scenarios where the rank of an elliptic curve increases from 0 to 2 within a quadratic field, a phenomenon that was initially observed in greater depth in a paper by Dietmann and Griffin for fields of degree 3. We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. Notably, this lower bound provides a more precise estimate than previous upper bounds for certain qubit states and their corresponding unitary dynamics. Furthermore, our study generalizes these findings to multi-level systems and provides new insights into the relationship between asymmetry, decoherence time, and distinguishability time. Our results offer a comprehensive understanding of how qubit states' structure influences their dynamics and can serve as a theoretical foundation for deciding when a qubit state has become irreversibly changed due to unitary or non-unitary evolution. This decision-making framework is critical for developing dynamic protection protocols for quantum memory. Our approach also involves developing a new measure for the difference between two unitary evolutions and demonstrates the utility of asymmetry measures in evaluating the similarity between unitary operators. Ultimately, our investigation paves the way for exploring other dynamics, such as repeated measurements or coherent decoherence, and prompts the question of whether our criteria and bounds can be applied to such dynamics. In doing so, our study raises intriguing questions about the fundamental relationship between the structure of qubit states, their unitary evolution, and the dynamics that govern their irreversible change. Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a non-degenerate simplex can be formed with vertices at $Q_n$. Various methods will be discussed for establishing upper bounds for the norm of $P$ in the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$. Additionally, when the dimension of the space is two, upper bounds of the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{3n}$ hold. However, for dimensions greater than two, counterexamples exist demonstrating that the norm of $P$ exceeds $\sqrt{n}$ explicitly. A counterexample is given for the interpolation projector associated with the symmetric simplex in $4$-dimensional space, where the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, and the norm of $P$ is greater than $4$. Consequently, no general upper bound of the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{n}$ holds for the corresponding interpolation projector $P$. Counterexamples can also be constructed for submatrices of the interpolation matrix $A$, such as upper triangular matrices with a determinant of a specific sign, but no such construction exists for the full matrix $A$. A lower bound of the form $\|P\|_{Q_n} \geq c \sqrt{n}$ holds under additional constraints, such as when the number of nodes is not an Hadamard number or when the matrix $A$ is positive definite. A method exists to further investigate upper bounds for the norm of $P$ through the solution of a variational problem. A further analysis of the upper bound $\|P\|_{Q_n} \leq c \sqrt{3n}$ is also presented for the interpolation projector

We investigated the carrier concentration distribution inside the hole, finding a linear decrease from the edge to approximately 0.7 times the hole radius. Notably, our findings enable a key step towards developing quantitative models linking device design to photon loss, a crucial aspect in designing low-loss quantum devices. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. Alongside ongoing missions, we highlight the potential for future research, including those aimed at understanding Venus's geophysical activity and interior structure through seismic and magnetic field studies, as well as those focused on better comprehending the planet's atmospheric escape mechanisms, geochemical cycles, and magnetospheric interactions through a combination of observational and modeling approaches. Ultimately, this work emphasizes the value of comparing Earth and Mars to better grasp the unique evolution of Venus. This comparison enables a more comprehensive understanding of the complex interior-exterior interactions that have driven the planet's development and will continue to shape Venus in the ages to come. This research is part of the ongoing effort to prepare for manned missions to Mars, which will require a deeper understanding of the Earth's sister planets, including their pasts, present states, and future trajectories. Recent breakthroughs in numerical computation, driven by GPU and TPU advancements, have significantly scaled tensor network algorithms for complex quantum simulation and machine learning applications. The quantum-inspired nature of these algorithms makes them mappable to parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs), which is now fueling proposals for leveraging near-term quantum devices to enhance algorithm performance. Furthermore, joint quantum-classical frameworks can exploit the unique strengths of TNs and PQC models. Nonetheless, approximating TN states using realistic quantum circuits remains a pending issue for the success of such approaches. Our study assesses novel and existing protocols for decomposing matrix product states into shallow quantum circuits consisting of stacked linear layers of two-qubit gates, incorporating both analytical decomposition schemes and constrained optimization of circuit unitaries. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of a sequential growth protocol, especially when computational resources are limited, leading us to anticipate that this protocol will become a crucial tool for integrating tensor networks and quantum circuits. Our code is openly available for further exploration and protocol customization. Orlov et al. introduced a sequential growth protocol for approximating matrix product states using shallow quantum circuits. Our study builds upon this concept, exploring both analytical and protocol-based decomposition approaches for decomposing matrix product states into quantum circuits composed of two-qubit gates, investigating the scalability of these protocols for realistic systems, examining the general applicability of previously proposed decomposition schemes, and exploring the impact of circuit depth on approximation accuracy. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of a sequential growth protocol, especially in resource-constrained scenarios, and validate its performance with realistic systems, while also making our code openly available for further customization.

The success of cancer diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes depends heavily on the properties and spatial organization of cells within tissues. Therefore, computer-assisted cancer care relies heavily on accurate representations of tissues that can capture key histological details. Building upon existing cell-graphs that encode cell characteristics and spatial relationships, researchers have been using machine learning to establish correlations between tissue structure and function. However, a single cell-centric approach falls short of describing the complex hierarchical organization within tissues. In response, a novel multi-scale graph representation of tissues has been proposed, comprising of multiple layers of histological entities, along with their relationships. A corresponding graph neural network is also proposed, allowing tissue structure to be linked to its functional behavior. Specifically, this method utilizes cell and tissue region features extracted from histology images to create HierArchical Cell-to-Tissue graphs. An associated neural network is designed to classify such graph representations, referred to as HACT-Net. As part of this work, a comprehensive dataset called the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset is created and employed to evaluate the efficacy of this method against pathologist assessments and current approaches. Experimental studies demonstrate the superiority of this method over alternative techniques and even expert pathologist assessments in breast tumor subtyping tasks. Notably, this technique has the potential to create closed loops in cancer care, linking tissue structure to function, and further improving its accuracy through feedback from clinical data. As such, it is anticipated that this model will contribute positively to the advancement of computer-assisted cancer diagnosis. In addition to cancer, this method is expected to be applicable to other diseases characterized by abnormal tissue architecture, such as liver fibrosis. Furthermore, extensions to this approach are seen as valuable avenues for further research. As a result, this method is expected to facilitate a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between tissue structure and function, and may ultimately contribute to more effective tissue architecture-based diagnosis. In doing so, it is hoped that this method will help give rise to computer-assisted cancer care informed by closed loops uniting structure and function. Specifically, it is anticipated that this method will enable the accurate prediction of tissue proteins from its structure, in turn enabling the prediction of tissue function from its structure, and ultimately, the prediction of tissue structure from function. As part of this work, a novel multi-scale graph representation of tissues is proposed, comprising of multiple layers of histological entities, along with their relationships. An associated graph neural network is also proposed, allowing tissue structure to be linked to its functional behavior.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. This study builds upon previous work, as we are investigating the properties of the posterior distribution when the process parameters are non-stationary and the memory of the process extends infinitely, scenarios which are commonly encountered in event-data scenarios. It is worth highlighting that the proposed methods are efficient and user-friendly, implemented in R using the R package named "hawkespack". This package not only generates data from nonlinear Hawkes processes but also estimates the process parameters, Granger connectivity graphs, and their corresponding posterior distributions. For further information, refer to the package vignette. Highlights of our research are further illustrated by means of real-world examples, such as analyzes of earthquake data and online message data, with focus on the interplay between modeling event-data and the associated challenges. It is our hope that this study will stimulate advanced research on Bayesian analysis of point processes and the exploration of new methods to analyze event-data. It is also our aim to introduce the "hawkespack" package as a user-friendly starting point for the exploration of event-data, encouraging users to contribute their own event-data datasets that can be freely downloaded via the package. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in pairwise interactions, a Fast Multipole Method variant addresses this by substituting interactions between distant particle clusters, which however introduces inaccuracies in angular momentum conservation. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM. This modified algorithm is compatible with existing FMM implementations and does not compromise on mass, energy, or angular momentum conservation. To facilitate easy adoption, our implementation is openly available for public use. Our modified FMM was successfully incorporated into the most recent version of the Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics One Solver (SPHOS) and utilized to simulate binary neutron star mergers, resulting in output consistent with existing research. Furthermore, this indicates the capability to accurately model gravitational waves, compact object formation, and heavy element creation during such events. This upgraded FMM, along with our particle integration conservation properties, is featured in the most recent open-source code release, which serves as a standalone FMM package accessible independently of SPHOS. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered when datasets are small and have few labeled images. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotated datasets of similar anatomical structures for training. Nevertheless, a challenge arises when adapting the model to cross-anatomy domains due to differences in image modalities and target structures' appearance. To overcome this, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA) that allows a model to segment similar structures in a target domain with only a limited number of target domain annotations, aided by existing annotations in a source domain. We employ Domain-Specific Batch Normalization to normalize anatomical feature maps from the two domains separately, introduce a cross-domain contrastive learning approach to promote extracting domain-invariant features, and integrate these into a Self-Ensembling Mean-Teacher (SE-MT) framework that leverages unlabeled target domain images and incorporates prediction consistency constraints. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the CS-CADA's ability to solve the complex cross-anatomy domain shift issue, resulting in the accurate segmentation of coronary arteries in X-ray images, aided by retinal vessel images, and cardiac MR images, aided by fundus images, with only a limited number of target domain annotations. Our method's performance surpasses baseline methods that employ traditional domain adaptation techniques in multiple datasets, showcasing the CS-CADA's versatility and capability in actual clinical applications. Furthermore, the CS-CADA's code is openly accessible at https://github.com/zwang83/CS-CADA.

As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. Additionally, possible applications include enhancing the efficiency of laser-powered x-ray generators and plasma-based particle accelerators, as well as the capability to handle multiple pulses within a single pulse train. This could enable the successful operation of future laser-driven plasma devices that require a high peak power but are constrained by available power supplies. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Moreover, we explore the properties of these natural constructs within the framework of differentiable manifolds. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the combinatorial differentiable manifolds of Gelfand and MacPherson and the recent work of Cohen and MacPherson on combinatorial superconnections, including the introduction of a combinatorial Cheeger-Greenleaf conjeture. We conjecture that the classes of Gelfand and MacPherson's combinatorial manifolds are equivalent to the Chern character of the combinatorial superconnections. This new perspective also leads to an innovative definition of combinatorial characteristic classes for superconnections. We also discuss the related Cheeger-Greenleaf conjeture for the manifolds of Gelfand and MacPherson. We provide a set of sufficient conditions for the validity of this conjeture on certain types of combinatorial manifolds. We conclude by proposing that Gelfand and MacPherson's approach to combinatorial manifolds serves as an intriguing framework for combinatorial differential topology. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. Consequently, SN~2020jfo may represent a transitional object between standard SNe~II and SNe~Ib, potentially exploding due to the collapse of a massive star that had already shed its hydrogen envelope. However, an alternative explanation could be that SN~2020jfo originated from a massive star with significant mass loss during its life cycle, resulting in a low-mass hydrogen envelope when it exploded. In this second scenario, SN~2020jfo would resemble the recently observed SNe~Ib like SN~2020dn and SN~2021bn. In both scenarios, SN~2020jfo provides valuable insights into the diverse phenomena of stripped helium supernovae. Additionally, its distinctive features make SN~2020jfo an important addition to the growing list of unusual supernovae, such as SN~2014aj, SNe~2008cn and 2009zen, and SN~2020dn, which are helping to expand the classification of stripped mass supernovae. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The proposed MuLE optics would not only significantly reduce the weight and cost of such missions but also increase their detection rate of X-ray binaries and other transient sources. The MuLE concept is also applicable to other Le optics-based systems employing a large field of view. We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations. This approach is complemented by an investigation of the adjoint operator, leading to the existence proof for a maximum principle for the adjoint operator. Furthermore, we derive an operator norm estimate for the adjoint operator, obtaining a bound in terms of the original operator's norm. These results can be applied to key examples, such as the Malmquist-type problem, for which we solve an associated Hamiltonian Malmquist-type problem. Additionally, we explore the existence of stationary solutions for a fully nonlinear parabolic equation with state feedback, leading to the convergence of sequences under a transversality condition. This research is grounded in the work of Jensen for fully linear equations. It is noteworthy that the symmetric concave property is optimal for the partial uniform ellipticity condition, a fact demonstrated through a counterexample. This counterexample is constructed through a technique involving the establishment of a continuous, symmetric concave function that is not partially uniformly elliptic. The proposed strategies and results have a significant impact on the study of fully nonlinear equations and their applications. They open up avenues for exploring new problems and validating existing theories for certain types of equations. Moreover, they demonstrate the efficacy of the partial uniform ellipticity approach in tackling fundamental issues related to the maximum principle, adjoint operators, Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations, and stationary solutions. This research thus provides a robust framework for investigating solutions to fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations. It also paves the way for examining more general systems of equations comprised of continuous, symmetric concave functions. Ultimately, the proposed methods can be adapted for studying similar problems involving partial differential equations. To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a later time without traditional force-based $N$-body calculations. Instead, the model used density and velocity fields at the initial stage to forecast final halo masses. When tested with parameters not seen during training, the model showed a strong relationship between input conditions and predicted halo masses. Furthermore, the inclusion of velocity information significantly improved the accuracy of halo mass predictions by reducing the scatter by nearly half, especially for more massive halos. Additionally, varying the power spectrum density (PSD) in the simulations led to a significant increase in the uncertainty of halo mass predictions, with a distinction made between collapse and stable regimes. Variations in PSD were found to influence halo mass predictions more significantly than mass density fluctuations do. Consequently, this implies that velocity plays a crucial role in halo mass evolution, particularly in response to changes in the large-scale structure of the universe. Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, specifically piano transcription. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues. Furthermore, employing a single recording of each note significantly improves performance, implying potential uses in large-scale song analysis. Additionally, low-rank factorization methods prove resistant to pitch-based noise, showcasing the technique's potential for handling imperfect input conditions. Nonetheless, efficient playback of our results reveals a notable gap between the proposed method and professional piano performances. To mitigate this, we explore the potential for the technique to handle individual notes with varying intensities. Ultimately, while the method shows promise for music transcription, significant improvements are needed before it can rival professional standards. The code for the proposed method is available online at the specified repository URL.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Specifically, on invoices, this approach reduces labeling time from 55 hours to just 5.5 hours, a 10x improvement. Our code and datasets are available for download at https://github.com/google-research-data/Selective-Labeling. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many social determinants remain unstructured and un-coded within electronic health records, often only present in the free-text notes made by healthcare professionals. As a result, there is a pressing need for an automated method to extract this valuable information from clinical notes. Our research centers on the development of an innovative multi-stage system combining techniques like named entity recognition, relation classification, and text classification to identify and extract relevant social determinants of health information from clinical notes with minimal human intervention.

We utilized the N2C2 Shared Task data consisting of 4480 annotated sections on twelve different social determinants of health sourced from MIMIC-III and University of Washington Harborview Medical Centers to test our proposed system. Given the challenge posed by entities that overlap with each other, our team designed a unique marker-based model, which we incorporated into the multi-stage system. 

In our experiments, our proposed system consistently demonstrated exceptional performance by achieving better overall Micro-F1 score and outshining existing state-of-the-art models when handling the critical issue of overlapping entities.

Ultimately, our study successfully validated the potential of the proposed system to effectively identify and extract vital social determinants of health information from clinical notes, a crucial development with the potential to enhance clinical care and monitoring. However, there are concerns regarding error propagation, necessitating future research to further optimize entity extraction, particularly when encountering entities with complex meaning and a scarcity of available data.

This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can divide the problem into manageable components, explicitly solve each part, and consequently derive a comprehensive solution despite the discontinuities. We also utilize numerical modeling to illustrate the efficacy of less frequent switching in minimizing costs for both scenarios. Furthermore, we explored the effectiveness of periodic control in the second scenario through numerical simulations, using a variety of parameters. Consequently, our analysis confirms that reducing switching frequency leads to a proportionate decrease in costs in both scenarios. Additionally, we found that in the context of periodic control, the optimal strategy often corresponds to the steady-state solution of the associated difference equation, and that this relationship holds regardless of the specific parameters used. Consequently, we were able to derive the condition that maximizes the optimal velocity, and found that it is bounded by the square root of the product of the two velocities. Finally, we applied our analysis to the broader class of straight swimmers described by the flagellum model, and obtained the same key findings. Consequently, we believe that our analysis is likely to be applicable to other swimmers with similar dynamics. Moreover, we propose that our method is likely to yield similar results for other optimal control problems involving systems that maintain a stable, periodic orbit in the absence of control inputs. Alongside our analytical solutions, we also provide numerical solutions for the discrete equation that underlies the optimal control problems we are exploring, and are particularly interested in the distinct states that can occur when the system is driven by a unimodal difference equation with constant parameters. To conclude, we think that our findings will contribute meaningfully to the ongoing research aimed at understanding the behavior of unimodal difference equations, and also have implications for the study of variable delay systems. Lastly, we propose that our results could inform subsequent research aimed at optimizing the performance of other swimming cells that share similar dynamics. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. As a result, we are able to create a more comprehensive and precise annotation set for the EMO20Q dataset. Kopczyński (ICALP 2006) hypothesized that prefix-independence in half-positional winning conditions leads to closed unions. Contrary to this hypothesis, we demonstrate that such conditions are not finite union-closed over limited scenarios. To disprove this hypothesis, we define a new set of bi-positional winning conditions known as 'energy conditions,' specifically tailored for total-imprisonment games on directed acyclic graphs. Within this new set, we prove that certain 'energy conditions' are positionally independent and, as a result, have closed unions. Furthermore, by combining two inherently unstable conditions within this new set, we derive a condition that is positionally dependent, thus invalidating the hypothesis proposed by Kopczyński. Building upon this contradiction, we establish the theoretical basis for analyzing the complexity of half-positional winning conditions in game theory. Alongside this breakthrough, we develop an applicable method for determining the computational complexity of specific game theory problems by constructing reducible instances from simple bi-positional energy conditions. Finally, we demonstrate the practical applicability of these concepts by applying them to existing game theory problems, including the derivation of an NP-completeness proof for a particular directed graph game. By tackling these research questions, this paper provides a theoretical framework for analyzing the complexity of half-positional winning conditions and offers a novel approach to solving complex game theory problems. This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100. To further investigate the methods' performance, we'll conduct multiple numerical experiments with two different meshes and two different sampling points. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use. Alongside the code, a simulation benchmark suite has also been made available online.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. This finding provides a practical solution to mitigate the spillover's impact or overcome the limitations of the Thomas-Fermi model in similar scenarios involving close contact between metals and reduces the complexity of simulations involving small gaps. Furthermore, we explore the temporal variation of the electron's response and find that both the spillover and gap size can lead to the emergence of distinct subcycles in metal regions near interfaces with photons with short lifetimes. This subcycle phenomenon is visible both above and below the Fermi level and is unaffected by the type of electron behavior when considering gaps larger than 0.5 nm. In such cases, the spillover's effect on this subcycle is more significant than that of the gap size. Ultimately, we suggest that future electron spillover studies should be preceded by a quantum hydrodynamics simulation of the local electron behavior to provide parameters for the Thomas-Fermi model, especially for understanding the quantum hydrodynamics's threshold behavior in the context of spillover. This research is applicable to a wide range of metal interfaces, including metallic surfaces in contact with each other, metals combined with semiconductors or insulators, and metal-molecule interactions in molecular switching devices. Consequently, our findings will contribute significantly to a deeper understanding of the physical mechanisms governing the behavior of electrons at metal interfaces and in reducing the limitations of local response models. This, in turn, will pave the way for further optimization of the performance of metal-based devices. The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved. Additionally, this work provides an overview of the strong normalization proofs in relation to the construction of dependent types in programming languages and discusses the implications of this research for the development of programming languages and type theory. This survey is intended for programmers and researchers familiar with programming languages and type theory, who can use this in-depth review as a foundation for further exploration of the subject matter. The associated technical report contains a more comprehensive literature review and is available as a separate download. MacIntyre, published by Elsevier in 2011. We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics. These models have proven accessible and instructive for our own educational path, and we hope they will resonate with readers looking to introduce these compelling topics in their own classrooms. 

Despite the simplicity of one-dimensional topological phases, there is an ongoing misconception that students cannot fully grasp their underlying mechanisms without advanced quantum many-body theory. In reality, the fundamental principles of one-dimensional topological phases can be understood using basic quantum mechanics and chemistry. 

We began our research on one-dimensional topological phases several years ago with the goal of creating a suite of publicly available numerical codes that could simulate and teach key concepts behind these phenomena. Along our educational path, we used the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model to explore various aspects of one-dimensional topological phases, starting from their electronic and transport properties, delving into electron-electron interactions, polarization, geometric phase, entanglement, and finally fermionic and bosonic multicomponent systems. 

Here, we invite your attention to a suite of publicly available numerical codes that we created to conduct these studies, along with previously unpublished results obtained using these codes. We also provide code snippets that can be used as a starting point for further research or educational presentations. 

Here is a list of the main concepts that we explored along with relevant code files: 

* Basic properties of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model (Code File 1)
* Electron-electron interactions (Code File 2)
* Entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix (Code File 3)
* Geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics (Code File 4)
* Multicomponent systems (Code File 5)

All code files can be found under https://github.com/eduardorj/sosh-1d-topology. We hope that this educational introduction, accompanied by freely accessible numerical codes, will inspire undergraduate and early graduate students to explore one-dimensional topological phases and, more broadly, the fascinating world of quantum electronics.

Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. Further analysis on the dimer's behavior highlighted the importance of exchange field orientation in determining YSR state splitting. This knowledge may contribute to the direct observation of magnetic dimer behavior on superconducting surfaces.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), we demonstrate significant enhancements to mask quality using the predictions of FourierMask. Compared to Mask R-CNN at the same resolution, FourierMask achieves comparable performance on the MS COCO dataset while delivering superior results at higher resolutions. Moreover, FourierMask surpasses Mask R-CNN at higher resolutions (36x) on the PASCAL VOC dataset, a more realistic dataset. Consequently, FourierMask proves that implicit functions integrated with Fourier transformations excel in instance segmentation and can efficiently handle high-resolution real-world images. The code and models are available at https://github.com/yunuis/FourierMask.

This study examines how the discrete nature of the frequency spectrum for a non-compact manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space affects its boundary points, focusing particularly on the Hausdorff dimension of those boundary points. Specifically, if a flat, extrinsically bounded two-dimensional surface is mapped onto a bounded, three-dimensional convex area, and the boundary points have a certain measure, the surface will have a discrete frequency spectrum. The theorem is relevant to recent research involving the construction of bounded, flat disks, and it answers a previously asked question about the frequency spectrum of certain surfaces. Additionally, this study demonstrates the precision of its results by showing counter-examples and a new method for identifying essential frequencies. This new method determines the essential frequencies of a surface by analyzing its connectivity components, and it raises questions about the dynamics of surfaces with limited connectivity. This research is part of an ongoing investigation aimed at understanding how the frequency spectrum of a surface affects its connectivity components. Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects. Developing efficient forward solvers for three-dimensional radiative transfer will be crucial for applying this method from space. By acknowledging the existence of optically thick cloud cores, where scattered photons do not contribute useful information, we can refine future 3D retrievals. Investigating this phenomenon using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we identified key insights to streamline cloud tomographic reconstruction. Notably, we determined the veiled core of optically thick clouds to typically be at an optical distance of around 5 from the cloud's boundary, allowing for more efficient use of computational resources and potential improvements to reconstruction algorithms. To test this new framework's feasibility, we developed a simulated stochastic solver for 3D radiative transfer and applied it to reconstructions of cloud tomographic slabs and spheres. Comparing these results to traditional 1D retrievals highlighted the superior accuracy of 3D reconstructions, especially for estimating cloud size. Slower convective clouds, where particles are larger and more compact, allowed for 3D reconstructions to recover core temperatures with high accuracy. However, this was not the case for faster clouds, where particles are smaller and more dispersed, likely due to the influence of cloud dynamics on radiative transfer. Despite this, we found that cloud tomography remains a viable technique for analyzing convective clouds even in cases where the core is not completely optically thick. Furthermore, our simulations demonstrated that cloud tomography can be an effective tool for monitoring changes in cloud morphology, particularly core temperatures, making it suitable for tracking high-latitude cloud changes over monthly cycles. Ultimately, we believe that refining 3D radiative transfer solvers utilizing satellite data will be crucial for applying cloud tomography from space. We examined how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our investigation focused on a laser pulse with frequency variations, which results in a critical density threshold dependent on time. The model we applied goes beyond the initial assumption of linear variation. Our analysis shows that in cases of negative frequency variations, the higher frequency component interacts with the target before the lower frequency component, whereas the reverse occurs in positive frequency variations. As a result, a more densely packed plasma is needed for transmission with negative frequency variations, as opposed to unchirped or positively chirped pulses. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties. Finally, by calculating the formation energies of these defects, we found that nitrogen defects form easier in anatase TiO2, whereas carbon defects form easier in rutile TiO2, and that interstitial N defects have the lowest formation energy of all considered configurations.  This could have significant implications for improving the photocatalytic properties of TiO2.  We hope that experimental verification of our results can be carried out in the future.
