Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays offer a rich understanding of galaxy clusters' dynamics. Maintaining equilibrium within the ICM is partially achieved by non-thermal pressure and the dissipation of turbulent energy. X-ray emission line mapping, essential for studying ICM turbulence, is complicated by the lack of high-resolution spectroscopy. Future X-ray detectors like the X-IFU on Athena will enable thorough investigations of ICM turbulence across multiple scales. Crucial metrics for such studies include line shift and broadening maps, as well as the second-order structure function. When analyzing these quantities, measurements are constrained by instrumental uncertainties and the inherent variability in cosmic observations. Here, the formalism established in a previous paper is expanded to account for the statistical uncertainty in line diagnostics, specifically structure functions. Statistical variance contributes to total variance in several ways, influenced by the detector's geometry, spatial binning, and the characteristics of turbulent fields. These terms hold significant importance for studying turbulence at smaller scales. A demonstration is conducted for the X-IFU using a simulated turbulent velocity map of a galaxy cluster resembling Coma. Results indicate excellent agreement with theoretical formulas for structure function estimation and its associated variance. These derived expressions can be applied to any X-ray measurement of turbulent structure functions and provide a framework for optimizing future instrumentation and observational strategies. Optimizing such measurements will be crucial for accurately studying ICM turbulence with a new generation of X-ray detectors.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Our methodology involves applying the Shimony-Tarui theorem from our previous work, and establishing the $\lambda$ value for structures with five vertices where every edge is either red or blue. Specifically, we show that the highest $\lambda$ value for such structures occurs at 7/8, and demonstrate the applicability of this method to similar problems. Additionally, we present an alternative approach using Erdos' lower estimate for the sum of squares problem, and establish the $\lambda$ value for structures with six vertices where at least one edge is of a specific color, such as green, with a $\lambda$ value of 1 - (1/2)^5, or 229/256. Notably, this last result holds even if no two blue edges share a common vertex. Our novel techniques allow us to re-prove Szariski's result for upper density in the context of Erdos-Rényi random graphs, and provide a simpler proof for the $\lambda$ value in the context of Erdos-Rényi random graphs with an specified color. Lastly, we explore the application of these methods to all-to-all communications games in graph theory. 

This work is a direct continuation of our previous paper, and deepens the upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically focused on the investigation of structures with an arbitrary number of vertices in every possible two-edge coloring of an infinite complete graph. We establish lower bounds for $\lambda$ values in various cases, surpassing former upper bounds for cliques and odd cycles, and present novel approaches applicable to similar problems. Our techniques also enable us to tackle Erdos' lower estimate for the sum of squares problem, as well as explore the application of these methods to all-to-all communications games in graph theory.

This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have significant abelian subgroups of a comparable size to the group itself. Specifically, G's polynomial diameter implies the existence of an abelian subgroup consisting of at least half of G's members, and this abelian subgroup can be generated by a quantity similar to the diameter itself. Consequently, the scale of the polynomial diameter is equivalent to the quartic scale of the group's size, and it surpasses previous lower bounds predicted by nilpotent group theories. Moreover, this research establishes a connection between a group's diameter and its nonabelian torsion elements, and it sets bounds on the group's diagonalizable subsets based on the polynomial diameter. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. To further highlight its effectiveness, the proposed design was integrated into an adaptive DVS system, demonstrating successful voltage adjustment and resulting energy savings of up to 12%. In addition, the proposed design was compared to existing temperature sensor designs, highlighting its unique features, outstanding performance, and compact design. Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap-stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has been observed but the exact stellar interior conditions responsible are still the focus of ongoing research. Studies have revealed that magnetic fields purely in the toroidal or poloidal configurations inevitably succumb to instability. In contrast, numerical simulations have consistently shown stability in the axisymmetric configurations of the magnetic fields found within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These stable configurations consist of intertwined toroidal and poloidal components resembling a twisted torus. Prior studies have identified rough limits to the ratio of the toroidal and poloidal magnetic energy. In order to define the conditions necessary for these stable configurations, we ran three-dimensional simulations utilizing the Pencil Code for non-rotating stars experiencing viscosity-driven dissipation. Our simulations were performed for both barotropic stars with constant specific entropy and stably stratified stars, while varying parameters including the level of stable stratification and magnetic energy in each component, confirming existing predictions for the stability boundaries. Additionally, we derived equations describing the equilibrium states and stability criteria in terms of the energy ratios and stable stratification parameters, thus defining the conditions necessary for stable twisted magnetic fields within non-turbulent stellar interiors. These conditions are met by stars with stable stratification holding at least 10% of their magnetic energy in the toroidal component, having a magnetic energy ratio of $|\beta_t/\beta_p| \lesssim 10$ and a stable stratification parameter of $Q \gtrsim 10$, which can be found in the stable regime of our stable stratification experiments ranging from $10^{-4} \lesssim Q \lesssim 10^{-1}$. The necessary conditions for stable twisted magnetic fields provide a theoretical framework for interpreting magnetic field data and offers a predictive tool for modeling the evolution of these fields. The ratio of toroidal to poloidal magnetic energy is the primary indicator for stable twisted magnetic fields, which can be applied to various types of stars with stable twisted magnetic fields. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse-graining changes. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. Additionally, our findings facilitate fresh perspectives on renormalization group flows, including understanding how the nature of the flow might be irreversible. We explore the application of our framework to one-dimensional and higher-dimensional models and anticipate it to contribute positively to further research into the renormalization group in quantum field theories. We also anticipate related studies could lead to an improved comprehension of phase transitions in statistical physics. Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, enabling users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options. By integrating multiple music databases simultaneously, Pied Piper can present users with a results page featuring songs that match their query, complete with accompanying audio and lyrics for each match. Furthermore, Pied Piper introduces an innovative ranking algorithm to ensure the display order of search results is both musically coherent and relevant to the user's query. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through comparative trials involving 5000 randomly generated queries, which showcases Pied Piper's capacity to deliver more accurate and user-friendly search results when compared to standard search engines and standalone music database searches. Additionally, we explore methods for enhancing Pied Piper by integrating additional music databases and leveraging user feedback. Given the existing implementation of Pied Piper, we outline practical steps for building a full-fledged web application that can be accessed via the desktop or mobile browsers through a user-friendly interface. Our aim is to introduce a more effective music search solution that can rival established search engines like Google and YouTube by integrating a user-friendly web interface with the existing meta-search engine. By doing so, we hope to provide music enthusiasts with a more suitable search alternative that can be used freely without charges. Ultimately, this proposal offers a starting point for developing a superior music search engine that can serve as a free alternative to existing music search solutions. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  In addition, we discovered that both protostellar and starless cores within the Dragon cloud exhibit similar spectral energy distributions, with no distinct differences in their characteristics.  This finding suggests that the conversion of cores to protostars may be a relatively quick process, likely occurring over a few core mass units, and without any significant alteration in the core's temperature or luminosity.  Therefore, it may be necessary to reevaluate the core mass function's lower limit in order to more accurately understand the origin of massive star formation.  Finally, we observed that both protostellar and starless cores within the Dragon cloud are embedded within dense gas environments, defined as high-density clumps, and are structured as small, compact clusters rather than solitary objects.  This leads to the hypothesis that the formation of large clumps plays a crucial role in the formation of massive star clusters.  Therefore, based on the characteristics of the Dragon infrared dark cloud, we propose that the formation of massive star clusters is initiated at an early stage of clump formation, prior to the formation of stellar clusters, and involves the birth of small compact groups of protostars within dense gas environments.  Future research is necessary to validate this hypothesis through observations and computer simulations.  In addition, we suggest enhancing core mass functions with a composite model that integrates a standard core mass function and a protostellar mass function, and propose using this model to analyze core populations within other infrared dark clouds.  Finally, we propose posing the question, "What is the origin of the mass function of new stars?" in relation to the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of newly formed stars, and challenge the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple dimension reduction techniques, spanning PCA to neural network-based encoders, to illustrate their influence on classification outcomes. Our results reveal that combining feature engineering with a method like PCA leads to better classification accuracy when compared to straightforward classification of raw data. Moreover, using contextual information represents a crucial aspect in achieving high accuracy. We have made our code publicly available to facilitate the classification of similar LiDAR data sets. However, we have not included actual data collections due to copyright restrictions associated with research publications. Instead, we advise utilizing existing publicly accessible data sets, such as the ones referenced in our research, for testing and comparing different classification approaches. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for further exploration of advanced classification techniques within complex 3D LiDAR data settings, especially those involving rotational transformations, by providing access to our code and presenting initial performance benchmarks. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. Additionally, this paper explores the general properties of these new operators and establishes their applicability to various special functions, including spherical Bessel functions, hypergeometric functions, and Whittaker functions. The created operators enable the construction of new zonal functions with (strict) positive definiteness for fractional dimensions, thus bridging the gap in positive definite quantum field theory. This development particularly benefits the Dunkl harmonic analysis on the real line, characterized by the failure of usual hypergeometric function convergence due to a fractional dimension. This paper's innovations provide a unified framework, enabling the introduction of a family of (strictly) positive definite zonal functions for fractional dimensions, valid for any non-negative space dimension, regardless of its rationality. Consequently, this implies the convergence of associated expansion series, such as spherical Bessel functions, hypergeometric functions, and Whittaker functions, for any fractional dimension, accompanied by associated Asymptotic Approximations. This paper's findings are accompanied by numerical examples, confirming the proposed method's efficacy. The created operators open up new research avenues in the context of analytical physics and special functions. As a by-product, this paper presents novel Asymptotic Approximations, expanding on the classical results by Watson, Erdelyi, and others. The methods introduced in this paper further facilitate the resummation of divergent series, revealing a powerful tool for the resummation of convergent series. The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased glimpse into hadronic interactions of cosmic rays. This paper introduces three new strategies to link neutrino and UHECR arrival directions. With upgraded data sets from IceCube Neutrino Observatory and ANTARES for neutrinos, as well as from Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array for UHECRs, statistical significance and accuracy are significantly improved. Specifically, three methodologies are presented to identify UHECR-UHE neutrino pairs and neutrino ensembles associated with UHECR arrival directions. Furthermore, to minimize potential biases, the statistical analysis is performed with a comprehensive set of controls that neutrino and UHECR datasets are randomly manipulated to prevent any dependence on real data. Applying these methods to real data, slight deviations from random expectations are observed with varying significance levels. Notably, the simplest pair search methodology yields significant p-values for protons and neutrons at 4.05*10^-3 and 6.08*10^-3, respectively. Moreover, when restricting UHECR energies to simulate interactions resulting in neutrino energies observed in IceCube, the p-values become even more notable at 3.67*10^-3 for protons. Additionally, substantial UHECR clusters are identified around approximately 20% of all neutrino events with energies exceeding 56 EeV, with the largest concentration found near the Vela supern remnant. Consequently, it is hypothesized that high-energy neutrino sources, which include UHECR clusters and supern remnant neutrino single events, may be closely linked to massive hadronic processes involving high-energy UHECR interactions that result in neutrino production. Further research is necessary to validate the findings and understand the underlying physics behind these hypothetical connections. The methods presented in this paper provide a statistical framework that is not limited to UHECR-UHE neutrino correlations and can be applied to any multivariate analysis involving UHECR and neutrino datasets. Ultimately, with upgraded and new-generation neutrino and UHECR facilities, a significant breakthrough in solving the UHECR enigma may be achieved in the near future. The strategies outlined in this paper are available online at https://github.com/ahmaddilelma/UHECR-Neutrino-Correlation.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to detect outliers through one-dimensional and two-dimensional projections of CNN features. Our approach to handle the anomalous class involved comparing two scenarios: first, where the anomalous class is integrated with typical classes; and second, where the anomalous class is excluded from the dataset. For the first scenario, we proposed an anomaly detection metric that assessed the CNN model's performance. For the second scenario, we presented a method to estimate the accuracy on normal classes when the anomalous class is excluded from the dataset. Additionally, we examined the impact of removing the anomalous class from the dataset. To diagnose skin cancer from metadata, we used a simple ensemble of decision trees. However, since the challenge lacked truly anomalous images, we defined an image as anomalous if its prediction probability for a specific class exceeded a certain threshold based on the entire dataset. Consequently, our best model's anomaly detection performance was evaluated under various threshold conditions. All methods presented in this report are publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/ISIC_2019.

When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of states, including both reflection-symmetric states and asymmetric states, are presented in this study. The relationship between the size of the membrane system and a particular natural scale dictates both primary state transformations from the unperturbed state as well as the start and form of additional secondary branches that occur during the membrane's response to changes in its surroundings. The membrane's behavior is such that when its size is held constant, variations in the inner fluid's density result in changes to the finger pattern while changes in the membrane's size produce distinct transformations in the pattern in a non-trivial manner. Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications. In fact, the sign of work becomes negative, indicating that energy is released from the system, not expended, and this effect diminishes over time as the system equilibrates. Notably, our approach also provides a framework for calculating nonequilibrium free energy differences directly from observable time averages, unencumbered by the need for reversible pathways. This advancement is further illustrated by deriving an expression for nonequilibrium free energy differences in terms of time-averaged microwork, which is directly measurable in experiments using nonequilibrium fluctuations techniques. Ultimately, our study showcases the effectiveness of microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics in analyzing complex dynamical systems involved in expansion or contraction processes.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, which may reflect the abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN. The calculated CCH over CN ratio is higher for cyclopentadiene but significantly lower for benzene. The formation of the cyclical compounds in TMC-1 can be attributed to a reaction pathway based on neutral-neutral reactions, which also suggests benzene's expected abundance should be comparable to that of cyclopentadiene. However, benzene formation might be impeded in TMC-1 by a side reaction based on CN, which could explain the low abundance of cyano benzene relative to cycloadducts of CNC and CCH with benzene. The expected abundance of the cyano and ethynyl derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are significantly lower than the noise level of current telescopes but considerably higher than detection limits of upcoming sensitive telescopes. Therefore, further observations in areas like TMC-1 and in other carbon chain-rich molecular clouds are necessary to confirm these predictions. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. The proposed models excel particularly in predicting target words that appear infrequently in sentences. We also analyze the theoretical advantages of our model and provide insights into its performance from both quantitative and qualitative perspectives. The code for our novel look-ahead attention model is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ZhuyunLi/LAAT. The paper's final version can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.12079, and we have achieved state-of-the-art results on the WMT 2016 English-to-German translation task at https://conferences.unige.ch/sci-nlp/2018/en/short-papers.html#sp15.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. Looked at in reverse, the sequence of events that led to accurate, reliable, and high-performance grid computing was predicated on making the software accessible to average users. Consequently, we outline the key characteristics of successful translational computer science projects, using grid computing as an illustrative example. Finally, we explore implications of this experience for the ongoing development of grid computing and potential applications to other areas in the field of translational computer science. In addition, we detail specific contributions that the GAT framework makes to addressing scalability issues in grid computing. Specifically, we present strategies for addressing both horizontal and vertical scalability concerns. Furthermore, we include future directions for the GAT framework that could be applied to other similar challenges in the field of grid computing and translational computer science. In conclusion, we believe that our perspective on the development of grid computing, fueled by a focus on direct application, can offer valuable lessons for other projects in the field of translational computer science. In addition, we feel that the GAT framework's approach to addressing scalability issues in grid computing is a relevant contribution that could be explored in other contexts. Consequently, we are making the GAT framework publicly available to facilitate collaboration and to stimulate discussion on related concerns in the field. Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills. We also make these data sets and visualizations publicly available to foster further research in this area. The effective management of urban roads plays a crucial role in the optimal operation of urban transportation systems and overall city functioning. Current monitoring techniques rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a groundbreaking approach of mobile sensing is presented, utilizing a large fleet of ridesharing vehicles to monitor and interpret the condition of urban roads as they traverse through the network. Our analysis assesses the sensing performance of this approach based on several key factors including road segments covered, data reliability due to repeated visits, and implicit inferences drawn from collected data combined with urban road topology. A model for optimizing routing is developed to balance maximum coverage and highest reliability of collected data, with the capability to be solved efficiently through a heuristic algorithm. Real-world data from over 20,000 ridesharing vehicles in New York City is utilized for thorough experimentation and analysis of sensitivity. Our results show significant advancements in road coverage and reliability improvement through this approach, achieving an overall coverage rate of up to 75.5% of all road segments with 97.2% of those implicitly covered, alongside a reliability boost of at least 31.1% compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, optimization of routing results in reliable data coverage within 5-10 minutes of driving time. A theoretical analysis and empirical validation of the model's reliability showcase its capability to provide reliable data in as little as 30 minutes of driving. This pioneering approach of using ridesharing vehicles for mobile sensing paves the way for utilizing other types of city mobility networks, offering potential applications in scientific research, traffic management, and vehicle service network optimization. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. As a result, our study highlights the potential of J/ψ invisible decays to set stringent limits on light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter, leading to a crucial role for J/ψ experiments in the search for these fundamental components of new physics. In addition, our analysis demonstrates the value of exploring J/ψ rare decays at next-generation J/ψ facilities, such as highly sensitive searches for J/ψ decays into muon pairs or other rare hadronic or leptonic final states, which could lead to groundbreaking contributions to the field of flavor physics. Consequently, our research emphasizes the scientific significance of thoroughly studying the J/ψ spectrum and its rare decays in upcoming experiments. Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis. Additionally, we compare the performance of our new methods with existing ones, including the explicit Runge-Kutta and general linear methods, on a set of benchmark functions. Further, we also consider the application of our new methods to differential-algebraic equations of index one by transforming them into stiff systems equivalence.Numerical experiments are performed using the solver daeStep from the PETSc library and our own implementation in C++, with source code available for the SGLM type odeStep. This work offers a preliminary exploration of variable stepsize SGLMs and p-stage SGLMs for differential-algebraic equations, and there are numerous directions for further research in this area.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. To achieve this, the authors split a typical density mask mask into two separate components, then trained two separate models to map images to binary masks and density masks respectively. To facilitate model generalization across multiple sclerosis plaque and colon adenocarcinoma tissue images, four diverse datasets were assembled for training. The unprecedented complexity of these training datasets, combined with the incorporation of plaque boundaries found in three of the datasets, led to outstanding performance, with accurate detection of complex nuclei structures, overlapping nuclei, and precise boundary estimation. In a benchmark test on unseen images from the four datasets, the proposed W-shaped network yielded outstanding results, surpassing state-of-the-art algorithms, demonstrating its capability to handle a wide range of challenging nucleus instances, and providing a reliable foundation for further cancer diagnosis tasks. Furthermore, the approach provides intuitive insights into cross-stage feature extraction, demonstrating the model's generalizability across different tissues and plaques. The authors also explore various applications of this approach, utilizing the dense masks to extract valuable information for cancer diagnosis, such as tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, necrotic regions and adenoma thickness. Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are then described as non-flat connections, from which conserved charges can be deduced using established formulas, albeit those of standard Chern-Simons theory. The soliton's stability and characteristics are determined based on holonomic constraints along cyclic paths, while in rotating hairy black holes cases, the theory allows recovery of the temperature and chemical potential. The entropy generated by the black holes in these scenarios remains consistent with that predicted by the Chern-Simons theory. The conformal equivalent to this framework describes General Relativity's interaction with a cosmologically constant scalar field. The redefinition of the Chern-Simons form for this system, using suitable composite gauge fields, is explored in a simplified form. In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Furthermore, we derive an analogous algorithm for the $k$-median problem with similar storage requirements, thus bridging the storage gap between $k$-means and $k$-median in high-dimensional spaces. Leveraging our core algorithms, we mitigate the impact of removing past data points by introducing an extended algorithm with increased space consumption, thereby mitigating the difficulty of maintaining $k$-means clustering accuracy in the face of evolving data streams. Experimental results validate the efficacy of our proposed algorithms in both synthetic and real-world datasets. Notably, our $k$-means algorithm outperforms contemporary algorithms in a cloud environment and matches or surpasses their performance in in-house settings, while our $k$-median algorithm exhibits comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art methods across various datasets and scenarios.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Additionally, we observe that utilizing outcomes as rewards enables seamless integration with state-based reinforcement learning methods. Our results highlight the hierarchy's potential to streamline the process of modeling complex grid worlds and provide a foundation for exploring more sophisticated multi-level architectures in recursive PEGs. Furthermore, we open-source our implementation to facilitate future research and cooperation in this domain.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in instances where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components in a 'cyclic' triple. 

Additionally, we introduce an alternative model based on comparing the medians of random variables rather than their order, which allows us to derive exact values for the probabilities associated with the median in a 'cyclic' triple and provide upper and lower limits for the same probabilities in instances where n is 4 or greater. Our analysis provides an insight into the distribution of the central component in an n-tuple and establishes that this distribution becomes increasingly uniform as n increases without bound. 

Our work is further expanded to explore 'cyclic' quadruples and the associated probabilities, which indicates a probability approaching 1 for any 'cyclic' quadruple, and enables us to identify the specific distribution associated with the order of these quadruples. We conclude our research by examining the probabilities associated with the order of 'cyclic' n-tuples of any length, and present an open question regarding the distribution of the central component in such n-tuples. 

Our analysis is supported by numerical data obtained through the use of a Monte Carlo algorithm, which involves the generation of random n-tuples based on specified probability

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be trained with more stability using limited training data. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters. Moreover, the proposed method achieves enhanced denoising performance, especially in complex scenarios such as CT density scaling and noise reduction, and can be easily adapted to other imaging modalities such as MRI. With significantly reduced complexity, the proposed architecture not only accelerates training but also makes the model more suitable for mobile and embedded devices. To facilitate further research, we have released the new proposed architecture along with code and data at: https://github.com/ResearchingAI/SSGAN-LDCT. Additionally, sample output images demonstrating our method's performance can be viewed at: https://researchingai.github.io/SSGAN-LDCT/.

Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method on wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects in rotating distorted halo nuclei. Our findings further highlight the importance of considering both single particle configuration and continuum effects when studying collective behavior in exotic nuclei. Finally, we propose that rotating distorted halo nuclei offer a crucial testing ground for coupling schemes used in nuclear many-body theory. Our research provides new perspectives on rotating exotic nuclei, offering a framework that researchers can use to study a wide range of topics, from shape evolution to pair correlations. Ultimately, our approach paves the way for a deeper understanding of the interplay between single particle and collective effects in the most tightly bound systems in the universe, phenomena unique to the behavior of exotic nuclear rotations.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing. Our research lays the foundation for future video enhancement research, with theoretical analysis and extensive experiments demonstrating the benefits of the proposed model.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. The inclusion of non-standard gauge boson states such as dark photons and axion-like particles is also explored through the incorporation of effective dark photon and axion-like particle codes. The output of this research will be useful in informing the design of future lepton colliders operating above a few TeV. The implementation of W/Z PDFs will be made publicly available as part of the MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO package. The code for forward beam spectrum simulation is also publicly available under the name of Forward-BS. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/owenscully/mbmmt. 

Authors employ a variety of baseline models, including graph neural networks and
recurrent models, and demonstrate that subsiding models outperform them in
multi-task settings. Moreover, they exhibit that their method achieves the highest
average rewards in both the mini-grid and Vizdoom games, surpassing the reward
expectations in the latter by 5% compared to the worst-case performance. 
Finally, they provide visual evidence highlighting the learning dynamics of 
their method, showing that isolated sub-networks specialize in task-specific 
dynamics. 

By using a single dynamics model and subdividing it into task-specific 
components, authors open up an interesting direction for future research in 
multi-task reinforcement learning. 

All models and data used in this research are available at https://github.com/owenscully/mbmmt.

Building upon these foundational results, we formally establish the converse: assuming a formal system meets specific criteria, we can construct a suitable arithmetical theory that yields the respective theorems, their strengthened forms, and a fundamental lemma concerning the consistency theorem. This construction offers a holistic understanding of these fundamental results within the context of first-order logic and its relationships to cognitive science and computer science. Furthermore, our proof strategy offers a paradigm for using theorems as data in a more general metatheoretic framework. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Additionally, we present an application of the three balls theorem to a type of Riemann-Hilbert problem within the R^n+1 complex plane. Furthermore, we outline how the three balls theorem can be used to prove a variant of the Schauder estimate for solutions to the Dirac equation Du = λu. This involves demonstrating the boundedness of the operator involved, which can be viewed as a corollary to the three balls theorem. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. Ultimately, despite some initial discrepancies, direct prediction proved the most robust in handling image and depth noise but fared poorly with segmentation noise, while other methods converged to similar performance levels across different noise levels but struggled in clean-signal conditions. Through additional testing in a real-world environment, we found the best method to be the direct prediction approach, which successfully calibrated the camera with satisfactory accuracy in a laboratory setting. However, its effectiveness in a more dynamic environment, such as on top of a mobile robot, remains to be investigated. The code and datasets used in this research are available for public access.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, our approach demonstrates the capacity to create realistic samples even when the mean of the posterior distribution is not accurate. One of the key advantages of our method is its ability to decrease the amount of training data required by utilizing a regularized version of the opponent, which led to accurate results when testing the method on public datasets such as MRI with multiple coils and Stacked Face dataset. We also show that the proposed method converges to a stable equilibrium by implementing a gan module with a fixed generator and analyzing the geometry of the resulting samples. Our code is available online at the address provided.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. We conclude by discussing the significance of invariant sets in the context of stability and the central manifold theorem. Notably, we provide a brief explanation of how the geometry of the central manifold influences the stability of the system in a fractional-order context. This discussion serves as a starting point for a more in-depth exploration of the topic, which includes a review of related stability theorems and their implications. We also introduce the basic concepts underlying the construction of the central manifold in a fractional-order system, which has not been comprehensively addressed in existing literature. We hope this introductory overview will prove useful for readers new to the subject, while also providing a concise reference for experts looking to apply these concepts to the analysis of fractional-order systems. Expertise required for this topic ranges from basic dynamical systems knowledge to advanced concepts involving the construction of the central manifold. This article aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the main ideas involved in constructing the central manifold in a fractional-order system, which has not been comprehensively addressed in existing literature. We hope this will prove useful both for readers new to the subject and as a concise reference for experts looking to apply these concepts to the analysis of fractional-order systems. We also hope to spark further exploration into the many fascinating aspects related to the construction of the central manifold in a fractional-order context. We look forward to seeing the exciting developments that future research will undoubtedly bring to this field. Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed in this paper that dynamically optimizes training levels across individual single-hop links, maximizing overall spectral efficiency. To tackle this optimization problem in the presence of channel state uncertainty and noise, a reinforcement learning solution inspired by the multi-armed bandit problem is proposed. Simulations show the new technique converges quickly in dynamic channel conditions and offers up to 75% better performance than conventional methods in terms of spectral efficiency. In addition, the proposed method is highly effective in mitigating interference in multi-access scenarios. To address implementation challenges, an architecture for hierarchical beam training is proposed based on existing protocols such as 5G New Radio. To take advantage of increasing computational power in edge nodes, a deep learning approach is also presented that can learn optimal training policies from historical data, leading to further performance gains. The results of this research can be applied to various multi-band communication scenarios, enabling efficient beam training in a rapidly evolving Terahertz frequency domain. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. The findings also suggest two screens are linked to distinct scintillation patterns observed simultaneously, implying very close distances between them. Furthermore, 17 isolated scintillation events with shorter durations were analyzed, providing insight into moving screens and their connection to the pulsar's velocity vector. The study reveals a substantial distribution of screen locations relative to the pulsar, with a significant discrepancy in locations that would result from a moving screen as the Earth orbits the pulsar. The screens play a crucial role in modifying the pulsar's electromagnetic signal, making their study vital for accurately interpreting scientific data related to pulsars. The methods employed in this research can be applied to a comprehensive re-examination of screen properties in the Milky Way's spiral arms. The analysis of moving screens may provide valuable information about the disk's rotation and perspective on the spiral arms, as well as the distribution of stellar imprints within the interstellar medium. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of scattering screens, shaped by the forces of gravity and charge, will offer a more comprehensive view of the complex relationships within our galaxy's dynamic system. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Additionally, subjective assessments confirm the superiority of QPNet's sound quality over the basic WN model. Furthermore, our study shows that a compact cascaded network can yield comparable performance to a full cascaded architecture with significantly fewer parameters. To facilitate reproducibility, the proposed QPNet models are openly available at https://github.com/yj151140/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet. 

Keywords: quasi-periodic signals, wavenet, pitch control, dilated convolutional neural networks, speech synthesis.

Planets similar to Earth, orbiting nearby stars with reduced energy output, are being extensively studied and several are suited for further analysis. Focusing on temperate worlds surrounded by thick H2 atmospheres, our models follow chemical transformations and gas circulation after H2O, CH4, NH3, and H2S molecules break apart under stellar radiation and various atmospheric conditions. According to our simulations, NH3 molecules are destroyed by solar energy in most scenarios, while generating HCN and other compounds in the process. However, if atmospheric temperatures rise above 180K, NH3 can regain some stability. Systems with extensive NH3 breakdown and moderate temperatures also create sulfur-containing compounds that could eventually combine with iron to form solid particles, albeit only in atmospheres where NH3 is present in large quantities. Yet, even in such cases the formation of solid particles is highly slow-blinking on cosmic timescales. Models indicating the existence of thick H2O or CH4 atmospheres forming around M stars appear inconsistent with observations of similar atmospheres around M stars, while also contradicting established understanding of M star atmospheric behavior. Lastly, our study highlights the need for a thorough assessment of how the presence of H2 and various molecules affects the formation of atmospheric opacities, when analyzing spectral energy distributions of exoplanet atmoses. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Moreover, this relationship enables the derivation of shadow functors for specific bicategorical THH constructions, such as THH of a category or a 2-category, consistent with their categorified counterparts. Additionally, this framework results in an explicit description of shadow functors for various bicategorical constructions, obtained through the application of Berman's extension to functors of a particular form, obtained in turn through a process of categorified localisation. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. All code and models are available for download at https://github.com/hjewell/sound-source- localization. The VGG-Sound Source dataset can be accessed via the following link: https://www. research.vgg.ucl.ac.uk/publications/2022/09/sound-source-localization- dataset.html. The dataset is also openly available via Pastebin: https://pastebin. research.vgg.ucl.ac.uk/104. Additionally, the dataset can be obtained from Pastebin for the following categories: animals https://pastebin. research.vgg.ucl.ac.uk/105, food https://pastebin.research.vgg.ucl.ac.uk/106, and activities https://pastebin.research.vgg.ucl.ac.uk/107. The dataset includes audio descriptions for 10,000 video clips, with a separate paper detailing the audio description generation process. The dataset demonstrates notable improvements over prior work based on image-classification methods, achieving a top-1 accuracy of 44.95% on the validation set and 45.06% on the test set. The dataset's effectiveness is further highlighted by the fact that models trained on it perform source localization on unseen video classes with a top-1 accuracy of 26.14%.
