Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Moreover, LGCN successfully applies metric learning to cross-domain graph classification, and it is plausible that it may enhance the understanding of complex biological networks represented in hyperbolic space. The LGCN framework is available at https://github.com/ghulghule/LGCN.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Additionally, a single output approach solves the inverse problem with a non-standard time-dependent source term. Though this strategy yields stability in the appropriate Sobolev space, it falls short of the desired stability estimate due to the limited information extracted from a single output. Consequently, an alternative approach involving multiple outputs is implemented to achieve the desired stability estimate. Notably, increasing the dimension does not improve the current estimate due to the overwhelming impact of the dimension on the Carleman estimate. Consequently, the current estimate does not match the optimal dimension-dependent decay rate implied by the Helmerowski-Lassas-Leung results for the full source term reconstruction in this higher dimensional scenario. This research is complemented by a numerical implementation utilizing a single output and the Tikhonov method. Results for the full source term reconstruction, though, can only be numerically achieved through an iterative process that leverages the uniqueness proof and successive approximation. Notably, this numerical approach for the full source term reconstruction outperforms the single output strategy in all tested scenarios. Ultimately, this research is underpinned by a theoretical framework that leverages the Carleman estimate, observability inequality, compactness-uniqueness argument, operator theoretical approach, and a single output approach, all of which are complemented by a numerical implementation of the Tikhonov method. In particular, this research demonstrates the utility of Carleman estimate in complex mathematical models and highlights the advantages of employing multiple outputs to achieve optimal stability estimates. In addition, this study illustrates the effectiveness of the Tikhonov method in conjunction with theoretical uniqueness and stability results for both single and multi-output scenarios. Furthermore, this research indicates that, although the strategy employing a single output yields uniqueness and stability results, the optimal estimate can only be achieved through the use of multiple outputs. In contrast, increased dimensions do not improve the current estimate due to the overwhelming impact of the dimension on the Carleman estimate.

A new method has been created that successfully transfers squeezed states into optical cavities even in stable conditions. The method builds upon conventional optomechanical setups, utilizing a three-level atom to facilitate the transfer. Two techniques were devised to observe the squeezed state transfer effect, including applying a controlled influx of squeezed phonons and simulating the system in an environment of phonon-squeezed vibrations. Our model demonstrates the ability to efficiently achieve this transfer in optomechanical systems. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of phonon-squeezed vibrations on optical signals, finding that they not only enable the transfer of squeezed states but also allow for phonon-squeezing of optical fields via the interaction with a phonon-squeezed environment. This could lead to the development of optomechanical systems that employ phonon-squeezzed vibrations to transfer and manipulate the states of optical and mechanical systems. Consequently, this may facilitate a more efficient implementation of quantum manipulation and estimation using optomechanical systems. 

This method includes a model that effectively transfers a squeezed state into an optical cavity, as well as two alternative methods for observing the squeezed state transfer effect. In addition, we explore the influence of phonon-squeezed vibrations on optical signals, discovering that they enable the transfer of squeezed states and allow for the phonon-squeezing of optical fields via their interaction with a phonon-squeezed environment. variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our exponential dual model
replicates the same findings as the 2011 linear dual model proposed by Newhouse,
which involved a direct relationship between standard deviations of delay
discounting and variance of impulsivity, but with a significant reduction in
estimation error. Notably, our results also indicate that the majority of
subjects' data aligns with the dual model rather than the single- or multi-
peaked model. Finally, we include a feature that allows users to visualize
their own delay discounting curves using our web-based tool. A companion
piece to this paper includes a comprehensive review of the topic and a
methodological critique of previous research in the field. A corresponding
data set, complete with estimates for each subject, is available for public
access through the MPI for Personal Data. For further information on delay
discounting, please refer to the book chapter "Delay Discounting" by Bueler.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This choice of gauge can be viewed as a minimal solution to the mass problem of linearized massive gravity.  Furthermore, when solving the linearized Einstein equations under this harmonic gauge, the coefficient of the unwanted degree of freedom becomes zero, while the coefficient of the massive mode is determined to be $m^2 =1/(2k^2)$ for a non-dynamical vector field, in agreement with the findings of de la Cruz-Domeneck et. al.  For the linearized massive gravity model, the choice of this particular harmonic gauge leads to a five decoupled second-order differential equations for the propagating modes, allowing for the computation of the poles via the inverse problem of spectral function reconstruction, resulting in a mass spectrum consisting of a scalar mode at $m^2 = 1/(2k^2)$ and a fourth degree of freedom at $m^2 = 1/k^2$.  This model can be generalized to higher derivatives and still maintain the correct number of degrees of freedom.  When considering an irreducible symmetric tensor field of higher derivatives, the Fierz-Pauli type mass term is not sufficient, requiring an additional term involving the double derivative of the trace, resulting in a linearized massive gravity model that models this type of interaction.  Interestingly, this model contains an extra degree of freedom; however, this excess can be removed when the harmonic gauge is chosen appropriately, leading to a healthy linearized massive gravity model with this type of interaction.  This discussion on linearized massive gravity also extends to an irreducible symmetric tensor field of higher derivatives in an $N=2$ supergravity context.  Finally, the implications of this discussion on a nonlinear massive gravity model are briefly considered.  This work is based on the research paper "Harmonic Gauge and Higher Derivative Theories of Linearized Massive Gravity" by H. N. Md. Abdul, S. K. Roudra, and R. Ma

The goal of this article is to solve the minimum value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$, where $|A|$, when A is a set of integers, and investigate the underlying structure of A to achieve this minimum value. Additionally, some open questions related to $h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A$ are proposed in this article. 

In Part 1, we establish the minimum value of $|h\hat{}_{\underline{+}}A|$ when A contains elements from {-1,0,1} and prove that this minimum value can be achieved. In Part 2, we discuss the applicability of our method to sets with more complex structures and propose new open questions.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. Notably, it differs from existing datasets in various ways, such as being based on tissue samples rather than biopsies, containing a larger set of images featuring neoplastic lesions, and including a significant quantity of normal polyp tissue. For evaluation purposes, we trained and tested a basic convolutional neural network model, achieving impressive results of 92.95% accuracy in distinguishing benign polyps from adenomas and colorectal carcinoma, and obtaining a mean grade of 1.53 in grading adenomas. These outcomes indicate significant potential for using UniToPatho in developing artificial intelligence models capable of automating colorectal polyp characterization. In addition to the dataset, we've made available the related analysis, including evaluation metrics and comparison with state-of-the-art classification and grading models, via the accompanying paper. The comprehensive dataset, including code and slides, is now available online at the specified link. A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. However, it should be noted that trapping modes significantly reduce the method's efficiency. As such, further research is needed to address this limitation. The introduced approach and associated algorithms are implemented within the OpenSource MATLAB package called FFTFS. This package is particularly suited for addressing frequency-independent acoustic scattering issues and can be obtained at no cost from the MITACS repository under the name Front Tracking Fourier Solver (FFTFS). It is available for download at http://casa.gsc.nrc.cn/ Mitchell_English.html. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. 

This work also provides a deeper understanding of the formation of chondrite textures, suggesting that the antipodal method can reproduce end-textures and beginning textures, while only being able to partially mimic the development of intermediate textures. 

Finally, analyzing the D-poor hydrogen isotopic signatures in combination with water content allowed for a more precise classification of the thermal metamorphism conditions in the chondrite rocks, offering a perspective on the internal structure of the parent bodies and providing a framework for a more detailed study of the matematic processes themselves.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. Additionally, our models excel in zero-shot settings and outperform models trained on specific data for 8 out of 10 tested scenarios. We also observe improvements in cases with limited additional data, advancing the capabilities of speech-to-text models. Our code and data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ghrua/zs-s2t. Our findings represent significant breakthroughs in zero-shot speech-to-text and offer feasible methods for building multi-language speech-to-text models with minimal data requirements. These models increase the feasibility of deploying speech-to-text systems in situations where only limited data is available for a particular language pair. They also facilitate the ease of adding new language pairs without necessitating additional data collection. Moreover, our models' ability to leverage supplementary data enables them to surpass direct training results, thereby creating potential applications in noise-reduced speech-to-text scenarios. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for further investigations into zero-shot speech-to-text and its interconnected areas, which include speech recognition, machine translation, and text-to-speech. Consequently, our models may serve as suitable starting points for developing other zero-shot speech-related systems. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. This work was also featured in the 3rd International Workshop on Advanced Imaging for Clinical Applications at the Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention Conference 2020 in Cambridge, UK. In this research, tangible results of a disease transplanted onto normal chest X-rays were presented, featuring cardiac enlargement, lung lesions, and pulmonary edema. These groundbreaking images confirmed the feasibility of GAN-based medical imaging enhancement and hinted at the vast potential of this technique. In the long run, this could empower AI systems to generate realistic medical images to support training and validation of diagnosis models, even in data scarce scenarios. In this research, a StyleGAN was utilized, but other GAN-based generators can also be explored for similar applications. Furthermore, the developed inverse mapping framework is general and can be applied to various medical imaging transplants. While successful outcomes were achieved with the CheXpert dataset, the quality of images may decline when using datasets with poorer resolution. To address this issue, integrating resolution-specific encoders or coarse-to-fine processing methods could provide better results. Additionally, utilizing real medical images with marked affected areas for target segmentation can enhance the accuracy of transplanted images. Although the developed technique yields artificial images comparable to real images, the method still lacks an effective way to generate synthetic images that can fool medical specialists. In the short term, this research can facilitate the development of new medical imaging scans without exposing real patient data. Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments. We also discuss potential applications of this algorithm, such as solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations, and suggest possible extensions, such as using this algorithm for other integral equations or modifying it for boundary value problems. We conclude by highlighting potential future research directions and suggesting that this algorithm could benefit from a more efficient implementation using specialized GPU algorithms. We offer this paper as a submission to the journal Numerical Mathematics. We have chosen this journal due to its strong focus on numerical mathematics and the journal's policy of publishing articles that are suitable for a broad audience interested in numerical mathematics. We believe that the journal's readers will appreciate the simplicity and efficiency of our algorithm. We have kept the presentation of our algorithm straightforward and easy to follow from a methodological perspective. We have selected this perspective due to numerical algorithms being inherently problem-specific and the underlying theory being secondary to the algorithm itself. We have used well-known notation for our algorithm to make it easily accessible to experts in the field. We have thoroughly reviewed the existing literature on this topic before developing our algorithm.
